0.title: Christ Is All: Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
0.overview:
No letter of Paul’s is more concentrated on who Christ is than Colossians. Its central argument can be stated in five words: Christ is all you need. The church at Colossae was being seduced by a sophisticated religious system: a blend of Jewish rule-keeping, the honouring of angels, harsh treatment of the body, and a philosophy of secret knowledge. Scholars call it the “Colossian heresy.” The false teachers were not asking the Colossians to abandon Christ; they were proposing to add to him, as though Christ alone could not give them everything. Paul’s response is the great hymn to Christ in chapter 1 and the argument of chapter 2: in Christ “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him” (2:9–10). There is nothing to add. He is enough.

Paul wrote the letter from prison, most likely in Rome, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon (with Philippians, the “Prison Epistles”). The church at Colossae had apparently been founded not by Paul himself but by Epaphras (1:7), one of Paul’s co-workers, during Paul’s extended ministry in Ephesus (Acts 19). Paul had never visited the church personally (2:1), and yet he writes with the pastoral urgency of a father: he is “struggling” for them (2:1), pointing them to Christ, in whom are hidden “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (2:3), and warning them against the plausible-sounding deception that threatens to take them captive (2:8).

The letter has two halves. Chapters 1–2 teach who Christ is: he is supreme over all creation (1:15–20), he lives in his people as their hope of glory (1:27), and all God’s fullness is in him, so nothing need be added (2:9–15). Chapters 3–4 show how to live: if Christ is everything, if you have died and been raised with him, if your life is hidden with him in God, then certain things must be put to death and certain things must be put on. With Paul, teaching always comes before living: who you are before what you do.

The Christ hymn of Colossians 1:15–20 is one of the most majestic texts in the entire New Testament. In six verses it covers the entire scope of Christ’s lordship: he is the image of the invisible God; the firstborn over all creation; the one through whom, for whom, and in whom all things were created and hold together; the head of the body; the firstborn from the dead; the one in whom all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell; the one through whom God reconciled all things to himself, making peace by the blood of his cross. This is not merely fine religious poetry; it is the fullest statement of who Christ is in Paul’s letters, and everything else in the letter is built on it. If Christ is who the hymn says he is, then the Colossian heresy, and every attempt in every generation to add to Christ, is not merely unnecessary but absurd.

Did Paul write Colossians? Some scholars doubt it, pointing to vocabulary and style unlike his undisputed letters, to the soaring hymn of 1:15–20, and to its close relation to Ephesians. But the letter names Paul three times (1:1, 23; 4:18), closes with his own signature, and is tied by its list of names to Philemon, which almost no one doubts is his. Differences of style are well explained by the subject (a new error to answer) and by the help of Timothy, who is named with him (1:1). The church received it as Paul’s from the beginning, and the more likely conclusion is that he wrote it.

Colossians is the answer to every form of Christianity that adds to Christ. It speaks directly to the believer who feels that faith in Christ alone is not quite enough, and that extra spiritual experiences, extra practices or extra revelations are needed to come fully to God. The letter says: you have been filled in him. You are complete. The fullness you are seeking is already yours, in the one in whom all fullness dwells. Seek more of him, not something more beyond him.

1.title: The Supremacy of Christ: Hymn, Mystery, and Ministry
1.overview:
Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, about 100 miles east of Ephesus. Paul had never visited; the church was planted by Epaphras, a local man. Now, writing from prison, Paul hears that teachers are offering the Colossians something more: secret knowledge, angelic powers to be honoured, food laws and festivals, and harsh treatment of the body (2:8–23). His answer is not a better technique but a bigger Christ.

Chapter 1 moves from thanks and prayer, to the great hymn on Christ as Creator, sustainer and reconciler of all things (vv. 15–20), to its application: former enemies reconciled, and the mystery now revealed, Christ in you, the hope of glory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul greets a church he did not found, thanks God for the faith, love and hope the gospel has produced in them, and prays that they will know God’s will and live it, strengthened and thankful to the Father who has rescued them into the kingdom of his Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Knowledge of God’s Will: Wisdom, Not Secrets

Paul’s prayer for knowledge of God’s will (v. 9) counters the false teachers’ offer of special knowledge. The knowledge he seeks is not mystical but practical: it is meant to be walked. True wisdom is the God-given capacity to live well in God’s world. The wisdom from above, as James says, is “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits” (James 3:17). It is visible in a life.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered a spiritual wisdom that was speculative and attainable only through special initiation. Now: Knowledge of God’s will is measured not by the height of its claims but by the life it produces: does it make you fruitful, enduring and thankful?

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace to you and peace from God our Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Colossians is Paul’s great letter on the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ. A teaching at Colossae was adding to Christ. Paul never names it and its exact shape is debated, but chapter 2 suggests it offered special insight, visions, the worship of angels, food laws and festivals. Paul answers not with a deeper secret but with a bigger Christ. Chapter 1 moves in four steps: thanks for the gospel bearing fruit (vv. 1–8); a prayer that they will know God’s will and thank the Father who rescued them (vv. 9–14); one of the Bible’s highest passages on Christ (vv. 15–20); and the application: once enemies, now reconciled, while Paul suffers to make known Christ in you, the hope of glory (vv. 21–29).

The setting. Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, east of Ephesus, near Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:13), overshadowed by its wealthier neighbours. Paul had never visited (2:1). Epaphras founded the church, probably during Paul’s three years in Ephesus, when all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord (Acts 19:10). Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon, sending the letter with Tychicus and Onesimus (4:7–9). Some scholars doubt Paul wrote it, but the names it shares with Philemon, accepted by almost all as his, and the early church’s witness give good reason to read it as his. So the greatest description of Christ’s lordship over the universe was written by a man in chains, to a small church in a fading town that he had never seen.

An apostle sent by the risen Christ. Paul writes to a church that does not know him personally, so he states his authority, and he roots it not in achievement but in calling. “By the will of God” says where his authority comes from: not from other people’s recognition or his own sense of calling, but from the risen Christ, who stopped him on the Damascus road while he was hunting Christians (Acts 9:5). An apostle is a sent man, and the sender is the point: the letter that will set Christ above every power in heaven begins by putting its own writer under him.

And Timothy our brother. Timothy was with Paul in prison, and he is named as co-sender, though Paul is the writer (see the “I” of 1:23–25). And Paul’s word for him is not assistant but brother: family before team.

Saints and faithful brothers. Saints are holy ones, set apart for God; faithful brothers are believing and trustworthy. They are holy by God’s action, and faithful in their own continuing trust. Paul gives them two addresses. In Christ: their true location, the place where their life is hidden (3:3). At Colossae: their earthly address, a small town with its markets, its temples and its ordinary pressures. Every believer has both, and the whole letter is about living at the second address as someone who belongs to the first. In Christ means being joined to him by faith, so that what is true of him is counted true of you: his death counts as your death to sin’s penalty, and his risen life becomes your life (Romans 6:4–5; Colossians 2:12).

Grace and peace. Grace (charis) takes the ordinary Greek hello, chairein, and fills it with the gospel: God’s free, undeserved favour. Peace is the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, everything set right with God. Grace is the source; peace is the fruit. The God who could have written to the Colossians as a judge writes to them as a Father. Before a word of correction, before a line of argument, he pronounces grace and peace over a little church in a declining town, and calls them holy. (Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add and the Lord Jesus Christ; the earliest do not.)

What it does not mean. Saint is not a level reached by a few but what God has done for all believers in setting them apart.

Why is Paul so formal with people he loves? Because he has to be. A rival teaching was claiming a higher authority than the gospel the Colossians first received, and a church that does not know Paul’s face needs to know that this letter is not one man’s view. Apostolic letters were read aloud in church as the word of the Lord (4:16), and they still are. When you open Colossians, you are not reading a pious friend’s advice. You are receiving what Christ’s appointed envoy was given to say.
verseByVerse.note: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, about 100 miles east of Ephesus, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had never visited; the church was founded by Epaphras. Paul wrote from prison, at the same time as Ephesians and Philemon.

verseByVerse.quote: We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We always thank God. Paul thanks God for a church he has never seen, not for success but for the faith, love and hope the gospel produced, because every evidence of grace is God’s doing. Thanksgiving runs through the whole letter (1:12; 2:7; 3:15–17; 4:2). A church that has forgotten how to give thanks is already open to the teachers who say it does not yet have enough.

The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. The full title identifies which God Paul addresses: not one deity among many in the crowded religious marketplace of Asia Minor, but the God who has revealed himself in Jesus Christ. It also names the basis on which we approach him: the God who is Father of the Lord Jesus is, by adoption, Father of all who are in the Lord Jesus (John 14:6; 20:17).

When we pray for you. Paul prayed regularly for people whose faces he had never seen, and his praying was not vague goodwill; it had names and places in it.

Should I thank God for Christians I find difficult? Yes, and Paul shows how. You do not have to approve of everything they do, or pretend their faults are not there. You thank God for what he has truly given them: their faith in Christ, the love they do show, the hope they hold. That is not flattery, because the gifts are real and the credit goes to God. And it changes you. It is very hard to keep resenting someone you have honestly thanked God for that morning.

verseByVerse.quote: since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your faith in Christ Jesus. Faith and love are the two great marks Paul looks for in a congregation. Faith looks upward: it is the soul resting its weight on Christ. Its value lies in its object: faith is not strong because the believer is strong but because Christ is; weak faith in a strong Saviour is safe, because it is the Saviour who saves.

Love for all the saints. Love looks outward to other people. It is the evidence that the faith is real, and it is for all of them: not only the believers who are like us, or easy to be with. The two are inseparable in Paul: faith working through love (Galatians 5:6). Faith that produces no love is not the genuine article (1 John 4:20), and we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

Does loving all the saints mean I have to like them all? No. Love in the New Testament is not first a feeling of warmth but a settled commitment to another person’s good. You may never find a particular believer easy company, and that is not a sin. But you can pray for him, speak well of him, help him when he is in need, forgive him when he wrongs you, and refuse to join in when others run him down. That is love, and over time God often adds the warmth to the obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hope laid up for you. Biblical hope is not the modern wish, as in “I hope it does not rain”, but confident expectation grounded in God’s promise: certain, though not yet received. “Laid up” is the language of a secured deposit, kept where nothing can spoil or steal it (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 1:4). No thief breaks in there, no market crashes there, no diagnosis reaches there.

Hope is the fuel. Paul says faith and love spring from the hope, which seems backwards. He is describing what keeps faith and love going day by day (1 Corinthians 13:13). A believer who has lost sight of what is coming finds faith shrinking and love growing cold. Those sure of heaven can afford to love sacrificially on earth.

A hope with a face. What is laid up in heaven is finally not a thing but a Person. Paul will soon call Christ in you the hope of glory (1:27), and tell the Colossians that their life is hidden with Christ in God (3:3). It is kept in heaven because Christ is there, and it is as safe as he is. And it will not be posted to us from a distance. It arrives when he does.

The word of the truth. Against a teaching that paraded itself as a higher wisdom, Paul offers no competing philosophy. The gospel is the word of the truth, not one opinion among many, because it corresponds to what God has actually done in Christ. And “gospel” (euangelion) was the word for an emperor’s public announcement of good news. This one announces that a King has won the decisive victory (Isaiah 52:7).

Is heaven a place I go to, or something that comes here? Both, in their order. When a believer dies, he goes to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). But the final hope is larger: Christ will return, the dead will be raised, and God will make a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–4). What is laid up in heaven now is kept there for us, and will be revealed when Christ appears (3:4). You are not hoping to float away from creation for ever, but to live in it renewed, with God.

In everyday life. When love feels too costly, look up before you look in. Ask what you are actually hoping for, and whether it is big enough to pay for what Christ is asking of you today. A forgiven grudge, a hard kindness, a long patience: none of them can bankrupt someone whose inheritance is kept in heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing—as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which has come to you. They did not go looking for the gospel in some distant shrine; it came to them, carried by a man from their own town.

Bearing fruit and increasing. The gospel is a living plant: not an idea humans spread by their own energy but God’s word, carrying the power to produce what it announces. The farmer only sows; the seed has life in itself (Mark 4:26–29). So we carry the gospel, and it does the work (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). And the whole world means that this is not a local cult or secret teaching but a message for all nations. The word that came to a small town in the Lycus Valley is the same word that is still running across the earth, alive with the life of the God who spoke it, and it has never yet returned to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

Understood the grace of God. “Understood” is a strong word: coming to know fully. To understand grace is to understand that you brought nothing, deserved nothing, and received everything. Those who have simply received the gospel are missing nothing (Galatians 1:6–9).

What does “in truth” add? The Greek en alētheia carries two ideas, and Paul probably means both. First, truly: their understanding was real, not a passing interest or a surface agreement, and it showed in the fruit growing in their lives since that day. Second, as it really is: they understood God’s grace accurately, in its true form, not a distorted version of it. Paul has just called the gospel the word of the truth (v. 5), and he adds that they learned it from Epaphras, a faithful minister of Christ (v. 7). That matters because false teachers were now offering the Colossians plausible arguments, philosophy and empty deceit (2:4, 8), and rules about food, festivals and self-denial (2:16–23).

Why it matters. Grace can be misunderstood in two opposite ways. Some turn it into permission to sin: if God forgives, why not carry on? (Romans 6:1; Jude 4). Others add something to it, so that Christ is not quite enough without extra rules, rituals or experiences: the very danger in Colossae (2:20–23; Galatians 5:4). Grace in truth is entirely free, and it changes those who receive it. The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).

Grace with a name. Grace is not a general mood of kindness in heaven; it has a name. John says that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17), and Paul that the rich Son became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). That is why grace cannot be topped up with rules or experiences. It is not a quantity God measures out but the gift of his Son, and the Son is not given in part.

How can I tell whether I have understood grace in truth? Look at both halves. Do you rest your hope before God on Christ alone, with nothing of your own added: not your church attendance, your good record, your feelings, your spiritual experiences? And is that grace changing you, so that you hate the sins you once excused and want to please the God who forgave you? If you find yourself thinking that God accepts you because you are doing well, grace has been distorted one way. If you find yourself thinking it does not matter how you live because you are forgiven, it has been distorted the other. Grace in truth gives you peace and makes you new.

In everyday life. When you share the gospel, remember whose seed it is: your task is to sow it faithfully and clearly, not to make it grow. That frees you to speak without pressure and to wait without despair.

verseByVerse.quote: just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphras. A native of Colossae (4:12), he probably heard the gospel from Paul in Ephesus and took it home to the Lycus Valley. Paul endorses his teaching: the Colossians did not receive a beginner’s version that now needs upgrading. They received the real thing from a faithful man.

Our beloved fellow servant. “Fellow servant” is literally fellow slave (syndoulos): someone whose whole existence is defined by belonging to a master. Paul regularly calls himself a slave of Christ (Romans 1:1), and here he names Epaphras his equal in that service. And “beloved” shows that Paul praises him out of real affection, not as a tactic.

A faithful minister. “Minister” (diakonos) is the word for a table servant, one who waits at another’s direction. The Christian leader is a servant who brings what his Master gives him, not a message of his own (Mark 10:44–45). Some manuscripts read on our behalf (ESV note): Epaphras then represented Paul among them. Either way, his faithfulness is the point. Christ the Lord took the form of a servant and came among us as one who serves (Philippians 2:7; Luke 22:27). Every faithful Epaphras is only following his Master to the table.

Why a minister of Christ, and not of the Father? There is a pattern in Paul. When he speaks of the source of salvation and the ultimate purpose of all things, he tends to name the Father (as in v. 3). When he speaks of the content and commission of the ministry, what is preached and served, he names Christ. Epaphras is a minister of Christ because it is Christ who commissioned him, Christ whose death and resurrection is the substance of the message, and Christ who sends those who go in his name, with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18–20). The Father, when speaking of source and purpose; Christ, when speaking of the mission.

What if the person who brought me the gospel later failed badly? It happens, and it is painful. But the gospel you received does not stand or fall with the messenger. What saved you was Christ, not the person who told you of him. Paul says he could rejoice that Christ was preached even when the preachers had poor motives (Philippians 1:15–18). Grieve the failure, pray for them, and if they wronged you, take it seriously. But hold on to what was true in what they gave you: the Christ you trusted is unchanged.

In everyday life. Thank God for the person who first brought you the gospel, and if you can, write and thank them. Faithful servants are rarely told what their faithfulness did.
verseByVerse.note: Epaphras was a native of Colossae who probably heard the gospel during Paul’s long stay in Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: and has made known to us your love in the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love in the Spirit. Love whose source and energy is the Holy Spirit himself. God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5:5), and Paul goes straight on to say what that love looks like: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). Love is the first fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22). This is the only explicit mention of the Spirit in Colossians, which focuses on Christ, and that is fitting, because the Spirit’s work is to make Christ known.

Two kinds of love. Natural love is real and good, but it prefers the lovable and dries up when not returned. Love in the Spirit can love the difficult and the enemy, because it draws not on human reserves but on God’s love.

The surest evidence. Anyone can adopt new religious beliefs; not everyone comes to love people they would not naturally love. When Epaphras reported the Colossians’ love, Paul heard: the Spirit is at work here (1 John 4:7).

May we pray to the Holy Spirit? The normal pattern of Christian prayer in the New Testament is to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit: through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18; Matthew 6:9; John 16:23). No prayer in the New Testament is addressed directly to the Spirit, and many Reformed Christians therefore keep to that pattern, as this commentary does. But it is not wrong to address the Spirit. He is fully God: lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God (Acts 5:3–4). We are baptised into the one name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). The Westminster Confession says that worship is to be given to God, the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and to him alone (21.2; 1689 22.2), and the Nicene Creed confesses the Spirit, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified. That is why the church has long sung prayers to the Spirit, such as Come, Holy Ghost, our souls inspire, and Breathe on me, breath of God. So: pray ordinarily to the Father, in the Spirit’s strength; and if you sometimes say, Holy Spirit, fill me with love, you are speaking to God.

What if I do not feel much love for other believers? Then ask for it, because that is exactly what the Spirit gives. Love in the Spirit is not something you manufacture by trying to feel warmer. Begin where you are: confess the coldness honestly, ask your Father to pour his love into your heart by the Spirit (Luke 11:13), and then act in love toward someone specific, even before you feel it. The feelings often follow the obedience. And look again at the cross. The Spirit’s way of producing love is to show us how much we have been loved (1 John 4:10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have not ceased to pray. Paul prays rather than merely explains, because accurate teaching alone does not change a life. God must bring the truth home to the heart (1 Corinthians 2:14). That is why the most faithful teachers are the most persistent in prayer, as Epaphras was, always struggling on their behalf in his prayers (4:12).

In the flow. Verses 9–14 are one long Greek sentence that climbs from knowing God’s will to thanks for the Father’s rescue, and that rescue brings Paul to the Son (vv. 15–20). So the prayer is not a detour before the doctrine. It is the road into it.

Filled with the knowledge of his will. The false teachers seem to have promised special knowledge. Paul prays for full knowledge of God’s will, a practical grasp of what God wants. And filled matters. The false teachers implied that the Colossians were half empty and needed topping up from their secrets. Paul prays that they will be filled from the source they already have, Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (2:3).

Spiritual wisdom and understanding. The two are near partners. Spiritual means given by the Spirit, not human cleverness, which was precisely the counterfeit the false teachers were selling.

Which word means applying God’s word? In the Bible, it is chiefly wisdom. The Old Testament word behind it (ḥokmah) means skill: it is used of craftsmen (Exodus 31:3–6), and in Proverbs it is the skill of living well in God’s world, choosing the right thing in a real situation. James says the same: who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works (James 3:13). Understanding is closer to insight: seeing what a situation really is, discerning, grasping how truths fit together (Proverbs 2:2–6; 1 Kings 3:9–12). So roughly: understanding sees, and wisdom does. Some interpreters, notably J. B. Lightfoot, described understanding as the critical faculty that grasps the bearings of things, how a truth bears on a particular case, which is why it is sometimes explained as applying truth; but the words overlap heavily, and in Scripture it is wisdom that is most clearly the skill of living. The pair comes from Isaiah’s promise that the Spirit of wisdom and understanding would rest on the Messiah (Isaiah 11:2). What Christ has fully, his people receive from his Spirit. And the purpose follows at once: so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord (v. 10). Knowledge of God’s will is meant to be lived.

Does this mean God will show me which job to take or whom to marry? Paul means God’s revealed will: the wisdom and understanding to live a life worthy of the Lord (v. 10). Within that will, God gives his people freedom to make wise choices, praying, seeking counsel and weighing what is good. He guides by his word and his providence, not usually by special messages about particular decisions. So if two jobs are both honest and both open to you, you are not missing a secret answer. Ask which would let you serve God and love others best, take advice from mature believers, decide, and trust him with the result. Scripture does settle some questions for you: a believer is to marry only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39).

In everyday life. Pray this prayer by name for someone else today, as Paul prayed it for people he had never met: Lord, fill them with the knowledge of your will.

verseByVerse.quote: so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
A manner worthy of the Lord. Knowledge of God’s will is never meant to stay in the head; walk in the Bible means the whole of daily life. “Worthy” first meant of equal weight, what balances the scales: a worthy life is one that fits the one it belongs to (Philippians 1:27; Ephesians 4:1).

The order of the walk. The order matters: we please God because he loves us, not so that he will. It is a loved child’s response (1 John 4:19). And Paul prays for knowledge and wisdom so that they may walk worthily. This is why prayer is not an extra added to the Christian life but what drives it.

What does a worthy walk look like? Paul does not leave us to guess. He defines it in the same sentence, with four marks: bearing fruit in every good work, increasing in the knowledge of God (v. 10), being strengthened for endurance and patience with joy (v. 11), and giving thanks to the Father (v. 12). Fruitful, growing, enduring with joy, thankful. Later he fills it in: compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forgiving one another, and above all love (3:12–14), lived out in marriage, in the family and at work (3:18–4:1). And the measure is the Lord himself: not any lord, but the one Paul is about to describe, the image of the invisible God, the one through whom all things were made, who made peace by the blood of his cross (vv. 15–20). He is gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). A life that fits him will look like him.

Fully pleasing to him. The aim of life is to please Christ (2 Corinthians 5:9). The Lord who needs nothing from us (Acts 17:25) takes pleasure in the obedience of his children, as a father delights in a child who loves him. Our small, ordinary acts of faithfulness can please him (Hebrews 13:16).

Bearing fruit. The same word is used of the gospel (v. 6), because the fruit in the believer is the gospel’s own fruit, the works God prepared beforehand for us to walk in (Ephesians 2:10). And every good work means the whole texture of daily life: the honest word when a lie would be easier, the kindness to the person nobody notices.

Increasing in the knowledge of God. Not accumulating information but deepening a relationship, in which knowing and living feed each other. Knowing God better produces a worthy life: you do not struggle as much to forgive once you have reckoned with how much you have been forgiven. And living worthily deepens the knowledge: if anyone wills to do God’s will, Jesus said, he will know whether the teaching is from God (John 7:17). The growth has no ceiling (2 Peter 3:18): you learn that he keeps his promises, and then you find him keeping them in a hospital corridor (Psalm 34:8).

What it does not mean. Not earning God’s approval: we are already accepted in Christ (1:22), and please him as children, not as servants anxious for wages.

Not a list of human rules or a Christian look. A worthy walk is not measured by a dress code, foods or special days: that is exactly the religion Paul rejects in this letter (2:16–23).

Not mere respectability. The Lord himself was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 11:19). A life that fits him will sometimes look out of place to polite society, and even to religious people.

Not perfection, and not only the spectacular. The worthy walk is growing, not finished, and it includes failing, confessing and getting up again (1 John 1:9). Enduring a long illness with patience and joy is as worthy of the Lord as any public ministry. And it is not in our own strength: Paul prays for this walk, because it is God’s work in us (v. 11).

Can someone as ordinary and inconsistent as me really please God? Yes, and Scripture says so plainly (2 Corinthians 5:9; Hebrews 13:16). You please him not because your obedience is flawless but because you are in his Son, so that your imperfect works are received through Christ, as a father treasures the crooked drawing his child brings him. The Westminster Confession says that believers’ good works, though imperfect, are accepted in Christ, God looking upon them in his Son (Westminster 16.6; 1689 16.6). So the smallest honest act done for his sake gives him pleasure. That is not a reason for pride. It is a reason to begin.

verseByVerse.quote: being strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being strengthened. The Greek verb means that the strength is given to them, and keeps being given: an ongoing supply from outside. Paul does not pray that they try harder, but that they be strengthened.

According to his glorious might. The measure is God’s own might, the same power that raised Christ from the dead (Ephesians 1:19–20), now at work in believers through his Spirit in the inner being (Ephesians 3:16). The one who thinks he needs only a little of God’s help has not understood how much genuine love, sustained faithfulness and real forgiveness actually cost.

Endurance and patience. God’s mighty power is given not for spectacular feats but for the two graces that keep a believer going. Endurance holds up under circumstances; patience is with people: the long-suffering that does not retaliate but waits for God to act. It takes nothing less than that resurrection might to keep a tired believer gentle with a difficult neighbour for twenty years. The might that flung out the galaxies and raised Christ from the tomb is put to work in the quiet places of a believer’s life: a hospital bed, a hard marriage, a long wait. God is not too great to bother with our endurance. He counts it worth his glorious power.

With joy. Not grim endurance, and not forced cheerfulness, but the deep gladness of one who knows the inheritance is secure, so that no present suffering is the final word (James 1:2–4; Romans 5:3–5).

Endurance first seen in the Lord. Both graces were Christ’s before they were ours. He endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). And Paul says that in his own conversion Christ Jesus displayed his perfect patience (1 Timothy 1:16), bearing long with the man who was hunting his church. So endurance with joy is the shape of the Saviour’s own life, and the power that strengthens us is his risen life at work in us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God removes trials, and joy does not mean pretending: the psalms of lament are in the Bible, and Jesus wept. Joy can sit alongside tears, because it rests on something deeper than the day.

How can I have joy when I am suffering? Not by denying the pain, but by looking past it to what it cannot touch. Your sins are forgiven (v. 14), your inheritance is kept in light (v. 12), you have been moved into the kingdom of the Son the Father loves (v. 13), and the Lord who holds all things together is holding you (v. 17). Joy in suffering is often quiet, more like a steady floor under your feet than a feeling of happiness. If you cannot find it today, ask God for it, because Paul is praying here for exactly that, and it is a gift, not an achievement.

In everyday life. Name the trial you are enduring and the person who most tries your patience. Ask God for his glorious power, not to escape your trial, but to endure it with joy, and not to change that person first, but to make you patient with them.

verseByVerse.quote: giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Giving thanks to the Father. The fourth mark of the worthy walk: a heart that has understood it has received everything as a gift.

Who has qualified you. “Qualified” means made fit, and the choice is pointed. The false teachers suggested the believers were not yet fully qualified: that they needed additional experiences, angelic mediators, or ascetic practices to be complete (2:18, 23). Paul cuts it off at the root: the Father has already qualified you, fully, not provisionally. This is the pastoral heart of the letter, a word for the anxious achiever as much as the rebel. Many church people quietly live as though they must still earn their place, by doing enough or feeling spiritual enough. The Father’s verdict ends that labour. He did not wait for us to become fit for his presence. He made us fit, at the cost of his Son.

The inheritance of the saints in light. Paul draws on the Old Testament language of the promised land, the inheritance God gave Israel as his gift, where the LORD himself was the portion of his people (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 32:9). In Christ it becomes the new creation, the resurrection body, the face of God seen unveiled (1 Corinthians 2:9). It comes as an inheritance comes to a child: as a gift, not as wages. And it is in light because it is in the full presence of God, with nothing in between, who is light (1 John 1:5; Revelation 21:23). It sets up the contrast with the darkness of v. 13.

Heirs because of the Heir. Why should strangers inherit anything from God? Because the Father has appointed his Son heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and everyone joined to the Son shares his portion: heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). Canaan was divided by lot among the tribes; this inheritance is not divided at all, because each of the saints receives it whole, in him.

What if I feel unworthy to stand before God? You are right that you are unworthy in yourself, and so is every believer. But the question is not whether you are worthy but whether God has qualified you, and if you trust Christ, he has. Your fitness for heaven does not rest on your feelings, your progress or your record this week. It rests on what the Father has done in his Son. Feeling unworthy can be a healthy humility, but it must not become a doubt about God’s verdict. Bring the feeling to the cross and leave it there.

verseByVerse.quote: He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Delivered. A rescue word, used of God snatching his people from Egypt. No one is delivered who found his own way out. Paul’s whole diagnosis is that without Christ we were dead, captive, bound: not struggling toward the light but at home in the dark (Ephesians 2:1–5).

The domain of darkness. “Domain” is a word for rule and authority: not merely a moral condition but an organised realm with a ruler, under the one Jesus called the ruler of this world (John 12:31) and Paul the god of this age (2 Corinthians 4:4). It blinds minds while presenting itself as normal. The person living in it does not feel trapped. He cannot see that he cannot see, which is why rescue requires a power from outside.

Transferred. The word was used of deporting whole populations. God moved us from one kingdom to another, and it is a completed action. The kingdom is not only future; everyone in him by faith has already entered it, a citizen of a different kingdom even while your feet still stand on the old earth (Philippians 3:20). To be transferred means that the voice with the last say over your life is no longer sin, fear or the crowd, but Christ, and that his protection, his laws and his future are now yours (Romans 6:17–18).

The Son of his love. And it is the kingdom of his beloved Son, literally the Son of his love, echoing the Father’s voice at the baptism: this is my beloved Son (Matthew 3:17). You have been brought inside the Father’s own love for the Son. The Father’s delight in him is the atmosphere of the kingdom, and you are secure there, because nothing can remove the Father’s love for Christ, and you are in Christ (John 17:23).

In the flow. His beloved Son introduces the one who fills everything until v. 21: you cannot understand the kingdom until you see whose kingdom it is.

If I have been rescued, why do I still struggle with sin and temptation? Because the transfer is complete but the war is not over. You have changed kingdoms, but you still live in enemy-occupied territory, with old habits that still pull and an enemy who still tempts. The difference is that sin is now a rebel in your life, not your rightful ruler (Romans 6:12–14). Every struggle against it is the struggle of a free citizen of Christ’s kingdom, not the hopeless effort of a captive. Fight it, confess it, and remember whose kingdom you belong to.

In everyday life. When a temptation comes dressed as normal life, call it by its name: that is the old country. You do not live there any more. And when you pray for a friend who does not believe, pray as Paul would: not merely that they will improve, but that God will rescue them, because that is what it takes.

verseByVerse.quote: in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Redemption. The word comes from ransom: captives freed when someone paid the price. We could not pay our own way out. Christ paid, and the price was his blood (Ephesians 1:7; 1 Peter 1:18–19). The debt was not overlooked but met in full, and Paul says we have this redemption now. Some later manuscripts add through his blood, borrowed from Ephesians 1:7; the earliest manuscripts do not have it here, but the truth is the same, as v. 20 will say.

The forgiveness of sins. Forgiveness means release, the dropping of a charge. It does not pretend the offences did not happen; it declares the charge answered and the record cleared, legally, finally, completely. Our debts are cancelled, the record nailed to the cross (2:13–14). And the One who cancelled the charge sheet is the Judge himself.

One event, two angles. Redemption answers the question, how did we get free? A price was paid. Forgiveness answers the question, what is our standing now? The debt is gone, the record clear (Romans 3:24–25). And the two words “in whom” matter. Redemption is not a commodity Christ hands over and leaves us to manage. It is found in him, and we have it because we have him.

Does God forgive sins I commit after I become a Christian? Yes. The forgiveness Christ won covers your whole life, because he paid for all your sins on the cross, when every one of them was still future. That does not make sin small; it cost his blood. When you sin as a believer, you are not cast out of the family, but you do grieve your Father, and you should confess it to him honestly. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9). Confession does not buy the forgiveness again; it brings you back into the enjoyment of it.

In everyday life. When an old sin comes back to accuse you, do not argue with your feelings; answer with the fact: in Christ I have redemption, the forgiveness of sins. And because you are forgiven so much, forgive the person who has wronged you a little (3:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In what may be an early Christian hymn, Paul sets out who Christ is: over the first creation as its maker and sustainer, and over the new creation as head of the church and firstborn from the dead, the one in whom all God’s fullness dwells and through whom God made peace by the blood of his cross.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ as Creator and Redeemer

The hymn holds Christ’s work in creation and redemption together: the one through whom all things were made is the one through whose blood all things are reconciled. So redemption is not rescue from a material world God has abandoned but the renewal of his creation. Abraham Kuyper’s famous claim, “there is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is Sovereign over all, does not cry: ‘Mine!’”, rests on passages like this one.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian error apparently involved a hierarchy of spiritual powers through whom one had to navigate to reach God. The hymn removes it: all these powers were created by Christ and are subject to him. Now: Whatever sets other mediators between the believer and God, whether saints, angels or spiritual powers, repeats the Colossian mistake. To see God, look at Christ. To reach God, come through Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The turn to Christ. Now, without warning, Paul speaks only of Christ until v. 20. This is his whole strategy against the error threatening the church: he answers false teaching not by matching its secrets but by showing the church more of Christ.

The Christ hymn. Verses 15–20 are often thought to be an early Christian hymn, in two stanzas: Christ and creation (vv. 15–17), Christ and the new creation (vv. 18–20). Whether Paul wrote it or quoted it, it is aimed at a teaching that made Christ one spiritual power among many. The stanzas mirror each other: firstborn of all creation (v. 15), firstborn from the dead (v. 18); all things created through him (v. 16), all things reconciled through him (v. 20). The one who made the world is the one who remakes it.

The image of the invisible God. The word is eikōn: not a mere copy, but the exact, living representation of the original. No one has ever seen God (John 1:18), and yet he has made himself visible, not in a symbol but in a Person: whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9; Hebrews 1:3). The God no one has ever seen has stepped into view in his Son, with a human face and nail-scarred hands.

Three echoes. An eikōn was the emperor’s head stamped on a coin, carrying the sovereign’s own authority (Mark 12:16). Humanity was made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27): Christ is the true image Adam failed to be, in whom the broken likeness is restored (3:10). And Jewish wisdom writing had called Wisdom an image of God’s goodness (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26). Paul lands all of it on one man: Jesus of Nazareth.

Firstborn of all creation. “Firstborn” speaks of rank, as the heir held first place in the family: not first created, but heir and ruler over all creation. God made David his firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth (Psalm 89:27), though David was the youngest son of Jesse. He is not the eldest member of creation’s family; he is the heir of the whole estate.

Where Christians differ: is Christ a created being? Ancient Arians (a fourth-century movement that denied Christ’s full deity) and modern Jehovah’s Witnesses take firstborn to mean that Christ was the first being God created, through whom he made everything else. This commentary’s view: Verse 16 gives the reason he is firstborn: “for by him all things were created.” If he created all things, he is not one of them. Firstborn here means supreme heir, not first created; Greek had a word for first created (prōtoktistos), and Paul did not use it. And verse 19 says all the fullness of God dwells in him. Christ is the eternal Son, uncreated, fully God, of one substance with the Father (John 1:1–3; Nicene Creed).

How do I answer a Jehovah’s Witness at my door about this verse? Gently, and from the passage itself. Ask them to read on to verse 16, and ask how someone who made all things can himself be one of the things made. Point out that the Bible calls David the firstborn although he was the youngest, so firstborn can mean first in rank. Then show them verse 19 and 2:9, where all the fullness of deity dwells in Christ. Their own translation adds the word other (all other things), which is not in the Greek; you can ask them why. Above all, be kind. You are not winning an argument but pointing a person to the Christ who made them.

If God is invisible, how can I know him? By looking at Jesus: read the Gospels and watch him touching lepers, weeping at a grave, forgiving the men who crucified him. That is what God is like. (See 1 Timothy 1:17 for the fuller answer.)
verseByVerse.note: “Firstborn” speaks of rank and supremacy, as the heir held first place, not that the Son was created.

parallels.desc: I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth

verseByVerse.quote: For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities — all things were created through him and for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By him all things were created. Literally in him: creation took place in the Son, with him as its centre and source (John 1:3; Hebrews 1:2). Creation is the work of the whole Trinity (1 Corinthians 8:6; Genesis 1:2), but Christ is in the spotlight because the false teachers were crowding him in among the spiritual powers (2:18). Paul plants him on the Creator’s side of the line: the One they would reduce to a creature made every creature.

Visible and invisible. The scope is exhaustive, to shut every door, and the unseen realm is where the Colossian error located its powers.

Thrones or dominions. These are unseen spiritual powers, angels good and evil, which the false teachers honoured or feared (2:15, 18). The four terms were probably used of angelic ranks. Paul is not teaching angelic grades; he borrows the impressive vocabulary and sweeps it all into one sentence: every rank, created by Christ.

You do not tremble before what your Lord made. The Colossians were taught that these powers controlled the road to God and had to be appeased, and Paul pulls the ground from under that fear with one fact: Christ made them. And even the fallen, hostile powers Christ disarmed at the cross (2:15) owe their existence to him: not an independent dark kingdom in even combat, but defeated creatures whose Maker is their Master.

Through him and for him. Through him: he is the agent of creation. For him: he is its goal, the one toward whom it all moves, made to find its meaning and end in Christ. In Romans 11:36 and 1 Corinthians 8:6 it is God the Father from whom and for whom all things exist; here Paul says it of Christ. Only God can be the purpose of creation, so this is a quiet but unmistakable claim to his full deity.

What it means to be made for Christ. If all things were created for him, so were you. He is not only where you came from, but what you are for. Man’s chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him for ever (Shorter Catechism Q. 1), and Colossians adds that this God is known in Christ. Four things follow.

Your life has a purpose that does not depend on success. You are not for Christ only when you are useful, healthy or impressive. A bedridden grandmother who trusts him, or a child with severe disabilities, is as truly made for him as a missionary or a preacher.

You belong to someone. You are not your own; you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

Nothing else will finally satisfy. Career, money or pleasure, good as they are, leave us restless when made the point of life. Augustine prayed: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you (Confessions 1.1).

Ordinary things are for him too. Work, food, marriage, music, a garden: everything created by God is good (1 Timothy 4:4), to be lived for him.

What living for him looks like. Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks (3:17). Work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men (3:23). He applies it to marriage, children and work (3:18–4:1). You do your job well because he is the one you serve; you speak as you would be glad for him to hear; you decide by asking what pleases him (2 Corinthians 5:9). And when you fail, you come back to him, because he has already forgiven you (1:13–14).

What it does not mean. Not that you must become a pastor or be doing something religious every minute. Not that God needs you: he is not served by human hands as though he needed anything (Acts 17:25). He made you for his glory and for your joy, and those two are not rivals. And not that your standing with him depends on how well you manage it: you are reconciled and presented holy in his sight through Christ’s death (1:22). Living for him is the response to that, not the price of it.

Like a key in its lock. A key made for one lock turns smoothly in the right door and jams in the wrong one. The van you drive, the shelves you stack, the bill you pay honestly, the patience you keep with a difficult workmate: done consciously for Christ, the key slides into its lock, and the most ordinary Monday becomes the thing you were made for.

Should I be afraid of evil spirits? No, not if you belong to Christ. Scripture takes them seriously: they are real, they deceive, and believers are to resist the devil and put on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7). But they are creatures, made by Christ, defeated at the cross (2:15), and unable to separate you from God’s love (Romans 8:38–39). You do not need charms, rituals, special formulas or anxious precautions. You need to stay close to Christ: pray, trust his word, refuse sin, and leave the powers to their Master. The safest place in the universe is in the hands of the One who made them.

Is it not vain for God to make all things for himself? Only if he were less than the best thing there is. When a person demands all praise, we call it vanity, because no person deserves it. But God is the one being who does, and he is the source of every joy we know. A God who pointed us to anything less than himself would be pointing us to something that cannot satisfy, and that would be unkind. And consider who the goal of creation is: the Son, who did not cling to his glory but laid it aside to rescue runaways (Philippians 2:6–8). His glory is not a tyrant’s vanity but a giver’s, and to live for it is to find the joy we were made for.
verseByVerse.note: Thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities are unseen spiritual powers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before all things. Before in time, and the present tense is startling: not he was before all things, but he is, the same kind of timeless present Jesus used when he said, before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58). And before in rank: to be before all things is to stand above them, first in authority and dignity. The false teachers were fitting Christ into the created order, but there is no rung of the ladder higher than Christ, because Christ is not on the ladder. He made it.

All things hold together. The word means to cohere, to be kept from flying apart, and its tense means has held together and goes on holding. Christ upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3). He is not a watchmaker who walked away. The atoms cohere, the planets keep their orbits, your next heartbeat comes, because Christ is actively holding it all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean scientific explanation is unimportant. The scientist who measures the laws of nature is measuring the faithfulness of the Son, whether he knows it or not.

If Christ holds everything together, why do things fall apart: illness, disasters, death? Because we live in a world that is held but also fallen. Christ sustains creation, but it has been subjected to futility because of sin, and it groans as it waits for its renewal (Romans 8:20–22). He does not prevent every breaking, but nothing breaks outside his hand, and he works even the breaking for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28). The same Christ who holds the stars was himself broken on a cross. He knows what falling apart feels like, and he is bringing all things to a day when nothing will be broken again.

In everyday life. On the day it feels as though everything is coming apart, say it to yourself: in him all things hold together, including this. Then do the next small thing in front of you, and leave the holding to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The head of the body. The second stanza: Christ and the new creation. Scholars debate whether head here means source, like the head of a river, or authority. In this letter Paul seems to hold both together: Christ is the source of the church’s life and its ruler (Ephesians 1:22–23; 4:15–16). The church is not merely like a body; it is Christ’s body.

Why the church comes in here. First, to bring the hymn home: the Lord of galaxies and angels is Head of the little flock at Colossae. Second, the false teachers were slipping angelic mediators between the believer and God, giving the church other heads to look to. Paul’s answer is that the church has one Head, and life and access to God flow from him alone. To go looking elsewhere is to let go of the Head (2:19).

The beginning. Origin, source, ruler. As he was firstborn over the old order (v. 15), so he is the beginning of the new order that dawned when he walked out of the tomb.

Firstborn from the dead. The first to rise to resurrection life, never to die again (1 Corinthians 15:20; Revelation 1:5). Lazarus and others were called back to the same mortal life only to die again (John 11:43–44); Christ passed through death into deathless life, the first human ever to do so. Firstborn, as an eldest brother is, the first of a great family who will follow him through the grave (Romans 8:29). Because the Head has risen, the body will rise too.

Preeminent. “Preeminent” means holding first place, and this purpose crowns the whole hymn: first in creation, first in new creation, over angels and over death. The Colossian error was a quiet demotion of Christ: high but not highest, sharing the platform with angels and rules. And it is God’s own settled purpose that his Son be first, with the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9–11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ needs the church to be complete. The church needs him. Nor does head mean that any human leader is head of the church. Pastors and elders are servants under the one Head, not substitutes for him.

What does it look like to give Christ first place? Think of a wedding ring. You may love a great many things, your work, your friends, your hobbies, all rightly enjoyed, but the ring says one person comes first, and everything else takes its place around her. A life is not put right by adding Christ to the list of things you love. It is put right when Christ is moved to the head of the list, and everything else, job, family, hobbies, not thrown away but reordered, learns to orbit him. In practice it shows in what you will not give up for anything else: time with him in his word and prayer, obedience when it costs, the worship of his people on the Lord’s Day. And it shows in how you decide: what does he want here?

verseByVerse.quote: For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the fullness of God. The Greek has no separate phrase of God; the ESV rightly supplies it, because Paul tells us one chapter on that in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (2:9). What dwells in Christ is nothing less than the entire divine nature, not a share.

In the flow. The For of verse 19 gives the reason for the verses on either side: Christ is first (v. 18) and can reconcile all things (v. 20) because the one who makes peace is God himself, not a go-between (see 2:9–10).

Fullness. Plērōma was perhaps a word the false teachers used for the totality of divine powers, spread out among angels and spirits. Later Gnostic teachers pictured it parcelled across a chain of intermediary beings, a ladder to climb. Paul turns the word: all the fullness, nothing left over, is in Christ alone. If the entire fullness of God is in Christ, the ladder of mediators is not merely unnecessary but an insult to the Son who holds it all.

To dwell. God dwelt in the tabernacle, and the Spirit dwells in believers by grace, but this is different altogether. The word means to take up permanent residence, not to lodge for a season and move on. God did not rest upon him as upon a prophet. The whole divine fullness took up residence in him, bodily: not a copy or an outflow of God, but God himself dwelling in the man Christ Jesus (John 1:14).

Was pleased. The language of free, delighted good pleasure, the same root as the Father’s voice at the baptism, with whom I am well pleased. Picture a vast firm whose owner you knew only through fragments passed down a chain of managers, until one Monday he walks onto the shop floor himself. God did not send fragments of himself down a chain of angels. He came himself, the whole of him, in a real man you could have stood beside (John 14:9; Hebrews 1:3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the fullness came to dwell in him at some point, as if he were not God before. Nor does it mean that Christ’s humanity was swallowed up by his deity: he is one person, truly God and truly man.

If I have Christ, do I need anything more? Nothing more of God, no. You do not need a second blessing to complete what Christ began, a secret teaching, a special experience, or a higher class of Christian. All the fullness is in him, and you are filled in him (2:10). You do need to grow: to know him better, to obey him more, to enjoy him more fully. But that growth is going deeper into Christ, not beyond him. Whatever claims to take you past Christ is taking you away from the only place God’s fullness is found.

verseByVerse.quote: and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To reconcile. To take two parties at war and bring them back to peace, turning enemies into friends; the Greek word is a strengthened form: to bring those who were estranged all the way home. Sin brought disorder and enmity into creation; through Christ, God restores harmony (2 Corinthians 5:18–19; Romans 5:10).

Through him. Through whom all things were created (v. 16), all things are reconciled. The hands that scattered the stars are the hands that were nailed to the beam. The Maker did not send the means; he became the means.

On earth or in heaven. Paul writes all things, not all people: the same sweeping phrase he used for the whole created order in vv. 16–17. The reach of the cross is as wide as the reach of creation. When Adam fell, the whole world was dragged down, subjected to futility and now groaning (Romans 8:20–22), so the rescue must be as large as the wreck: a renewed creation, the curse lifted, all things at peace.

The blood of his cross. The means is not special knowledge but Christ’s death, and peace is not a bare ceasefire but a relationship set right. There was real war: God’s holy wrath against sin, and our settled hostility. That wrath is no flash of irritation; it is the fixed resistance of a pure God to all that wrecks what he made, and a God without it would not be good (Habakkuk 1:13). God did not wave the conflict away. He satisfied his own justice and bore his own wrath in the body of his Son, so the peace is righteous, not cheap (Romans 3:25–26; 5:1). Blood is Scripture’s shorthand for a life laid down in sacrificial death (Leviticus 17:11). Paul lands the cosmic vision on a beam of wood outside a city wall: the reconciliation of the universe was achieved on one particular afternoon, by one particular death.

Where Christians differ: will all things, including all people and demons, be saved? Some read “reconcile all things” as universal salvation. This commentary’s view: Paul means that Christ restores all creation to its proper order under God. Believers are reconciled as friends (vv. 21–22); hostile powers are pacified by being disarmed and defeated (2:15), not saved. The same Paul teaches eternal judgment (2 Thessalonians 1:9). The whole universe will be brought back into peace with God, with evil judged and removed, and creation itself set free (Romans 8:19–21).

Two kinds of peace. Paul himself guards the point three verses on: this hope is yours if indeed you continue in the faith (v. 23). The restoration happens in two very different ways. For those who come to Christ, it is the reconciliation of glad children welcomed home. For the hostile powers, and for all who refuse him to the end, it is the peace of a conquered enemy, disarmed and put under his feet (2:15). One day every knee will bow, some in joy and some in defeat, but all in submission (Philippians 2:10–11).

What does the blood of the cross have to do with my peace with God? Everything. Your peace with God is not a mood you work up or a truce you negotiate by behaving well. It was made, once, outside Jerusalem, when Christ bore the penalty your sins deserved (1 Peter 2:24; 3:18). That is why it is solid: it rests on something finished. And that is why it is free: there is nothing to add by climbing angelic ladders or keeping man-made rules (2:13–15). When your conscience accuses you, do not look first at your feelings or your record. Look at the cross, where peace was made, and rest there.

Is it not primitive to say that peace was made by blood? Only if it means an angry god bribed with a victim, and the Bible means something else. Blood means a life given up in death, and here the life is God’s own, given in his Son. The Judge does not make someone else pay; he pays himself. The alternative is not a kinder God but one who shrugs at evil, at cruelty, betrayal and abuse, and calls it nothing. No one who has been badly wronged wants a God like that. At the cross God took evil with full seriousness, and took its cost on himself.

For worship. The cosmic Lord is the crucified Saviour, and his throne is shaped like a cross. The rebels did not sue for terms; the King paid the price of the treaty himself and signed it in his wounds. That peace is wide enough to hold the stars and near enough to hold a single forgiven sinner, and the day is coming when nothing in heaven or on earth will be at war with God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — Reconciled and the Mystery Revealed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns the hymn on his readers: once enemies, they are now reconciled through Christ’s death, if they continue in the faith. Then he describes his own costly service of the mystery now revealed, Christ in you, the hope of glory, which he proclaims to bring everyone to maturity in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ in You: Union with Christ

“Christ in you, the hope of glory” (v. 27) is the New Testament’s shortest statement of union with Christ, the believer’s being joined to him. The mystery hidden for ages is not only that Gentiles would be included in God’s people, but that Christ himself would live in them by his Spirit. Union with Christ is the root of every benefit of salvation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that they needed further experiences and secret knowledge to be complete or mature. Paul says the mystery that makes for maturity is already in them. Now: To the believer seeking a higher experience: the one in whom all fullness dwells is dwelling in you. What you are seeking is already yours; seek to know him more fully.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you. The camera turns from the glory of Christ to the readers. It is one thing to say Christ reconciled all things; it is another to hear that this includes you.

Once alienated. The word means estranged, shut out from a belonging that ought to be yours. Sin left us alienated from the life of God (Ephesians 4:18), without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12). Once: for the believer, a country left for good. But it is the present address of every soul not yet in Christ (Isaiah 59:2).

Hostile in mind. Underneath the estrangement lies enmity, in the very seat of thinking and willing: not neutral, but opposed. This does not mean every unbeliever consciously hates God; most never give him a thought. It means the natural mind will not have him on the throne. The mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot (Romans 8:7). The polite indifference of the respectable man and the open scorn of the scoffer are two faces of one enmity.

Doing evil deeds. The deeds are the symptom, not the disease: we are not alienated because we do wrong; we do wrong because we are alienated. And evil is measured by how a deed stands towards God: in this sense every deed, even a kind one, is evil when it is done with no thought of him. That is why even our righteous deeds can be like a polluted garment (Isaiah 64:6): not because kindness is worthless to a neighbour, but because it is offered by a heart still turned away.

But I was never a bad person. Paul is not saying the kind neighbour and the cruel criminal are equally wicked; many outside Christ are better company on a Monday than many a churchgoer. He measures people not against each other but against God: is a life turned toward its Maker or away? The respectable man and the criminal are not equally far down the road, but on the same side of the one line that finally matters.

The decent man on your old street. Think of the most decent man you knew growing up: paid every bill, lent out his ladder, and would have said cheerfully he was not religious, he just did no harm. Not raging against heaven, simply running his own little kingdom, his Maker nowhere in his thoughts.

The Son who was shut out for us. What we were, Christ took in our place. The Son who had lived in the Father’s love from eternity was numbered with the transgressors, and on the cross he cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34). He bore the estrangement our hostility had earned, so that those who were far off might be brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13). That is why this dark verse is not a portrait of despair. It is the measure of what he carried.

Why does Paul make me remember all this? Not to shame you, but to make you grateful. Paul paints the old life this dark for one reason: so that the grace of the next line blazes all the brighter (Ephesians 2:12–13; Titus 3:3–5). A believer who forgets what he was soon forgets what grace cost, and grows proud, cold or harsh toward those still outside. Remembering keeps you humble before God and gentle with unbelievers, because you know you were once exactly where they are, and only grace moved you.

verseByVerse.quote: he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has now reconciled. Once alienated, now reconciled, and the subject is he: God, in Christ. The offended party is the one who makes peace; we brought nothing to the table but the very hostility that needed reconciling. Not God meeting us halfway, but God crossing the whole distance to fetch his enemies home.

A finished peace. He has reconciled is a completed act: not a probation you must keep passing, but peace accomplished at the cross (John 19:30). You do not wake each morning to re-earn God’s welcome. You wake already reconciled, and live the day from a settled peace, not toward one you are still trying to win.

His body of flesh. Paul insists on the physical. The false teachers prized mystical experience and may have despised the body; Paul nails reconciliation to flesh and blood. The One in whom all the fullness dwells had to become flesh to die for flesh. Our peace did not cost God a word; it cost him a body (Hebrews 10:10).

Holy and blameless and above reproach. The goal is the last day. Present is the language of a bride led to her husband, an offering set before God. Holy: belonging wholly to God. Blameless: without blemish, the very word for a sacrificial lamb without defect. Above reproach: a courtroom word, unaccusable, a person against whom no charge can be made to stick. All of it before him, through Christ’s work, not their own (Ephesians 5:27). Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up, heard the seraphim cry holy, holy, holy, and cried out that he was lost (Isaiah 6:1–5). That this God should look at sinners and find nothing to charge them with is grace beyond telling, and it is true only because of the death Paul has just named.

But I never feel holy or blameless. How can this be me? Two truths set you free. First, this is your standing, not your feeling. It is not a description of how holy you have become but a verdict about how God sees you in Christ, whose own flawless record was credited to your account while your sin was counted his and paid for (2 Corinthians 5:21). Above reproach is the literal truth of your case in heaven’s court right now: the charge sheet torn up. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies; Christ Jesus is the one who died (Romans 8:33–34). Second, what God now counts you to be, you will one day be in full. Paul says to present you, and a day is coming when Christ will set his people blameless before the throne with great joy (Jude 24; Ephesians 5:27): the holiness counted yours now finished in you completely, the feeling at last catching up with the fact.

The gap and who closes it. Your sense of falling short is the gap between your standing, already perfect in Christ, and your experience, still being made holy. And the closing of that gap rests not on your grip on God but on his grip on you, for he does not begin a work he fails to finish (Philippians 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a minister.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If indeed you continue. That little if can land on a tender conscience like a cold draught. The condition is real. The faith means both their believing and the gospel believed. The people who will be presented holy are the people who keep believing to the end.

Stable and steadfast, not shifting. Building words: founded on a foundation, firmly seated, not budged. The false teachers were moving them off the simple gospel onto a deeper teaching dressed as progress. Stay put. The deepest thing in the universe is not beyond the gospel; it is the gospel.

Proclaimed in all creation. Not a claim that every person had heard, but the language of a public announcement open to the whole world. Why trade a place in a worldwide, God-driven gospel for a little local secret society?

I, Paul, became a minister. Servant, not master or self-styled expert: he did not invent the gospel; he serves it.

Where Christians differ: does this condition mean believers can lose salvation? Some read “if you continue” as showing that true believers may fall away and be lost, and many earnest Christians hold this out of a proper respect for the warnings. This commentary’s view: Perseverance is the evidence of genuine faith, and the warning is one of God’s means of producing it. Those who are truly reconciled will continue, because God keeps them (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; 1 Peter 1:5). Those who finally abandon the faith show they never truly had it (1 John 2:19). The condition is real and must be heard; it is how God keeps his people steadfast (the Westminster Confession, chapter 17; the 1689 London Baptist Confession, chapter 17).

Perseverance and preservation. The continuing is not a weight laid on your own grip for fifty years; it is itself God’s gift and work. Perseverance and preservation are two sides of one coin: the saints persevere because God preserves them.

The climber and the rope. A climber roped to a guide must keep climbing, but when his boot slips, the rope holds. So the if is not meant to torment you. It is a summons to keep going, and, for the one who keeps clinging to Christ through all his stumbles, the very proof that God is holding him.

Kept by the prayers of Christ. The deepest reason true believers continue lies not in them but in their Saviour. On the night before Peter’s denial, Jesus told him, I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:32), and Peter, though he fell, did not fall away. The same Lord always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). For every true believer, the if of this verse is answered by the prayers of the One who died for him.

What about someone I know who seemed to be a believer and has walked away? Do not pronounce the final verdict; that belongs to God, and the story is not over. Some who wander are true believers in a season of serious backsliding, and God brings them back, as he brought back Peter after his denial. Others, if they never return, show in the end that their faith was not the living kind (1 John 2:19). You cannot always tell which, and you do not need to. Pray for them persistently, keep the door open, love them honestly, and tell them the truth about Christ when you can. The God who keeps his own is also the God who seeks the lost.

How do I know my faith is the kind that continues? Not by looking for a feeling of certainty about the future, but by looking at Christ now. Are you still trusting him, however weakly? Do you still come back to him when you fail? Do you still want to be his? Those are the marks of a faith God is keeping. Then use the means he uses to keep you: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people. A believer who cuts himself off from these is not proving his security but endangering his steadiness.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I rejoice in my sufferings. Paul writes in chains (4:18), after floggings, stonings and shipwreck (2 Corinthians 11:23–28), the cost of carrying the gospel to the Gentiles. He does not enjoy pain for its own sake.

Three reasons for joy. First, the suffering is for your sake, spent on people he loves. Second, to suffer for Christ is to be drawn into fellowship with Christ himself (Philippians 3:10). The apostles left the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer for the name (Acts 5:41). Third, his joy rests not in the pain but in what it accomplishes: through a prisoner’s chains the gospel runs free and a church is built.

What is lacking in Christ’s afflictions. One of the hardest phrases Paul wrote. It cannot mean Christ’s atoning sufferings were insufficient, that his death left a deficit for Paul to make up. The letter has just declared the opposite (1:20, 22). And the word Paul uses for afflictions (thlipseis) is never used in the New Testament of Christ’s atoning death.

Two kinds of suffering. There is Christ’s atoning suffering, the once-for-all work of the cross, which we receive but never share. And there are his ongoing afflictions in his suffering people as the gospel advances in a hostile world.
