For Christ is so joined to his church that to strike the church is to strike him: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). There is an appointed measure of such affliction still to be borne before the end, and Paul takes up his share, not adding to the atonement but taking his portion of the cost of spreading it. Not one tear shed for Christ’s name is lost, and not one blow borne for his church is wasted.

For the sake of his body. His suffering builds up the church, and that is what turns hardship into joy. The place where Paul sat in chains was not a dead end; it was a pulpit (Philippians 1:12–14).

Where Christians differ: the merits of the saints. Roman Catholic teaching has used this verse to support a treasury of merit: the sufferings of saints added to Christ’s, applied to others through indulgences. This commentary’s view: Christ’s atoning work was complete and finished (John 19:30; Hebrews 10:14). Nothing can be added to it. Paul’s sufferings did not atone for anyone; they were the cost of bringing the gospel to them. There is no treasury of merit and no need for indulgences.

Does this apply to my sufferings, or only to Paul’s? In its measure, to yours. What was true of the apostle holds for every believer: when you bear loss or scorn for Christ’s sake, it is not meaningless misfortune but a share in the afflictions of Christ, counted into the great work he is doing and borne for the good of his people. Being passed over at work for refusing to lie, losing a friend because you follow Christ, the long labour of caring for a believer in need: these are not wasted. And even suffering that is not directly for the gospel, illness or grief, can be borne for the church’s sake when you bear it trusting God, because others are strengthened by watching you. But do not go looking for suffering, and do not call the results of your own folly persecution (1 Peter 4:15–16).
verseByVerse.note: Paul does not mean Christ’s atoning suffering was incomplete; he shares in the afflictions that Christ’s people must still endure.

verseByVerse.quote: of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The stewardship from God. A steward was not the owner but the servant entrusted with the keys to give out the master’s provisions. He does not own what he handles, did not appoint himself, and must give account. So Paul stands among the Colossians as a servant dispensing what belongs to Another, for their benefit (1 Corinthians 4:1–2).

All of it comes down. The gospel, the mystery, the revealing, the stewardship are God’s, and even the strength to carry it out is his energy that he powerfully works within me (v. 29). From first to last everything descends from heaven; not one thread ascends from earth. The same grace that made a persecutor into a steward reached down for you (Ephesians 3:7–8).

The word of God fully known. The word of God here is first the gospel message (v. 5). Fully known has a double force: Paul preaches the gospel completely, nothing edited out to please his hearers (Acts 20:27), and he carries it to its full reach, out to the Gentiles. The false teachers wanted to add to the gospel, as though it were lacking. Paul says it is already full: his task is not to supplement it but to declare the whole of it.

The mystery. A mystery in the Bible is not a baffling puzzle but something once hidden in the mind of God and now revealed by him: a truth no one could have worked out, which God has chosen to bring into the light (Ephesians 3:3–6; Romans 16:25–26). Its content comes in v. 27: Christ in you, the hope of glory. The irony: the pagan mystery religions (cults with secret rites for members only), and very likely the false teachers too, traded in secret knowledge for an inner ring. Paul takes their favourite word and turns it inside out.

Hidden, yet there all along. Hidden for ages, yet there in the Old Testament, veiled: the offspring who would crush the serpent (Genesis 3:15), the promise that in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), the Servant given as a light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6). Like a sealed letter lying on the table for generations, it waited to be opened, and Christ opened it (Luke 24:27).

Now revealed to his saints. Not unearthed by philosophers but unveiled from above: God comes down and tells. And it was revealed to all believers, not a spiritual elite (1 Corinthians 2:14). God drew back the curtain in his Son and put the secret of the universe into the hands of tradesmen, slaves and housewives in a small town.

Are there still hidden truths God reveals today to special people? Not new truths of the gospel. The mystery has now been revealed and written down by the apostles, and the faith was once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). God still opens blind eyes to see what is in his word (Ephesians 1:17–18), and a believer may suddenly see a passage he has read a hundred times. But that is illumination of what is written, not new revelation beside it. Christians who believe God still speaks through prophecy today generally agree that nothing said that way can add to Scripture or stand above it. Anyone who claims to have a secret truth that the ordinary believer with an open Bible cannot reach is offering exactly what Paul refused.

In everyday life. You hold, in an ordinary Bible on an ordinary shelf, the secret that kings and prophets longed to see (Luke 10:24). Open it today as if that were true, because it is.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chose to make known. The unveiling was owed to no one: God could have kept his secret locked in his own heart through all eternity. God chose to tell his secret to outsiders and rebels, a wonder before it is a doctrine (Matthew 11:26).

Among the Gentiles. The astonishing part: the Gentiles are included. To a Jewish mind they were the outsiders, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12). That God’s richest glory would be displayed among them was the part no one saw coming (Ephesians 3:6). And the Colossians are those Gentiles: this is about them. It leaves no room for spiritual snobbery, and Paul piles up words to say it: the riches of the glory of this mystery.

Christ in you. The greatest treasure God ever kept hidden turns out to be a Person (Galatians 2:20). Not Christ far above you, reached only through angels and rituals, the very thing the false teachers were selling, but the living Lord himself, taking up residence within his people, in the humblest believer. “In you” is plural: among you, and in each of you.

The hope of glory. Christ in you now guarantees glory to come: resurrection, glorification (God’s final work of making his people perfectly holy and raising them in bodies like Christ’s own, Philippians 3:21), and a share in his glory. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory (3:4; Romans 8:17–18). The present indwelling is the pledge and down payment of the coming splendour.

The King in the cottage. Imagine the King leaving his palace to live, day and night, in a labourer’s cottage. He did not move in to leave you in the cottage for ever: Christ in you is the King in the cottage; the hope of glory is the palace that must follow. He has moved in, and he means to take us home. Glory is not a maybe for those he indwells. It is as certain as he is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers become divine. It means Christ dwells in them by the Spirit, uniting them to himself.

How can Christ be in me if he is in heaven at the Father’s right hand? Both are true, and the link is the Holy Spirit. In his human body Christ has ascended and is in heaven, from where he will return (3:1; Acts 1:11). But by his Spirit he dwells in every believer: anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him, and if Christ is in you, your spirit is alive (Romans 8:9–10). This is not a feeling you must produce. It is a fact about every believer, whether you feel it or not, and it is why you are never alone, never beyond his help, and never without hope.

verseByVerse.quote: Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Him we proclaim. The first word is emphatic: Him. Not a system or a ladder of disciplines, but a Person, to be known, trusted and loved. You do not get Christ by keeping the rules; you begin to keep his commands by having Christ (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Warning everyone. True ministry warns as well as comforts. To warn is to counsel someone out of harm’s way. It is what Paul did at Ephesus night and day with tears (Acts 20:31). Here it is chiefly the warning against being lured from the all-sufficient Christ. To warn is love: a father shouts at the child wandering into the road precisely because he loves him.

Teaching everyone. Teaching builds up in the truth, with the wisdom found in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (2:3), and the skill to fit it to each real life so that it takes root. And mark the drumbeat: everyone, three times. No elite here.

Mature in Christ. “Present” is the word of v. 22, with the great Day in view. “Mature” means full-grown, brought to the intended end: a word some mystery cults used for their initiates.

What maturity is not, and what it is. Not mere head knowledge, nor a higher tier for an elite few, the very thing the false teachers dangled. What it is: growing up into Christ, rooted, steady, discerning, Christlike in character, no longer blown about by every new teaching, able to stand and feed yourself from God’s word (Ephesians 4:13–15; Hebrews 5:13–14). A sapling and an oak share the same life: maturity is the new convert’s Christ-life grown up.

Is warning only the pastor’s job? No. Paul uses the same word when he tells the whole church to teach and admonish one another in all wisdom (3:16). Every believer is meant to speak the truth in love to others. But how you do it matters. Warn someone you actually love, in private first (Matthew 18:15), humbly, aware of your own weakness (Galatians 6:1), with the aim of their good and not your relief. Begin with Christ, not with a list of their faults. And be willing to be warned yourself. A church where no one ever lovingly says, I am worried about this, is not gentle; it is neglectful.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this I toil. The shift to I toil shows what the goal costs Paul. “Toil” means to labour to the point of exhaustion, the bone-weariness of a field hand at harvest.

Struggling. The word for the athlete straining every sinew in the games, from which we get agony.

His energy. Yet the power he strains with is not his own. “Energy” and “works” are the same root, doubled for emphasis: God’s might, energising him from the inside. It is Christ’s power by the Spirit who dwells in every believer (Romans 8:11). Here is the balance the whole Bible keeps: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:12–13). Maximum effort and total dependence held together in one breath: not fifty-fifty, but fully Paul’s striving and fully God’s working (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Neither passive nor self-driven. Two ditches. One is “let go and let God”, as if all effort were unspiritual; but Paul toiled to the point of agony, and this ditch breeds a stalled faith that blames God for its barrenness. The other is “it is all up to me”: white-knuckled willpower that breeds pride when it works and burnout when it does not, self-reliance in religious clothes.

Set the sails. Work hard, and lean hard. A crew must hoist and trim the sails, but it is the wind that drives the boat home, filling only the sails hands have set. So set the sails: pray, fight sin, feed on the word, serve the church, keep going. And let the wind of God’s own power carry you on. The sweat is real, and it is yours; the strength is real, and it is God’s.

I am exhausted. Does this verse mean I should work even harder? Not necessarily. Paul’s toil was aimed at one thing, Christ’s people growing mature, and powered by Christ’s strength, not by guilt or the fear of letting people down. If you are worn out, ask whether you are carrying things God never gave you, or carrying the right things in your own strength. The same Lord who works powerfully in his servants also gave the Sabbath rest and told his tired disciples to come away and rest a while (Mark 6:31). Rest is not a failure of devotion. Sometimes the most faithful thing you can do is sleep, and trust him to hold what you put down. And be honest about what drives you. Sometimes the weariness comes not from Christ’s call but from a hunger to be needed, praised or in control, and that master is never satisfied. Christ’s yoke is easy and his burden light (Matthew 11:30); a burden that never lightens may not be his.

For worship. The risen Christ does not stand at a distance watching his servants strain. He works in them, with all his energy, powerfully. Every sermon faithfully preached, every prayer that struggles for a church, every tired act of love for his people is his own power moving through weak hands. The labour is ours; the might, and the glory, are his.

Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel,<sup>6</sup>which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing—as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth,<sup>7</sup>just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf<sup>8</sup>and has made known to us your love in the Spirit.<sup>9</sup>And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,<sup>10</sup>so as to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God;<sup>11</sup>being strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy;<sup>12</sup>giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.<sup>13</sup>He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son,<sup>14</sup>in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.<sup>15</sup>He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.<sup>16</sup>For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him.<sup>17</sup>And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.<sup>18</sup>And he is the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent.<sup>19</sup>For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,<sup>20</sup>and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross.<sup>21</sup>And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds,<sup>22</sup>he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him,<sup>23</sup>if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a minister.<sup>24</sup>Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church,<sup>25</sup>of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known,<sup>26</sup>the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints.<sup>27</sup>To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.<sup>28</sup>Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.<sup>29</sup>For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.

2.title: Fullness in Christ: Warnings Against Every Supplement
2.overview: Now Paul names the danger. Teachers are offering the Colossians a “philosophy” that sounds wise: keep food laws and holy days, practise harsh self-denial, honour angels as mediators, and pursue visions. Its message is Christ plus. Paul’s answer is Christ, in whom all fullness dwells and in whom believers are filled. The cure for sin is not more rules but union with the risen Christ, which chapter 3 unfolds.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Rooted and Built Up in Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells a church he has never visited how hard he labours in prayer for them, so that they may be strengthened, united in love and sure of Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden. Then he gives the command on which the whole chapter turns: as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him.
verseByVerse.theology:
All the Treasures of Wisdom Hidden in Christ

Colossians 2:3 has shaped how Reformed Christians think about learning. Writers such as Abraham Kuyper drew on the conviction that all true wisdom and knowledge come from Christ and hold together in him. This does not mean that only Christians can know things. It means that whatever is truly known is “thinking God’s thoughts after him,” knowingly or not, in a world that Christ made and holds together. So the Christian can study anything without fear, knowing that every true path leads back to the One in whom all wisdom is hidden.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy offered a secret wisdom that seemed to go beyond the gospel. Paul’s answer: you are not lacking wisdom; you have only begun to explore the One in whom it is stored. Now: A believer who turns to a therapy, a spirituality or a philosophy for what Christ supposedly cannot give has accepted the false teachers’ premise. He may learn from every honest source, while treating Christ as the source and the test of all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Colossians 2 confronts the false teaching directly, and answers it with Christ. Paul prays they will know Christ, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom, and keep walking in him (vv. 1–7); warns against philosophy not according to Christ, in whom believers are filled, forgiven and freed from the powers (vv. 8–15); and refuses every judgment over food, festivals, angel worship and man-made rules (vv. 16–23). Christ is enough.

How great a struggle. “Struggle” (agōn) is the root of our word agony: the all-out exertion of the wrestler in the contest, the same root he used of his ministry in 1:29. He writes in chains (4:18), so how does he struggle for a church he cannot reach? Chiefly on his knees, as Epaphras was always struggling on their behalf in his prayers (4:12). Pastoral love is hard, hidden work, aimed at a goal: that their hearts be encouraged and brought to full assurance of Christ (v. 2).

And for those at Laodicea. Laodicea lay about 10 miles from Colossae, a wealthy banking and textile city, the church later rebuked as lukewarm (Revelation 3:14–22). Paul wrote them a letter too, and wanted the two churches to swap letters (4:16). The same danger threatened the whole valley.

Not seen me face to face. These would include Hierapolis (4:13) and other churches in the valley. Paul would not have known these people in the street, yet he agonises for them, simply because they belong to Christ. A hired hand cares only for what the flock does for him; the true shepherd cares for the flock itself (John 10:12–13). The church is held up by hidden hands folded in prayer, and above them all by the pierced hands of the great Shepherd, who knows his sheep by name in every valley of the earth, and who prayed for us before we were born (John 17:20).

How do I struggle in prayer for someone? It is not about straining to feel intense or praying for hours. It means praying with persistence and with purpose: coming back to the same people again and again, asking for the things that matter most (as Paul does in v. 2 and in 1:9–12), and refusing to give up when nothing seems to change. It may mean praying when you are tired, or setting aside time you would rather spend elsewhere. Struggling prayer is ordinary prayer that keeps going, because you care what happens to that person’s soul.

In everyday life. Choose a church you have never visited and keep praying for it: a persecuted church, a struggling plant, a missionary’s congregation. Learn one name from it and pray for that person by name.
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea lay about 10 miles from Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Paul asks for. What he does not ask is telling: not that they be wealthy, comfortable or successful, nor even that the church grow in numbers.

Encouraged. “Encouraged” (parakaleō) means braced, given courage to stand, because the false teachers press in with plausible arguments (v. 4) and a wavering heart is easily swept away. This is the strengthening the Spirit himself gives, for he is the Helper whom Jesus sent (John 14:16), whose very name comes from the same root.

Knit together in love. “Knit together” (symbibazō) is used of the joints of a body (v. 19), and what binds them is love (Romans 5:5). The lone sheep is picked off; the flock knit together stands. Heresy isolates and flatters the few; love weaves the whole body into one. And love is the soil in which true understanding grows.

Full assurance. “Full assurance” (plērophoria) is faith brought all the way to certainty, and it is assurance of understanding: not a leap in the dark but a confidence that rests on actually grasping the truth. God’s great desire for you is not that you be clever or initiated but that you be sure: rich in the settled, glad certainty of knowing the Lord Jesus (2 Timothy 1:12).

God’s mystery, which is Christ. The mystery is not a secret doctrine for initiates, but a person: Christ (1:26–27). To know him is to know God’s mystery. The false teachers dangled mystery as a prize beyond Christ; the mystery is Christ. (The KJV, following later manuscripts, has a longer reading; on either reading the mystery is Christ.)

Is it proud to be sure I am saved? No. It would be proud to be sure because of your own goodness, but Christian assurance rests on Christ, not on you. God wants his children to be sure: John wrote so that those who believe in the name of the Son of God may know that they have eternal life (1 John 5:13). Here Paul prays for the riches of full assurance. Doubts come to many believers, and they are not proof that you are not his. But the remedy for them is to know Christ better: his promises, his finished work, his faithfulness. The more clearly you see him, the surer you will be.

verseByVerse.quote: in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the treasures. “In whom” means in Christ, the mystery of v. 2. Knowledge is the understanding of God and reality; wisdom, the skill of living rightly in its light. “Hidden” (apokryphos) means not out of reach but treasured up, as gold is kept in a vault, ready to be found by those who seek him. Christ is the strongroom in which God has stored everything worth knowing.

The sharp edge. The false teachers peddled hidden wisdom for the initiated few. Paul turns their prized word back: all the hidden treasures are in Christ. So there is no wisdom worth having outside Christ, and no lack of it inside him. The Christian does not graduate from Christ to something higher; he goes ever deeper into Christ, who is himself the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). God did not scatter his wisdom across the universe in fragments for the clever to collect. He stored it all in his Son, and gave his Son to us.

Two freeing things. First, you need not look anywhere else. You may fear the real riches belong to scholars and mystics. Not so: you have Christ, and need only go further into him. Second, the treasure has no bottom. A whole lifetime of knowing Jesus will not exhaust the riches stored in him.

The deed to the mine. Imagine a man chasing one get-rich scheme after another, then told the deed to the richest mine in the country was made out in his name long ago, and the mine runs so deep a thousand lifetimes could never empty it. That is you and Christ (Matthew 13:44).

Does this mean non-Christians can know nothing true? No. By God’s common grace unbelievers discover a great deal that is true, and Christians may learn from them. Paul is speaking of the wisdom that saves and makes sense of everything, which is found only in Christ. The doctor who sets your broken arm may not believe, and his skill is still real and a gift of God. But only in Christ do you learn who made the arm, why you are here, and how a sinner can stand before God.

verseByVerse.quote: I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That no one may delude you. This is why Paul has pressed Christ’s all-sufficiency so hard. The Colossian heresy’s exact shape is debated, but the letter points to a mixture of Jewish rule-keeping (food laws, festivals, circumcision), harsh self-denial, the veneration of angels, and claims to secret knowledge. Its method was not to deny Christ outright but to add to him: Christ plus these rules, plus these mediators, plus this deeper experience. “Delude” (paralogizomai) means to deceive by false reasoning, to talk someone out of the truth the way a swindler reasons a man out of his money.

With plausible arguments. “Plausible arguments” (pithanologia) is persuasive speech, fine-sounding words. Error does not arrive looking false; it comes dressed as wisdom (v. 23): “Faith in Christ is a fine beginning, but for real fullness you must also keep these days and honour these powers.”

The little word plus. The packaging changes; the pattern never does. The giveaway is always the little word “plus”: Christ is not quite enough; add something. Paul’s safeguard: know Christ fully, and you will not be talked out of him (2 Corinthians 11:3).

What it does not mean. Argument is not wrong; Paul himself reasoned and persuaded (Acts 17:2–4; 18:4). The question is not whether an argument is clever, but whether it leads to Christ or away from him.

What if I cannot answer an argument against my faith? You do not have to win every debate to be right. Many false teachings sound convincing because their teachers are skilled speakers, not because they are true. If you meet an argument you cannot answer, do not panic and do not pretend. Say honestly that you will think about it, then take it to Scripture and to a wise believer or a good book. Christians have faced most arguments before. Meanwhile hold on to what you know: Christ died, Christ rose, and his word has not failed you. A question you cannot yet answer is not a reason to let go of him.

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With you in spirit. Present in thought, prayer and care (1 Corinthians 5:3): the language of love that leaps over distance, and beneath it the truth that believers are bound together in Christ by one Spirit, and miles cannot sever that bond.

Rejoicing. A man in chains rejoices, not over his release but over the spiritual health of a congregation he has never seen. John says he has no greater joy than to hear that his children are walking in the truth (3 John 4).

Good order. “Good order” (taxis) means orderly arrangement, and it was often used of soldiers drawn up in disciplined ranks. The church was still holding the line.

Firmness. “Firmness” (stereōma) is solidity, and many hear in it, beside taxis, the solid front of a battle line or a fortress wall that does not give way. Under the plausible arguments of v. 4, their line holds. And the firmness comes from faith in Christ: their solidity is not self-manufactured grit but rests on its object, a line that holds because the One it leans on cannot be moved (1 Corinthians 15:58; 16:13).

Why does Paul praise them before warning them? Because that is how love corrects. He is not flattering them to soften the blow; he is telling the truth about what God has done in them, and the truth is good. A church that hears only warnings grows discouraged; a church that hears only praise grows careless. Paul gives both, in that order, so that they will hear the warning as coming from a friend who is on their side. When you need to correct a fellow believer, a child or a colleague, begin by honestly naming the good you see.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore. The hinge of the letter: because Christ is supreme and all-sufficient, here is what to do. Doctrine becomes duty.

As you received. “Received” (paralambanō) is the word for receiving a tradition handed down. And what they received was not just teaching about Christ but Christ himself, as Lord: received as Master, not an optional extra bolted onto the old life.

So walk in him. Walk is the whole daily conduct of life: the way you began is the way you go on. You came to Christ with empty hands, resting on him alone, receiving him by grace; so keep walking the very same way. The heresy is cut at the root: you do not graduate from Christ to higher teachings. You do not move on from him; you go on in him. Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? (Galatians 3:3).

Rooted and built up in him. Two pictures, cheerfully mixed (Ephesians 3:17): a tree sunk deep into the soil, a house rising on its foundation. Even the Greek tenses differ. Rooted (errizōmenoi) is something done once with lasting effect: firmly planted once and for all. Built up (epoikodomoumenoi) is still going on: continually, day by day. Anchored and rising, settled and growing. The Christ we received with empty hands at the beginning is the Christ who carries us to the end: the soil we are rooted in and the bedrock we are built on, who never runs dry and never gives way. In him means you are joined to Christ by faith, so that what is his becomes yours and his life flows into yours, the way sap flows from the vine into the branch (John 15:4–5).

Established in the faith. “Established” (bebaioumenoi) means confirmed, made firm. In the faith as Epaphras taught it (1:7). The mark of truth is not novelty but faithfulness to what the apostles handed down. When a teaching promises more than the plain gospel of Christ you were first taught, that is precisely the moment to be on guard (Jude 3; 2 Timothy 1:13–14).

Abounding in thanksgiving. Overflowing, and no afterthought. A heart overflowing with thanks for all it already has in Christ has no appetite for the false teacher’s offer of something more. Ingratitude is the crack through which discontent creeps in, and discontent is exactly the foothold the heretic needs; gratitude bolts the door. But thanks does not come naturally. Israel was fed with bread from heaven every morning and spent the journey murmuring, and we do the same.

How do I go deeper without going beyond Christ? By going further into the same things, not into new things. Read the Gospels again and again and get to know him. Learn what his death and resurrection accomplished, and what union with him means. Keep the means of grace he has given: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of his people. Obey him in the next thing he asks, because obedience opens understanding. Deep Christians are not people who found a secret; they are people who kept looking at Christ for a long time.

In everyday life. Thanksgiving must be cultivated, deliberately, against the grain of a forgetful heart. Stop, count the mercies, and name them: a Saviour, sins forgiven, Christ living within you, the sure hope of glory, until the grumble shrinks. You will find it nearly impossible to grumble and give thanks in the same breath, so fill your mouth with the better of the two (1 Thessalonians 5:18; Colossians 3:15–17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns against being taken captive by a philosophy that is not according to Christ, and gives the reason: in Christ the whole fullness of God dwells bodily, and believers are filled in him. Then he lists what God has already done for them in Christ, down to the defeat of the powers at the cross.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cancellation of the Debt and the Disarming of the Powers

Verses 13–15 give two vivid pictures of what the cross achieved. One is from the law court: the record of debt (cheirographon) that listed our guilt has been cancelled and nailed to the cross. The other is from the battlefield: the rulers and authorities, who held people through guilt and the law’s accusation, have been disarmed and led in triumph like conquered kings behind a general. Together: freedom from guilt and from spiritual bondage.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian teachers treated the elemental spirits and cosmic powers as threats to be kept happy by ritual. Paul says those powers are disarmed and paraded in defeat; you do not placate them, you stand in Christ’s victory. Now: A Christian who lives in dread of spiritual attack or dark forces needs to hear the same thing. The devil is real and still to be resisted, but he is a beaten enemy, and the believer stands on a victory already won.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Takes you captive. “Takes captive” (sylagōgeō) means to carry off as booty, to kidnap. A physical kidnapping everyone would see; when a teaching carries off a mind, almost no one notices, least of all the captive, who feels enlightened. Spiritual captivity wears the disguise of progress, which is why Paul shouts rather than whispers.

By philosophy and empty deceit. “Philosophy” (philosophia) means love of wisdom. Not all careful thinking (Paul reasoned with the philosophers at Athens), but this particular philosophy. In the Greek, philosophy and empty deceit form one phrase: a philosophy that is empty deceit. It promises fullness and delivers a void, while in Christ you have been filled (v. 10).

According to human tradition. Its source is human, what Jesus charged the Pharisees with: leaving the commandment of God to hold to the tradition of men (Mark 7:8).

The elemental spirits of the world. “Elemental spirits” (stoicheia) may mean the basic principles of religion, the ABCs, or the spirit powers thought to control the world, perhaps through the calendar and the stars, which people felt they must appease, as in Galatians 4:3, 9. To crawl back under them is to return to the slavery Christ broke.

Not according to Christ. The decisive test, and a freeing one: you do not need to master every false system to be safe. You need to know one thing surpassingly well: Christ.

Where Christians differ: should Christians study philosophy? Some take this verse to forbid all philosophy. This commentary’s view: Paul condemns philosophy that is empty deceit, rooted in human tradition and not according to Christ. Christians may study philosophy, and many great Christian thinkers have, but must bring every thought captive to Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5) and judge all systems by Scripture. Philosophy is a good servant and a bad master.

The bank teller. A bank teller spots forged notes not by memorising every counterfeit but by handling the genuine so constantly that anything false feels wrong at once. Know Christ deeply, and a teaching that diminishes or adds to him will feel wrong, however clever it sounds (1 John 4:1).

What does captivity to human philosophy look like today? Rarely a robed philosopher. More often it is the quiet assumptions of the age, absorbed without noticing: that you are what you feel, that truth is whatever works for you, that the physical world is all there is, that God exists to make you happy, that freedom means having no master. Some come from outside the church, some from inside it, dressed in Christian words. You do not need to be afraid of every idea. Ask of each: what does this say about Christ, about sin, about how a person is made right with God? If the answer pushes Christ to the edge, it is not according to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “Elemental spirits” may mean the basic principles of religion or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole fullness of deity. For gives the reason for the warning of v. 8: there is nothing to add to Christ, because all of God is in him and nowhere else. The whole fullness (pan to plērōma): nothing left over. “Deity” (theotēs) is the strongest word available: Godhead, the divine nature itself, not just divine qualities. Christ is not a creature filled with divine attributes but the One in whom the complete divine nature resides.

Dwells bodily. “Dwells” (katoikeō) is present tense: continues to dwell, permanently, to take up residence, God at home in Christ, even now that he is risen and reigns in heaven. And “bodily” (sōmatikōs): all of God, in a body you could have stood beside. Few verses state the full deity of the incarnate Christ more plainly.

Three blows against the error. Against their angels and elemental spirits: if all the fullness of deity is in Christ, those powers have no fullness to offer, so why seek lesser mediators? Against any idea of a scattered fullness, spread thin across a chain of angels and powers: Paul says it is concentrated, entire and undivided, in Christ alone. And against their contempt for the body: that one word bodily rebukes every teaching that seeks God by escaping the physical, for God himself dwells bodily in Christ.

Is Jesus still a man now, in heaven? Yes. The Son did not take a body for some thirty years and then lay it aside. He rose bodily, ascended bodily, and dwells (present tense) bodily, and he will return in the same way he went (Acts 1:11). That means there is a human being at the Father’s right hand who knows what it is to be tired, tempted, grieved and in pain (Hebrews 4:15). The God you pray to has a human face and human scars. He is not distant from what you are going through; he wears your nature still.

How can the infinite God live in a human body? Not by being squeezed into it. The Son did not stop upholding the universe when he lay in the manger (1:17; Hebrews 1:3); he added a human nature to the divine nature he always had, without either being changed into the other. We cannot picture how: a God we could fully explain would not be God. What Scripture gives us is not a puzzle to solve but a Person to bow before: the holy and infinite God has come near enough to be touched (1 John 1:1).

verseByVerse.quote: and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Filled in him. And carries us from Christ to ourselves. The fullness (plērōma) dwells in Christ, and you have been filled (peplērōmenoi) in Christ: the same root. What is true of the Head overflows to the members.

Three things in four words. The Greek tense describes a finished act with lasting results: you have been brought to fullness, and remain so. The verb is passive: God filled you; you did not fill yourself. And it is in him: yours not by your own attainment but by union with Christ. The heresy said they were lacking; Paul says they are already complete. Filled means that everything you need to be right with God and to know him is already yours because you belong to Christ: his righteousness counts as yours (2 Corinthians 5:21), his Spirit lives in you (Romans 8:9), and his Father is your Father (Galatians 4:6).

Head of all rule and authority. Christ rules over the very powers the false teachers urged the church to revere. Paul has said Christ created them (1:16), and he will say Christ disarmed them at the cross (2:15); here he is their head. Why seek help from angels or spirits, when you are joined to their Lord?

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have nothing more to grow into. They grow in experiencing what they already have. Nor does it mean you are sinlessly perfect or divine. It means you lack nothing for salvation or access to God.

If I am complete, why do I feel so incomplete? Because there is a difference between what you have and what you have yet to enjoy. A man with a fortune in his account who frets that he is poor does not need to earn more; he needs to wake up to what is already his. Your sense of lack is real, and some of it is the right longing for the glory still to come (Romans 8:23). But do not let it become a reason to chase extras. Much of the heart’s restless hunger, for more approval, more success, more spiritual experience, is a search for a fullness you already have in Christ. The answer to feeling incomplete is not a new experience or technique but a deeper grasp of what you already have in Christ, and a patient trust that he will finish what he started.

In everyday life. If you carry a vague dread of fate, of dark forces, of whatever pulls the strings behind life, say it plainly: the One I belong to is the head over every power that exists.

verseByVerse.quote: In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A circumcision made without hands. The false teachers were pressing physical circumcision. In Christ you have already received the true circumcision of the heart, which the Old Testament promised (Deuteronomy 30:6; Romans 2:28–29), done not by a knife but by God. This is what the Bible elsewhere calls the new birth, or regeneration: God himself giving a dead heart new life and new desires (Ezekiel 36:26; John 3:3–8). So the Colossians need no physical circumcision.

By putting off the body of the flesh. What is cut away is not a scrap of flesh but the body of the flesh: the whole old sinful self, stripped off like a garment (3:9). That does not mean a believer no longer feels sinful desires. It means the person you were in Adam, ruled by sin, died with Christ, so sin is no longer your master, even when it still tempts you (Romans 6:6–7).

By the circumcision of Christ. Either the circumcision Christ performs, or Christ’s own circumcision, his death, in which his body was cut off and in which the believer shares. Either way, union with Christ achieves what circumcision pointed to, and no human knife can add to it.

Buried with him in baptism. Paul sets baptism beside circumcision as a sign of the same reality. Baptism signifies union with Christ in his death and burial (Romans 6:3–4): the old life is not merely improved but put in the grave alongside Christ’s buried body.

Raised with him through faith. Rising in baptism pictures resurrection with Christ, the fact on which 3:1 builds. And it happens through faith: not the water by itself, but the power of God laid hold of by faith. Faith is the empty hand that receives; God’s power actually raises.

Who raised him from the dead. The same power raises believers to new life. Paul says God raised Jesus; elsewhere the Spirit raised him (Romans 8:11), and the Son says he has authority to take up his life again (John 10:18). The resurrection is the one act of the triune God, and the greatest display of power in history is the very power that raised you with him and is at work in you now (Ephesians 1:19–20).

Why all this, in the middle of a warning? The false teachers were saying: you need more; be circumcised, keep our rules, climb higher. Paul’s reply is to show what has already happened to you in Christ. You have received the true circumcision, the old self cut away by God. You have died and been buried with Christ, that chapter closed. You have been raised with him by the same power that raised Jesus from the grave. What, then, could anyone add? You cannot improve on death and resurrection.

Where Christians differ: does baptism replace circumcision? Paedobaptists (who baptise the infant children of believers) argue from this verse that baptism replaces circumcision and so belongs to infants. This commentary’s view: the circumcision Paul links with baptism is the heart’s, made without hands, and the raising happens “through faith,” so the sign belongs to believers, while we warmly respect brothers who read it differently. (See Acts 7:8 for the fuller answer.)

Where Christians differ: does baptism itself save? Some churches hold that God gives new birth through baptism. This commentary’s view: Paul ties the raising to faith, not to the water; baptism is God’s appointed sign of union with Christ, not working apart from faith. (See 1 Peter 3:21 for the fuller answer.)

I trust Christ but have never been baptised. Should I be? Yes. Baptism is Christ’s own command to his disciples (Matthew 28:19), and in the New Testament those who believed were baptised, usually very soon (Acts 2:41; 8:36–38; 16:33). It does not make you a Christian, but it is the way Christ has given for you to confess publicly that you are joined to him in his death and resurrection. If you are unsure or afraid, talk to the pastor or elders of your church. And if you were baptised as an infant and now trust Christ, ask them to help you think it through from Scripture, with patience and charity toward the church that baptised you.

In everyday life. When an old sin pulls at you today, say: that person was buried with Christ. Then live as the raised person you already are (Romans 6:4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dead in your trespasses. Not sick or struggling, but dead: unable to respond to God or contribute one thing to our rescue (Ephesians 2:1, 5).

The uncircumcision of your flesh. The Colossians were Gentiles, outside the covenant, and the phrase pictures the unrenewed heart: dead in guilt, shut out as strangers.

God made alive together with him. One word in Greek, synezōopoieō: resurrection language. God did for us exactly what he did for Christ in the tomb. This is regeneration, the new birth: you do not improve a corpse, you raise it (Ephesians 2:5). Not God helping those who help themselves, but God giving life to those who had none.

Forgiven us all our trespasses. “Forgiven” (charizomai) is built on the word for grace: forgiven freely, graciously. Paul shifts to us, including himself. And then the word to stop the heart: all. Past, present and future; the one that haunts you at three in the morning, the besetting sin you keep stumbling back into. God did not pardon most and keep a private reserve of charges. And it is no cheap amnesty. It is possible only because Christ bore every one of those sins himself (Psalm 103:12; Micah 7:19).

The record of debt. The record of debt is one Greek word, cheirographon: a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor himself, an IOU. It stands for our guilt before God’s law, a debt beyond all paying, and God cancelled it. The word for cancelling (exaleiphō) means to wipe out, as writing was washed off papyrus: not deferred or reduced but erased, as though the debt had never been written (Isaiah 43:25).

Nailing it to the cross. When the Romans crucified a man, they nailed his charge above his head; over Jesus it read, King of the Jews (John 19:19). But Paul says it was our certificate of debt that was nailed up at Calvary. Jesus was nailed there, so how was our record nailed with him? Because our debt was laid on him. This is penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty that we deserved, in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; Galatians 3:13).

What was nailed to the cross: the law, or our debt? Some take it as the law of Moses itself, which condemned. The more likely reading is that it is the record of our debt, our signed guilt before God’s law, which Christ cancelled by paying it. Either way, the law can no longer condemn those in Christ. That does not abolish God’s moral will: the ceremonial law is fulfilled, but love still keeps the commandments (Romans 13:8–10).

If all my sins are forgiven, why must I still confess them? Because forgiveness has two sides. As our Judge, God has forgiven us once for all; there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). As our Father, he still wants us to confess the sins that spoil our fellowship with him, and Jesus teaches us to pray daily, forgive us our debts (Matthew 6:12; 1 John 1:9). We confess not to stay saved, but because we are his children. A son who has broken his father’s window is not disowned, but he does not pretend nothing happened either.

Is it fair for an innocent person to pay someone else’s debt? It would be unjust to force a stranger to pay. But Christ was not a stranger dragged in against his will. He came willingly (John 10:18), he is the Head who joins his people to himself, and he is God himself bearing the cost of God’s own pardon. A holy Judge cannot tear up a just account as if it did not matter (Exodus 34:7); that would make sin small. At the cross the debt was neither ignored nor dumped on an unwilling victim. It was paid in full by the One who loved us and gave himself for us (Galatians 2:20).

In everyday life. When guilt accuses you today, name the sin that haunts you most, and say over it: forgiven, all of it, nailed to the cross. Then go and forgive someone who owes you far less.

For worship. The charge sheet with your name on it was fastened to the cross in the flesh of the Son of God and carried into the grave, and it never came back out. It is buried in the tomb of Jesus, and the empty tomb is the receipt stamped paid in full.
verseByVerse.note: The “record of debt” was a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor; the charge against a crucified man was nailed above him.

verseByVerse.quote: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who the rulers and authorities are. Not human kings but the spiritual forces of evil (Ephesians 6:12), the powers Christ created (1:16) and rules (2:10), and the very powers the false teachers were urging the church to fear and appease (2:18). They are real, personal, malevolent beings, and they held humanity in a threefold grip: as the powers behind our sin, as accusers wielding the law’s condemnation against us (the record of debt of v. 14), and through the fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15).

He disarmed. “Disarmed” (apekdyomai) means stripped, as defeated soldiers were stripped of weapons and armour. And what was the powers’ great weapon? Not brute force, but our sin and its just condemnation. The devil is the accuser of our brothers (Revelation 12:10); his whole case rested on the unpaid debt of our guilt. So v. 15 is welded to v. 14: the debt was their weapon. Once the record of guilt is wiped out and sin is fully paid, the accuser has nothing left to accuse with, the jailer has lost his keys, death has lost its sting.

Open shame. Made a public spectacle of them, before the whole watching unseen world of angels and powers, and through the gospel and the church wider still (Ephesians 3:10). The irony: at Calvary it looked as though the powers of darkness had won: the rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8), and behind them stood the darkness of this hour (Luke 22:53). But in that very act they were undone. Their apparent triumph was their defeat.

Triumphing over them. “Triumphing” (thriambeuō) is the technical word for a Roman triumph. A Roman general paraded through the city with conquered kings in chains behind his chariot; Paul casts the powers as those captive kings. What looked like Christ’s defeat was his triumph, and the very instrument of death became the chariot of victory. “In him” may also be translated “in it”, that is, in the cross.

The point for Colossae. The climax of the argument: the cross did not only forgive your sins (v. 14); it defeated the very powers the Colossians were told to appease. Why bow to, or bargain with, or tremble before an enemy your own Lord has already conquered and led in chains?

If Satan is defeated, why does he still seem so active? Because he is defeated but not yet removed, like an army that has lost the decisive battle and still fights on in the hills. He still tempts, deceives and accuses, and the New Testament tells believers to be watchful and to resist him (1 Peter 5:8–9; Ephesians 6:11). But he cannot condemn you, because your debt is paid; he cannot own you, because you belong to Christ; and he cannot win, because his end is fixed. Think of a fierce guard dog on a short chain: it still barks and lunges and frightens the timid, but it is bound and cannot drag down the one who belongs to its Master. Stand in Christ’s victory, and the devil will flee from you (James 4:7).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman general celebrated victory by parading his captives through the streets.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The conclusion follows. Since Christ has done everything, no one may judge believers over food and holy days, which were shadows of him, or disqualify them for lacking severity, angel worship and visions. They died with Christ to that whole order of human rules, which look wise but have no power against the flesh.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shadow and Substance

Verse 17 gives a key for reading the Old Testament, and Reformed interpreters have leaned on it heavily. The ceremonial law, its festivals, sabbaths, food laws and sacrifices, was truly given by God and truly pointed ahead. But it was a shadow, not the substance, and the substance is Christ. To go back to the shadow misses what the law was always saying.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian teachers made Jewish days and food laws part of their system. Paul says these were shadows, and Christ has come. Now: The same answer meets any movement that makes Old Testament ceremonies the mark of true spirituality. What those ceremonies taught about holiness and love is fulfilled in Christ and worked out in us by the Spirit; the ceremonies themselves have reached their goal in him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one pass judgment. Therefore draws the conclusion from everything before it: filled in Christ (v. 10), forgiven at the cross (v. 14), with the powers disarmed (v. 15), believers are free. The false teachers were passing judgment: condemning the Colossians for not keeping their rules, making them feel second-class, disqualified. Paul forbids it flatly. Your standing is in Christ, not in menus and calendars.

In questions of food and drink. The food laws of Moses, rules about clean and unclean food, and perhaps ascetic rules besides (v. 21).

A festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. The three kinds of holy days in Israel’s calendar: annual festivals, monthly new moons, weekly Sabbaths (1 Chronicles 23:31; Hosea 2:11). All three are included. And there is a reason these things can no longer be made binding, which Paul gives next: they were a shadow of the things to come (v. 17), signposts pointing forward to Christ. The rest the Sabbath pictured is found in him (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the feasts are fulfilled in his death, resurrection and gift of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 5:7; 15:20). To make them a condition of acceptance is, in effect, to deny that Christ is enough.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath. Some say Christians must keep the seventh-day Sabbath; others, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, that the fourth commandment carries over to the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath. This commentary’s view: Paul includes the Sabbath among the shadows fulfilled in Christ (v. 17). Christians are not bound by the Mosaic Sabbath law, and no one may judge them or bind their conscience over it (Romans 14:5). Christ is our rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). The Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is the day the church gathers (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10): his gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest out of joy and wisdom, not a binding law with rules about work. The Westminster and 1689 view (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8) is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect.

Does this include the weekly Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), hold that Paul means only the ceremonial sabbaths of Israel’s festivals, and that the weekly Sabbath remains a creation ordinance (a pattern God gave at creation for all people, Genesis 2:3), now kept on the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath. That view is held by many godly believers and deserves respect. But Paul’s list, festival, new moon, Sabbath, is the Old Testament’s standard way of naming the yearly, monthly and weekly holy days together (1 Chronicles 23:31). The more likely reading is that the weekly Sabbath is included, a shadow fulfilled in Christ. Christians gather on the first day as a glad and ancient practice, but no day binds the conscience (Romans 14:5).

The same error in modern clothes. The exact rules change; the pattern never does. It is the same error whenever a secondary or man-made practice is made the measure of true spirituality and people are judged by it. “A real Christian would never touch a drink.” “You must follow this diet or this fast to be holy.” “You must keep, or must not keep, Christmas or Lent.” “You must use only this Bible translation, sing only these songs, school your children in this one way.” Wherever someone takes a matter Christ has left free and turns it into a test of whether you are accepted by God, and looks down on you for failing it, that is the Colossian error in a Sunday suit.

So may I judge a brother who keeps these things? No. The rebuke cuts both ways. Do not let anyone make you feel like a second-rate Christian over such things, and do not sit in judgment on a brother who differs from you (Romans 14:1–4). The believer who keeps Sunday strictly and the one who keeps it more freely, the one who abstains and the one who drinks with thanksgiving, are both accepted by the same Christ. And this is no licence to despise all discipline. The gospel never frees us to sin, only from it. It is liberty of conscience: Christ alone is the ground of our acceptance, and no one may add a single rule to him (Galatians 5:1).

verseByVerse.quote: These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A shadow. These, the food laws and holy days of v. 16, are a shadow (skia): the dark outline an object throws, with the shape of the thing but none of its substance. You cannot shake a shadow’s hand. The whole ceremonial law was exactly that: a God-given shadow cast ahead of a coming reality, and the reality it traced was Christ (Hebrews 8:5; 10:1). The Passover lamb outlined the Lamb of God. The Day of Atonement outlined his once-for-all sacrifice. The Sabbath outlined the rest he gives. The tabernacle outlined God come to dwell with his people. A shadow is real and useful: it truly tells you something is on its way. But it was never meant to be clung to as though it were the thing itself.

The substance. The word for substance is literally body (sōma), and the contrast is beautiful: the shadow set against the body that casts it. The solid body that threw this entire shadow play, the whole Old Testament system of feasts and foods and sacred days, is Christ himself. And once the body has arrived, why cling to its shadow? When your friend walks through the door, you do not keep staring at his silhouette on the wall. To return to the ceremonial rules now that Christ has come is to prefer the outline to the person. You have lost nothing by leaving the shadows behind. You have gained the very One they were all pointing to.

In the flow. The word for substance, body, echoes verse 9: the fullness of deity dwells bodily in Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament is worthless. Shadows are real and point to the real thing. Studying them helps us see Christ. Nor does it mean that God’s moral law, summed up in love for God and neighbour, was a shadow; it is the ceremonial rules, the signposts, that have reached their destination.

How should I read the Old Testament laws, then? Ask what each one was pointing to: the sacrifices to Christ’s death, the food laws to the clean heart he gives (Mark 7:19), while the moral commands still show God’s will (Luke 24:27). (See 1 Corinthians 9:8–10 for the fuller answer.)

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one disqualify you. “Disqualify” (katabrabeuō) comes from the games: to rule against someone, like an umpire denying a prize. The false teachers set themselves up as umpires over the Colossians’ faith, pronouncing them out of the running unless they took up the teachers’ programme. Paul’s reply: do not let anyone rob you of a prize already yours in Christ, for the Father has already qualified you (1:12). And the programme had three strands.

Insisting on asceticism. “Asceticism” (tapeinophrosynē) is literally humility, but here it is false humility: harsh self-denial used as a spiritual technique. The false teacher insists on it, or delights in it: self-imposed severity, probably including rigorous fasting, as a path to higher spirituality (named again in v. 23). It looked humble, even impressive, but it was a performance of lowliness, not the real thing.

Worship of angels. Either worshipping angels, or joining in the worship angels offer, in visionary experiences. The false teaching seems to have mixed Jewish rules, strict self-denial and mystical experiences of the angelic world. Either way, giving religious devotion to angelic beings as mediators and guardians, channels through which to approach God, is plainly wrong. It dethrones the one Mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5) and bows to the very powers Christ is head over (2:10). Angels themselves refuse it: when John fell down to worship one, the angel told him not to, but to worship God (Revelation 19:10). Christ needs no angel to bring us to God, because he is God come to bring us home.

Going on in detail about visions. “Going on in detail” (embateuō) means entering into, and some ancient inscriptions seem to use it of initiates entering a sanctuary. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add not (things he has not seen); the earliest lack it, so most modern Bibles read what he has seen. The teacher paraded the things he claimed to have seen, mystical experiences won through his disciplines, and built his authority on them: “I have seen what you have not; follow me and you can too.” It was spiritual one-upmanship by experience, making private revelations rather than Christ and his word the measure of who is advanced.

Puffed up without reason. The sensuous mind is literally the mind of his flesh. For all the impressive display, the man is simply puffed up, swollen, inflated, and without reason, for there is nothing actually there. And here is the irony at the heart of it. The man who beats his body to escape the flesh, who scales the heavens in visions to rise above it, is driven the whole time by the flesh: by the fallen nature’s craving for status and superiority. The austerity feeds his pride; the visions feed his self-importance; his humility is vanity in disguise.

Still with us. All three strands are still with us: holiness equated with severity; the fascination with angels, spirit guides and other mediators slipped between the believer and Christ; and the experience-chasing that rates a Christian by his dramatic encounters. Beneath them all runs the same error: a spiritual elite making ordinary believers feel disqualified unless they add some practice or experience to Christ, and, underneath the show, the same fleshly pride (1 Corinthians 8:1). The safeguard, in every age, is the next verse: hold fast to the Head.

Where Christians differ: praying to angels and saints. Some traditions encourage prayer to angels or departed saints for help and intercession. Those traditions distinguish such requests from worship, and many sincere believers practise them. This commentary’s view: Paul warns against worship of angels, and Scripture forbids worshipping any creature (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9). There is one mediator between God and man, Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and he always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). Believers pray to God through Christ alone.

What if a Christian friend tells me about a dramatic vision or experience? Listen kindly, and do not mock. God is free to work in his people’s lives in ways that move them deeply. But test it by Scripture, and ask where it points: to Christ and his word, or to the person and their experience? Be wary of any experience that is used to claim a higher rank, to add teaching beyond the Bible, or to make others feel second-class. The closed canon of Scripture (the complete, finished collection of God’s written word) is sufficient for faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17). You do not need someone else’s vision to know Christ fully; you have his word, and his Spirit to open it.
verseByVerse.note: The false teaching seems to have mixed Jewish rules, strict self-denial and fascination with angels and visions.

verseByVerse.quote: and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Holding fast to the Head. “Holding fast” means to grip tightly, to cling, and the Head is Christ (1:18; 2:10). In a single phrase is Paul’s diagnosis of the whole heresy: for all the visions and disciplines and angel talk, they had let go of Christ. They shifted their grip from the Saviour to rules, experiences and spiritual beings, and that is fatal, because everything depends on keeping hold of the Head. All true spirituality holds on to him. Letting go is the exact opposite of being rooted and built up in him (2:7), and the phrase implies our part: hold on, do not drift, do not loosen your grip when something newer and more impressive comes along.

From whom the whole body. The church, the body of Christ (1:18). Christ is the Head, the church his body, and from the Head, and nowhere else, the whole body draws its life.

Joints and ligaments. Medical language: the connecting tissues that both link the parts and carry the supply down from the head to every limb. Life flows from Christ the Head, through all the connections, into every member, so that the body is at once fed and held together, and therefore grows. Believers grow through their relationships with one another in the church (Ephesians 4:15–16).

A growth that is from God. True growth comes from God, through Christ, not through rules or visions. The increase is his own doing, not something the body manufactures by technique (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

The branch and the vine. Here is the whole thing in a picture. Cut a branch from the vine and it does not grow; it withers, because all the life was in the vine (John 15:5). Sever a hand from the arm and no exercise will make it grow. That is exactly what the false teachers were unwittingly doing. By drawing people off Christ onto their rules and visions, they were cutting the branch from the vine, offering a fancier life while severing it from its only source.

Can I grow as a Christian without belonging to a church? Not as God intends. Paul says the body grows through its joints and ligaments, the connections between believers. A Christian was never meant to be a severed limb. Other believers teach you, correct you, pray for you, need your gifts, and show you Christ in ways you would never see alone. There may be seasons when you are cut off by illness, persecution or distance, and God is not limited then. But if you are able, join yourself to a faithful local church, and be known there. Holding fast to the Head and staying joined to the body go together.

In everyday life. Your growth is not a technique to master but the fruit of staying joined to Jesus, in faith, his word and prayer, while God supplies the increase. Think of one believer through whom God has fed you, and tell them.

For worship. Every ounce of life in the church flows down from her risen Lord. He feeds the smallest member through the plainest joint: a word from a friend, a prayer in a kitchen, a sermon in a small hall. The Head who was crowned with thorns now crowns his body with a growth that is God’s own, and no member joined to him has ever been starved.

verseByVerse.quote: If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations— “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” (referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If with Christ you died. The if is not a doubt but a settled fact: since you died with Christ. The elemental spirits (stoicheia, as in v. 8) are the basic governing principles and powers of the old order: the whole system of religious rules and the forces behind it. United to Christ in his death (2:11–12), you were severed from that old regime and released from its authority, for death dissolves every old bond (Romans 7:1–6). The elemental rules have no more claim on you than a master has on a slave who has died.

In the flow. Verse 20 begins the last paragraph of the chapter, and it opens with “If with Christ you died”, where if means since. Colossians 3:1 will open with its partner: “If then you have been raised with Christ”. The two belong together. Here Paul shows what your death with Christ frees you from, man-made rules; there he shows what your resurrection with him frees you for, a life set on Christ above.

Submit to regulations. “Submit to regulations” (dogmatizō) means to be subjected to decrees. To take up that world’s regulations again is to behave as if you were still alive in the world, as if the death had never happened. It is a freed slave voluntarily walking back into the slave quarters and picking up his old chains.

Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch. The slogans of the false teachers, and their character is plain: every one a prohibition, a religion of forbiddings, and pettily piled up, rules multiplying, each stricter than the last. Touch is lighter than handle, so even the faintest contact is banned.

Things that all perish. Then Paul lets the air out of the whole thing. Food and drink are used up and gone, and cannot touch the soul: as the Lord said, what goes into the stomach does not defile the heart (Mark 7:18–19).

According to human precepts and teachings? From Isaiah 29:13, quoted by Jesus against the Pharisees, who taught as doctrines the commandments of men (Mark 7:7). Human rules, not God’s commands. Rules God never gave cannot bind a soul God has freed.

An appearance of wisdom. They look impressive and spiritual: wise, rigorous, deeply devoted. The fasting looks like devotion, the strict rules like holiness, the severity like depth. That is exactly their danger: a convincing surface with no reality beneath. And rules appeal to the heart for a reason: they can be measured. I can tick them off, compare myself with others and feel I have earned my place, which is religion used to save myself. But no one keeps even God’s own commands perfectly; the only obedience that ever earned a place is Christ’s, and God counts it to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). The irreligious person who sees through that pride is right about the pride, and he needs the same Christ, who alone can make the proud and the careless clean.

Self-made religion. “Self-made religion” (ethelothrēskia) is will-worship: worship invented by one’s own will, worship a man chooses for himself rather than worship God commands. The word is not found in any earlier Greek writing we have, and Paul may have coined it; either way it exposes the root: self-will dressed up as devotion.

Of no value. For all the show, the system fails at the one thing it claims to do: it cannot curb sin. Rules cannot change the heart. They may restrain behaviour outwardly, but they feed pride and leave sinful desires untouched. Starve the body, and the flesh (the sinful nature) does not die; it grows fat on pride, swelling with self-righteous satisfaction in its own discipline. Rules may even inflame the very sin they forbid (Romans 7:5–8). Only union with Christ, dead and risen, defeats the flesh (3:1–5).

Weeds cut at ground level. Such rules are like cutting weeds off at ground level: the garden looks tidy for a day, but the roots are alive and the weeds come straight back. Only Christ digs out the root. The cure for sin is not a tighter rule book; it is a living Saviour. You have died and been raised with him, so the way forward is not to climb back under the rules but to hold fast to the Head and live the new life from above, where Christ is seated (3:1; Romans 8:13; Galatians 5:16).

Where Christians differ: rules for holiness. Many churches add rules beyond Scripture: no alcohol, no dancing, strict dress codes, as tests of holiness. This commentary’s view: Christians may make wise personal choices and churches may give wise counsel, but when human rules are made a test of spirituality or bound on others’ consciences, they become self-made religion. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and nothing is to be required beyond his word (the Westminster Confession 20.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2). The power to defeat sin is found in Christ, not in rules.

Does this make fasting and self-discipline pointless? No. Jesus expected his disciples to fast (Matthew 6:16–18), Paul disciplined his body and kept it under control (1 Corinthians 9:27), and bodily training is of some value (1 Timothy 4:8). What Paul condemns is rules imposed as the way to holiness or acceptance with God. Discipline as a means of growth, done in faith, is good.

So how do I actually fight a sin I keep falling into? Not by rules alone, though wise boundaries can help: if you know you are weak, do not walk into temptation (Romans 13:14). The heart of the fight is Christ. Remember that you died with him and were raised with him, so sin is no longer your master (Romans 6:11–14). Set your mind on things above, where he is (3:1–2). Put sin to death by the Spirit, not by willpower alone (Romans 8:13): pray, confess it honestly, bring it into the light with a trusted believer (James 5:16), fill your mind with his word, and feed on his love. The flesh is starved most effectively when the soul is feasting on Christ. And if you have fallen again, do not conclude that you are lost: hating the sin and still fighting it is itself the Spirit’s work in you (Galatians 5:17), so go straight back to Christ, for your standing rests on him, not on your record.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,<sup>2</sup>that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,<sup>3</sup>in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.<sup>4</sup>I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.<sup>5</sup>For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.<sup>6</sup>Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him,<sup>7</sup>rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.<sup>8</sup>See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.<sup>9</sup>For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,<sup>10</sup>and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.<sup>11</sup>In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ,<sup>12</sup>having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.<sup>13</sup>And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses,<sup>14</sup>by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands.
