This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.<sup>15</sup>He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.<sup>16</sup>Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.<sup>17</sup>These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.<sup>18</sup>Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,<sup>19</sup>and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.<sup>20</sup>If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations—<sup>21</sup>“Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch”<sup>22</sup>(referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings?<sup>23</sup>These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.

3.title: Set Your Minds on Things Above: The Old and the New
3.overview: Chapter 2 showed that rules cannot defeat sin. Chapter 3 gives the real cure: union with the risen Christ. Raised with him, believers set their minds on things above, where he reigns; their life is hidden with him and will appear with him in glory (vv. 1–4). So they put the old sins to death and put on the new self, in a people where Christ is all, and in all (vv. 5–11). As God’s chosen and beloved, they clothe themselves in Christ’s own character, with his peace ruling and his word dwelling richly among them (vv. 12–17). Then Christ’s lordship enters the home: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters, each with a duty, and those with power given the harder command (3:18–4:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Set Your Minds on Things Above
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything that follows rests on these four verses. Believers have died and been raised with Christ, so their minds are set where he is. Their real life is kept safe with him, out of sight for now, until he appears and they appear with him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hidden Life and the Security of the Believer

Colossians 3:3 is one of the plainest statements in the New Testament of the believer’s security. The Christian’s life is kept in the safest place there is: with Christ, in God. Reformed teaching therefore grounds assurance not in the believer’s performance but in where he is: in Christ, kept by God, where nothing can reach the life that matters.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were told their spiritual safety depended on handling the angels rightly, keeping the festivals and food laws, and reaching special spiritual states. Paul says their life is hidden with Christ in God, where none of that can touch it. Now: A Christian whose sense of security rises on good days of prayer and falls on days of failure needs the same word. His life is kept by the One stronger than everything that threatens it.

verseByVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Colossians 3 shows the true way to holiness, after chapter 2 tore down the false way of rules. The power for a holy life is not a stricter regime but union with Christ, and from that union flow a new mind, new conduct, a new worship and a new household. The whole chapter answers one question: what does a person do with his days once Christ has become his life?

Raised with Christ. The “if” turns the argument. All through chapter 2 Paul pulled down the rule-bound, ascetic religion of the false teachers, ending with the verdict that its rules are of no value against the flesh (2:23). Now comes the positive alternative, built on two halves of one truth: died with Christ, you are free from the world’s rules (2:20); raised with him, you seek what is above. The cure for a failed religion of rules is a new direction: not down into severity to the body, but up toward the risen Christ. The “if” means since, as in 2:20: Paul is not asking whether they belong to Christ; he is building his command on the fact that they do.

Raised already. “Raised with Christ” is not a promise about the distant future but a statement of what has already happened. United to Christ (2:12), you share his resurrection now. God counts you as one with his Son, so that his death for sin and his rising to new life are reckoned as yours (Romans 6:4–5). And the Spirit who raised Jesus now lives in you, giving a new heart that loves God and wants what is above (Romans 8:11; Ezekiel 36:26). The false teachers urged the Colossians to climb to heaven through fasting, visions and the worship of angels. Paul says they need not climb a single rung, for in Christ they are already raised and seated there (Ephesians 2:5–6). Every other way is a ladder. The gospel is the news that someone came down the ladder, took hold of you, and carried you up.

Seek the things above. The verb (zēteō) is present tense: keep seeking, keep pursuing, keep making Christ’s kingdom your aim and your treasure. It is the reorientation of a life’s desires, aims and ambition around the risen Christ, because where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:21).

Seated at the right hand. Paul locates the things above with precision. They are not a vague spiritual atmosphere; they are wherever Christ is, and Christ is seated at the right hand of God, the place of supreme honour and authority promised in the psalm the New Testament quotes more than any other (Psalm 110:1). And he is seated. The old priests stood day after day because their work was never finished; this priest sat down because his was (Hebrews 10:11–12). The powers the false teachers feared are disarmed beneath his feet (2:15), and the crucified one reigns there as your representative and advocate (Romans 8:34). The same Jesus who hung on the cross bearing your debt now sits on the throne of heaven, not as a stranger to us, but as our head, our brother and our high priest, with our names on his heart. Our head is there, so our hearts belong there.

How do I actually seek the things above in an ordinary day? Begin by deliberately turning your attention to where Christ is: a few minutes with Scripture and prayer in the morning, before the day’s demands start talking. Then carry one question into the day: what does the risen Lord want done here, and how would he value this? When you make a decision about money, time or ambition, ask which choice treats Christ’s kingdom as the treasure. Gather with his people on the Lord’s Day, where heaven’s realities are preached and sung. And when you notice your heart has drifted to anxiety or getting, do not berate yourself; simply turn it back. Seeking is a direction you keep returning to, not a feeling you must sustain.

In everyday life. Before your day fills with earthly concerns, lift your heart to Christ seated in heaven. Then, at some point in the afternoon when the pressure is highest, stop for ten seconds and remember where he is: not anxious, not hurried, not wondering how it will turn out, but seated. Your work today is real and it matters. It is not, however, holding up the universe. Someone else is doing that, and he has sat down.

verseByVerse.quote: Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set your minds. Verse 2 deepens verse 1. The verb (phroneō) means the settled bent of the mind, the whole orientation of a person’s thinking and valuing, the same word Paul uses when he says have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus (Philippians 2:5). Seeking engages the will; setting the mind engages the thoughts. There is nothing above to set the mind on but Christ, and Christ is enough to fill a mind for ever. We are invited to think about the most glorious being there is, and to find that he has been thinking about us first.

Not on earthly things. The counterweight is deliberate. Earthly things here are not the earth itself, which God made and called good, but the perishable things treated as ultimate: the food rules and regulations of 2:21–22, and the sinful desires Paul is about to name in 3:5. The ascetic and the sensualist look like opposites, but they have the same address: one is preoccupied with what he must not touch, the other with what he must have, and neither is looking at Christ.

The expatriate. Think of a man working abroad. He does his job well and is kind to his neighbours, but his heart is set on home: he is not crushed when the local currency falls, and he does not mistake the posting for his life. So it is with the Christian, for our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ (Philippians 3:20).

If my thoughts drift constantly, am I failing at this? No; the command assumes drift, which is why it is in the present tense: keep setting. A mind is set the way a compass needle is set, not by never moving but by always swinging back to north. You do not fix your thoughts by grim concentration. You feed them. What you read, watch, scroll and talk about will shape what your mind returns to when it is idle, so give it things worth returning to: Scripture memorised, a psalm sung, a truth about Christ turned over on the commute. Wandering is the condition of every believer this side of glory. The question is where you come back to.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you have died. “For” gives the ground beneath the command. Why seek the things above? Because that is where your life actually is. The verb is past and finished. In union with Christ’s death, the old you, the self that belonged to the world and lived for its things, has died and been buried with him (2:20; Romans 6:2–7). This is not a claim that you feel dead to sin; God counts you as having died with Christ when he died: sin’s right to rule you and the law’s sentence against you were dealt with there, once for all. The old master can still shout, but he no longer owns you.

Hidden with Christ in God. The verb (kryptō) is in the perfect tense: it has been hidden, and it stays hidden. It carries two senses. First, hidden means safe. Your life is stored away in the most secure place in the universe, and it is double-wrapped: your life in Christ, and Christ in God. No one can reach in and snatch it, for no one will snatch them out of my hand, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand (John 10:28–29). Second, hidden means concealed. Your true life and glory are not on display yet, and for now they look ordinary and often weak. But hidden is not lost. It is stored, waiting for the day it will be unveiled (v. 4).

Treasure in a strongroom. Your real life is not held in your own trembling hands; on your worst day, when you feel like a failure and a fraud, it is still safe, because it hangs not on your performance but on Christ. And you may look ordinary, ageing and weary, like an acorn in winter ground that looks nothing like the oak, but the glory is real and it is coming: we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared (1 John 3:2). You do not have to achieve your life, guard it or prove it.

What it does not mean. “You have died” does not mean you can no longer sin or feel temptation. The rest of the chapter commands believers to put sin to death precisely because it is still active in them. What died was your old identity and its claim on you, not every trace of its habits.

If my life is hidden and safe, why does it so often feel fragile? Because you are looking at the part that is not hidden: your moods, your health, your circumstances, your recent failures. Those are real and they do fluctuate. But Paul is not describing how your life feels; he is describing where it is kept. A deposit in a bank vault does not become less safe because the depositor has a bad week. When you feel fragile, do not try to feel stronger. Look away from yourself to the place where your life is, and remember who is holding it. Assurance grows by attending to Christ, not by taking your own temperature.

For worship. The God who hid Moses in the cleft of the rock while his glory passed by has hidden us in his Son, and the Son in himself. Our Saviour went into the darkness of the tomb so that our lives might be hidden in a place no darkness can reach. His keeping is stronger than our weakness, and he has never lost one whom he hid.

verseByVerse.quote: When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ who is your life. The pattern is hidden now, revealed then. Paul does not say Christ merely gives us life, as though it were a gift we hold apart from him. He says Christ is our life: its source, its substance and its centre. Your pardon is his death, your righteousness is his obedience, your new heart is the work of his Spirit, your future is his glory. So Paul could say, it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me (Galatians 2:20). This is the final answer to a heresy that offered Christ plus something: Christ is not part of the package. He is the whole of it.

Appears. The word (phaneroō) means to be brought out of hiding into open view. Now he is unseen by the world; but a day is fixed when he will be revealed in glory before the whole creation. Mark the word when, not if. It will be one appearing, public and visible to all (Matthew 24:27, 30–31). This commentary does not expect a secret rapture before it, since the New Testament describes Christ’s coming for his people and his coming in glory as one open event; but believers who do expect one long for the same appearing, and that shared hope is Paul’s point.

Appear with him in glory. Your destiny is bound to Christ’s. You, who look like nothing much now, will share his glory. We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2; Romans 8:17–19). He will not be ashamed of us on that day. He who is our life will show us to the universe as his own, robed in a glory he won and gives away.

The hinge of the chapter. Having settled who you are and who you will be, Paul draws the conclusion: put to death therefore (v. 5). Future glory is the great motive for present holiness. Everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure (1 John 3:3). People who know where they are going start dressing for it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will become divine or be absorbed into God. They will share his glory as glorified human beings, body and soul, still creatures, still themselves, made perfectly like their Lord. Nor does it mean that glory waits until the end with nothing before it. Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23); the soul does not sleep. But the full public unveiling, with resurrected bodies, comes when he appears.

What will glory actually be like? Scripture gives us more than we often notice. It will be a body raised imperishable, never again sick, ageing or dying (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). It will be a character finally free from sin, so that you will love God and others without the drag you feel now. It will be seeing Christ face to face, which is the heart of it. And it will be shared: you will appear with him and with all his people, in a renewed creation (Romans 8:21). Glory does not mean becoming a spotlight; it means being made fully what God always meant you to be, and reflecting his light without distortion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Put to Death, Put Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because of who they now are, believers put to death the sins of the appetites and strip off the sins of the temper and the tongue. They have already put off the old self and put on the new, which God is renewing in his image, and in that new humanity the old divisions no longer count.
verseByVerse.theology:
Putting to Death What Christ Has Already Condemned

John Owen’s Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers is the classic Reformed treatment of Colossians 3:5, and his principle, “be killing sin, or it will be killing you,” follows Paul closely. Mortification (putting sin to death) is not the harsh self-punishment of the Colossian teachers that Paul has just condemned (2:23). It is applying the cross, by the Spirit, to particular sinful desires: these belong to the old self that died with Christ, and by the Spirit I put them to death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were offered a programme of outward denial to deal with the flesh, and Paul says it has no value against it (2:23). True mortification differs not in severity but in its source: union with the crucified and risen Christ. Now: A Christian fighting sin by willpower alone is using the wrong weapons. The fight is real, and it is fought in prayer, by the Spirit, among God’s people, with the cross as its ground.

verseByVerse.quote: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put to death therefore. “Therefore” reaches back to verses 1–4: become what you are. You died to the old life as a finished fact (v. 3); now you put to death its lingering expressions, daily. This is not the asceticism Paul has just condemned, rules imposed from outside that cannot touch the flesh (2:23), but the killing of sin from the inside, by people already dead and raised with Christ.

The violent word. The verb (nekroō) means kill, execute. Not manage, not tame: kill. Sin is an enemy to be executed, not a pet to be domesticated. The killing is done not by rules that punish the flesh but by the Spirit: if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live (Romans 8:13). John Owen, the great Puritan, put it in a sentence his readers never forgot: be killing sin, or it will be killing you.

A sentence already passed. Why can a believer fight sin with hope instead of despair? Because the enemy he is told to execute has already been condemned. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, God condemned sin in the flesh (Romans 8:3), and our old self was crucified with him (Romans 6:6). At the cross sin lost its right to rule us; in the daily fight it loses its grip. The believer is carrying out a sentence already passed and paid for, by the power of Christ’s risen life within him.

What is earthly in you. Literally, your members which are on the earth: the sinful desires and habits of the old life that still cling to the believer and work through his body. Paul is not calling the body evil; he is naming the places where sin still has a foothold and saying that the foothold must go.

From the act to the root. The four words dig from the outward act down to the inward root. Sexual immorality (porneia) is the broad word for every sexual act outside marriage: the outward deed. Impurity (akatharsia) moves inward to the defiled imagination and the polluted inner life. Passion (pathos) goes deeper, to the ungoverned lust that masters a person. Evil desire (epithymia kakē) reaches the very bottom: the wrong craving of the heart itself. Sin runs all the way down into what the heart wants, which is why rules alone can never cure it: they trim the deed and leave the desire alive.

Covetousness, which is idolatry. Covetousness (pleonexia) is greed, the restless craving for more. Why call it idolatry? Because to covet is to set the heart’s supreme desire and trust on something other than God, looking to created things for the security and worth only God can give. Whatever a man treasures above God is his functional god, and the greedy man bows at an altar he would never admit was there (Ephesians 5:5; Matthew 6:24). It climaxes the list because it lays bare the idolatry beneath all these sins, and it wears a respectable coat. Take care, said Jesus, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions (Luke 12:15).

How do I actually put a sin to death? Name it plainly, as the enemy it is, not as a weakness or a phase. Refuse it at the first stirring, not after you have entertained it for an hour. Starve it: remove what feeds it, whether that is a device in the bedroom, a route home past the shop, a friendship that always ends the same way, or the shopping app on your phone. Flee the situations where you know you fall (2 Timothy 2:22). Bring it into the light with a trusted believer. And do all of it leaning on the Spirit’s power and on Christ’s finished work, not gritting your teeth to earn God’s favour, but fighting from a favour already yours. The fight is from acceptance, never for it.

What if I have been fighting the same sin for years and keep losing? Then you are in a real war, which is itself a sign of life; the dead do not fight. Long struggle does not prove you are not a Christian. What would be alarming is making peace with the sin. So keep going, but look at how you are fighting. Have you been fighting alone and in secret? Tell someone. Have you been fighting the act and ignoring the desire underneath? Ask what the sin promises you, and seek that in Christ. Have you been fighting from guilt instead of grace? Go back to the cross every time you fall, at once, not after a period of self-punishment. The Spirit is patient, and he finishes what he begins (Philippians 1:6).

Is this not simply a repressive view of sex? No, it is a high one. The world often treats sex as an appetite like hunger, to be satisfied wherever it can be, and then wonders why so many people end up used and lonely. Scripture treats it as a gift so precious that God fences it within the lifelong promise of marriage, where two people give themselves wholly and are not discarded (Genesis 2:24; Hebrews 13:4). The command to kill immorality is not God frowning at pleasure. It is the Maker guarding a gift from the misuse that ruins it, and guarding people from being treated as things.

For worship. Covetousness grasps, and the Son of God let go. Though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He was offered all the kingdoms of the world and would not bow to get them; he carried our idolatries to the cross, and now his Spirit finishes in us what he finished there. When Christ himself is our life, the idols lose their grip, because we have found the one treasure they were all pretending to be.

verseByVerse.quote: On account of these the wrath of God is coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wrath of God is coming. Between the two lists of sins (vv. 5 and 8) Paul gives the reason they must be killed: the wrath of God is real and on its way, with a day of judgment fixed, and that makes the fight urgent (Romans 1:18; Ephesians 5:6).

What God’s wrath is. It is not a bad temper or a petty loss of control, God flying off the handle. It is the settled, holy, righteous opposition of a perfectly good God to all evil: his just, judicial response to sin. Far from being a flaw, it is a mark of his goodness and flows from his holiness: he is of purer eyes than to see evil (Habakkuk 1:13). A God indifferent to the abuse of children, the exploitation of the poor and the betrayal of a marriage would be no good God. Those who have been badly wronged often understand this most quickly.

One appearing, two outcomes. Paul has just written of the day when Christ appears (v. 4), and now of the wrath that is coming. They are one event. God will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and he has given assurance of it by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The appearing that will be glory for those whose life is hidden in Christ will be judgment for those who refused him, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). For some his face will be the face of their life; for others, the face of their Judge.

A textual note. Many manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add the words upon the sons of disobedience, which appear in the parallel at Ephesians 5:6. Whether or not Paul wrote them here, the meaning is the same: God’s wrath falls on those who persist in these sins without repentance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that believers will face God’s wrath. Christ bore it for them in their place, so that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1), and we wait for Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10). There was a day when the wrath of God against these very sins came down, and it did not fall on the guilty. It fell on the Lamb of God, who drank the cup to the bottom, so that for everyone who trusts in him, not one drop remains. He was forsaken so that we would never be. The point is not to frighten Christians about their standing but to show them how serious sin is, and why they cannot treat it lightly.

If Christ has taken the wrath for me, why should this warning move me? Because it shows you what your sin really is and what it cost. A man who has been pulled from a burning house does not wander back in to collect a souvenir. The warning keeps you from treating as harmless the very things that brought the cross on your Saviour. And it is a test: a person who carries on in these sins with no fight and no grief, while claiming to be safe, should ask honestly whether he has ever been rescued at all. For the believer who is fighting, the warning drives him not into fear but back to the shelter, where the wrath has already fallen on someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once walked. Paul is not claiming that every person outside Christ commits every sin on the list, or that all are equally vile. People apart from Christ differ enormously, and many are outwardly decent and restrained, because God’s common grace holds back the full flood of sin in the world. He is saying that this was the Colossians’ own former road, and that these sins are the direction a heart turned away from God naturally runs, whether or not every sin shows in every person.

You too. There is tenderness in those two words. They keep the believer humble, for he was once where others are still trapped, and grateful, for grace lifted him out. Such were some of you, Paul tells the Corinthians, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:11; Titus 3:3–5).

Once, but now. Once sets up the pivot of the next verse: but now. This letter has already said what stands between the two. You, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds, he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him (1:21–22). The way out of the old country was not a better effort but a body nailed to a cross. That was your old country. You have emigrated, and he paid for your papers. Do not move back.

If I was a Christian from childhood, does “once” apply to me? Yes, though it may look different. You may never have walked in open sexual sin or drunkenness, and that is a mercy to thank God for, not a credential to boast in. But Paul’s point is that the heart apart from grace is turned from God at the root, and that was true of you too. The pride, self-will and quiet idolatries of a well-behaved child are the same country with tidier streets. Grace lifted you out as surely as it lifted the man with the dramatic story, only earlier, and that is more grace, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put them all away. Where verse 5 said kill, treating sin as an enemy to be executed, verse 8 says take off (apotithēmi), like stripping off filthy clothes and throwing them aside. And “all” sweeps up both lists. The first list (v. 5) was sexual and greedy, the sins of the appetites; this one is relational and verbal, the sins of the temper and the tongue. And here is the uncomfortable point: these are the sins respectable church members can commit for decades without anyone calling it sin.

Anger, wrath, malice. Two words for temper, and many read them as two kinds. Anger (orgē) is the settled, smouldering kind: the grudge nursed, the banked fire of resentment that will not go out. Wrath (thymos) is the sudden kind: the flare-up, the outburst that explodes and subsides. Beneath both lies malice (kakia): the ill will itself, the meanness of spirit that wishes another person harm, or is quietly pleased when harm comes to him.

Slander and obscene talk. Slander (blasphēmia) is injurious speech that runs a person down; it is the same word used for blasphemy against God, and the overlap is not an accident, because to tear down someone made in God’s image is to speak against his Maker (James 3:9). Obscene talk (aischrologia) is foul, shameful, abusive speech. The tongue is the drain through which the heart empties, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:34).

Reviled, he did not revile. Every sin on this list was once aimed at one man. False witnesses slandered him, the high priest called his words blasphemy, and passers-by hurled abuse at the cross (Mark 14:55–65; 15:29–32). And when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). He bore our sins in his body on the tree (2:24), the sins of our mouths among them. The anger and slander we are told to put away were carried by him, and his silence under them is the pattern of the new self.

How do I tell slander from a legitimate warning? Scripture itself names real dangers and sometimes real names (2 Timothy 4:14), so not every negative word is slander. Ask three questions. Is it true? Slander trades in falsehood and in the exaggeration that makes a story more interesting; a warning is accurate. Is it necessary, for a good end? A warning protects someone from harm; slander only wounds, entertains, or makes the speaker look better. And why are you saying it, and to whom? A faithful warning is given reluctantly, in love, usually to the person who can do something about it; slander is told with relish, behind the back, to anyone who will listen.

Is all anger sinful? No. Jesus looked around at the Pharisees with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5), and Paul says be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26). Anger at real wrong can be righteous: anger at cruelty, at injustice, at the abuse of the weak. What Paul tells us to put away is selfish anger, the kind that is about my rights, my comfort and my pride, and that wants to hurt. It is the kind that sits beside malice and slander in the list. A useful test: righteous anger is about God’s honour and other people’s good, is slow to arise, and moves toward putting things right. Sinful anger is about me, is quick, and moves toward getting even.

How do I put these off when I have tried to “just stop” so many times? Not by white-knuckle willpower in your own strength; that is the chapter 2 asceticism that cannot conquer the flesh. Putting off always comes paired with putting on (vv. 10, 12). You overcome a sin not by leaving a hole where it was but by replacing it: take off anger and put on compassion; take off slander and speak well of people behind their backs; take off lying and become a teller of truth. Sin is expelled not by a vacuum but by a stronger affection. And it flows from who you already are: you strip off these sins because you have already put off the old self (v. 9). It is the work of a lifetime, done by the Spirit. The old clothes feel familiar and you keep reaching for them, so you keep taking them off, day after day, while God keeps remaking you. Progress, not yet perfection (Ephesians 4:22–24).

In everyday life. Pick the one sin on this list your family would name if asked about you, and next time it rises replace it with its opposite. And if the words have already come out, go back and apologise without explanation. A sentence that begins I’m sorry, but is not an apology.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not lie to one another. One more sin of speech, and not only bald untruths but half-truths, spin, flattery, broken promises, exaggeration, and the whole family of deceit. “To one another” presses it home: lying poisons the trust that holds the new community together (Ephesians 4:25). The devil is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44); to deceive is to wear the old father’s likeness.

Put off the old self. The old self, literally the old man, is not merely a bundle of bad habits but the whole person you used to be in Adam: your old identity under the reign of sin, together with its practices. Scripture says it was crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6). Both verbs here, put off and put on, are most naturally read as completed past acts, done decisively at conversion: the old self was taken off once for all, and the daily putting away of his leftover habits (vv. 5, 8) simply lives out a change that has already happened. Like a discharged soldier, he may still reach for the old uniform, but its officers cannot give him orders (Romans 6:14).

Put on the new self. This is the new person you now are in Christ, the new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), your settled identity in union with the risen Lord. And it is corporate as well as personal, which is why verse 11 says the old divisions of race and class now fall away. Christ is forming not only new individuals but a new humanity.

Being renewed in knowledge. Yet the new self, already put on, is not static. The tense changes to the continuous: it is being renewed, made new day by day. And it is passive, because God is the one renewing it (2 Corinthians 4:16; Romans 12:2). The decisive change is done; the transformation is ongoing. And it is renewal in knowledge (epignōsis): not the secret knowledge the false teachers offered, but the personal knowledge of God as he really is in Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (2:3). Knowing God rightly is itself transforming.

After the image of its creator. This reaches back to Genesis. Man was made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27). The image was defaced, though not erased, by the fall, and it is now being restored in Christ, who is himself the image of the invisible God (1:15). To be renewed after the Creator’s image is to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29; Ephesians 4:24). Salvation is not self-improvement. It is new creation, God stamping his own likeness on the soul again. The Creator did not discard the ruined portrait, but sent his Son to bear its ruin and to make it new, and one day the restoration will be complete, and every one of his people will bear his likeness without a blemish.

Where Christians differ: is it ever right to lie, for example to protect life? The Hebrew midwives deceived Pharaoh, and Rahab hid the spies. Some Christians hold that deceiving people set on murder is not the lying Scripture forbids, since God dealt well with the midwives (Exodus 1:20). Others, with Augustine and Calvin, hold that every lie is a sin, though God may honour the faith and courage behind it. This commentary’s view: the first reading is more likely. The ninth commandment forbids false witness against a neighbour, and those bent on murder have no right to the truth they would use to kill; Rahab, and those who hid Jews from the Gestapo, stood in the same place. But such cases are rare and extreme, godly believers have differed on them, and they are not the subject of this verse. The command here is about trust among believers: Christians should be people whose word can always be relied on, in the small things as in the large.

What counts as lying in everyday life? More than most of us admit. The excuse that is not quite the reason. The figure rounded up on the claim form. Saying you are fine when you mean you are not, to avoid a conversation that needs to happen. Letting a false impression stand because it flatters you. The CV that implies more than it says. Agreeing to do something you have no intention of doing. Truthfulness does not require you to say everything you think; silence and tact are not lies. But whatever you do say should be true, and you should not set out to make anyone believe what is false.

verseByVerse.quote: Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not Greek and Jew. In the new self of verses 9–10, the new humanity Christ is forming, the old human divisions disappear. Paul names the great dividing lines of his world. Race: Greek and Jew, the deepest divide of all. Religion: circumcised and uncircumcised, the mark that had separated the covenant people from everyone else.

Barbarian, Scythian. Culture. A barbarian was anyone whose speech sounded like babble to Greek ears, the ancient way of calling someone uncivilised. And the Scythians, nomads from north of the Black Sea, were the Greek byword for savagery. Paul reaches for the most extreme example he can. Even they are welcome as equals in Christ.

Slave, free. Class. A slave was legally property, and slave and free seldom ate as equals. In the church they did. Philemon, a slave owner in this very congregation, was about to welcome back his slave Onesimus, who had probably run away and now came home with Tychicus, the bearer of this letter, as a beloved brother (4:9; Philemon 16).

Christ is all, and in all. Christ is all: everything, the sum and substance, the one thing that finally counts. And Christ is in all: the same Christ lives in every one of his people, Jew or Greek, slave or free, polished or rough, and that indwelling is what makes them one. He lives in each by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10), the same Christ in the Scythian and in the Pharisee. And the same Christ in whom all the fullness of God dwells (1:19) lives in plain, ordinary believers. Christ is in you, the hope of glory (1:27; Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 2:14–16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean cultural, ethnic or social differences simply disappear. A Jew remained a Jew and a slave remained a slave, and men and women remain men and women. Paul himself goes straight on to give different instructions to wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters (3:18–4:1). The differences are not erased but dethroned: they no longer decide a person’s worth, his standing before God, or his place in the family.

What does this look like in a church today? It means the businessman and the unemployed man share the bread and the cup as equals, and the elders are chosen for godliness, not for wealth or education or ethnicity. It means a congregation does not sort itself, without anyone deciding to, into tables of people who look alike. It means you take seriously a believer from another culture who prays and worships differently, as a brother and not a curiosity. And it means looking honestly at your own instincts: who do you naturally assume will be the most mature Christian in the room, and why? The world ranks; the church must not, because Christ does not.

For worship. Christ has made one people out of every kind of person, without flattening them into sameness. He broke down the dividing wall in his own flesh, and now the Jew and the Scythian kneel at the same table, the slave and the master call the same Father, and none of them has anything to boast in but him. Heaven will be full of every tribe and language and people and nation, every voice singing one name.
verseByVerse.note: Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were thought of as the most uncivilised of barbarians.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having stripped off the old, believers put on the new. Because God has already chosen and loved them, they clothe themselves in compassion, humility, patience, forgiveness and love, and let Christ’s peace, Christ’s word and Christ’s name govern their life together.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Virtues of the New Self as the Character of Christ

The virtues of 3:12–15 are a portrait of Christ himself. Sanctification is growing conformity to his image (Romans 8:29), and these are its features, not produced by moral effort alone but are the fruit of the Spirit in those united to Christ (Galatians 5:22–23).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian church mixed Jew and Greek, slave and free, people with very different habits of living together and quarrelling. In a world built on honour and revenge, humility and forgiveness looked strange. Now: They still do, and a church that truly puts on compassion, humility and forbearance will look unlike other communities, because these are the features of the One who was raised for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put on then. The clothing image continues: having stripped off the old sins (vv. 8–9), you get dressed in the character of Christ. The Christian life is never merely stopping the bad; it is clothing yourself with the good, daily, in the strength of the Spirit, acting in compassion and patience even before the feeling arrives. And Paul names who you are before he names a single virtue, with three titles that once belonged to Israel (Deuteronomy 7:6–8).

Chosen, holy, beloved. Chosen (eklektoi): God set his love on you and picked you out before you had done anything to deserve it, even before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). Holy: set apart as his treasured possession. Beloved: dearly loved, sharing the belovedness of his beloved Son, into whose kingdom he has transferred you (1:13). You do not put on these graces to become chosen and loved; you put them on because you already are, and the beloved can afford to love.

Compassionate hearts, kindness. The first garments are tender ones. Compassionate hearts is literally bowels of mercy, the ancient way of naming the deep, gut-level feeling that moves when someone else is in pain. Kindness (chrēstotēs) is that compassion turned into action. Compassion feels; kindness acts. Every one of these five virtues is a portrait of Christ, who was moved with compassion for the crowds because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36). He was kind to the outcast, humble enough to wash feet, meek before Pilate, and patient with disciples who never seemed to understand. He bore with us when we were unbearable, and he forgave us while we were driving in the nails.

Humility. Strikingly, this is the very word the false teachers had twisted into ascetic show (2:18, 23), but here it is the real thing: a right estimate of yourself before God, knowing you are a sinner saved by sheer grace and therefore above no one, so that in humility you count others more significant than yourselves (Philippians 2:3). It is not wallowing in self-hatred; that is self-absorption with a long face. Humility is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less.

Meekness, and patience. Meekness is not weakness. The Greeks could use the word for a wild horse broken and tamed, all its power still there but now under control. Meekness is strength under control: the gentleness of someone who could retaliate and chooses not to. Jesus was gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29), and he overturned the temple tables (John 2:15). Patience (makrothumia) is literally long-tempered: slow to anger, the same patience God shows to us, now worn toward others.

Bearing with one another. Bearing with one another means putting up with each other’s rough edges: the brother who talks too long, the sister who is always late, the personality that grates. Most church life is not about great wrongs. It is about small frictions, and love absorbs them without keeping a tally.

As the Lord has forgiven you. Then come the real wrongs, if one has a complaint against another. To forgive (charizomai, the verb built on the word for grace) is to release the debt, refusing the grudge and the revenge, just as God cancelled the record of debt that stood against you (2:14). The measure is as the Lord has forgiven you: freely, fully, at great cost, and while you were still his enemy (Romans 5:8–10). The forgiven man cannot easily hold a small debt over his brother (Matthew 18:21–35).

Must I forgive only when the other person apologises, or at once? Both, in different senses. The forgiving heart, the release of bitterness and the readiness to forgive, you must have at once, whether or not the other ever asks: whenever you stand praying, forgive (Mark 11:25). You never nurse a grudge until the offender grovels. But full reconciliation, the forgiveness spoken and received and the relationship restored, is completed when the other turns and repents (Luke 17:3). Restoration by its nature takes two. So forgive from the heart at once, holding nothing back, and stand ready, even eager, to welcome the other back the moment he turns.

Must I seek reconciliation with someone who abused me? No, not in the sense of resuming closeness or trust. Forgiving from the heart means letting go of revenge and handing the wrong over to God, who judges justly. It does not mean trusting a dangerous or unrepentant person, resuming contact, keeping the abuse secret, or giving up church discipline or the protection of the law; the governing authority is God’s servant to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4). Reporting a crime is not a failure to forgive. Reconciliation needs genuine repentance and changed behaviour shown over time, and safety comes first. A church that pressures a victim to reconcile has misunderstood both forgiveness and love.

Above all, love. Love is the outer robe pulled on over the whole wardrobe. It is not mainly a warm feeling or romance, for you can love a person you do not naturally like. It is a settled commitment of the will to seek another’s good at cost, regardless of merit or return.

Binds everything together. Love is the bond (syndesmos, a ligament, a belt, the same picture as the ligaments of the body in 2:19) that ties all the other graces, and the whole body, together. Without love the rest fall apart and ring hollow (1 Corinthians 13:1–3): humility without love becomes a pose, patience without love becomes cold endurance, and forgiveness without love becomes a transaction. And it is by this, Jesus said, that all people will know that you are my disciples (John 13:34–35).

What it does not mean. Forgiveness does not mean pretending a serious wrong did not happen. It names the wrong and then releases it; it does not always remove the consequences or immediately restore trust. Nor does bearing with one another mean tolerating anything at all; serious, persistent sin in the church is to be dealt with (Matthew 18:15–17), gently and with the aim of restoration.

How do I forgive when I still feel the hurt? Forgiveness is first a decision and then a process. You decide, before God, that you will not pursue revenge, will not keep bringing the matter up as a weapon, will not dwell on it to feed your resentment, and will not speak of it to others in order to damage the person. Then, when the memory returns with fresh pain, which it will, you make the same decision again and hand the wrong back to God. Feelings usually follow slowly. Pray for the person by name; it is hard to keep hating someone you pray for. And look again at the cross, where your own debt was paid.

verseByVerse.quote: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The peace of Christ. The peace of Christ is the peace he won and gives, the peace he made by the blood of his cross (1:20). It is first peace with God (Romans 5:1), and out of that comes the settled calm he leaves with his people, for peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you (John 14:27), and the peace that should reign between them.

Rule. The word (brabeuō) is the umpire’s word: the referee who makes the call and settles the contest, the official at the games who awarded the prize. So let Christ’s peace be the umpire in your heart. When you are torn, when relationships are strained, when a decision pulls you two ways, let his peace make the call, not anger, fear or self-will. Much of our turmoil comes from wanting to control what only God controls: how others see us, how things turn out. Christ’s peace gives us not that control but the One who has it.

Called in one body. This peace is part of your calling (1 Corinthians 7:15), into the one body of Christ, the one new humanity of verse 11. So this peace is not merely a private calm but the bond meant to keep the whole church one. In the context of verses 12–14, the umpire is most often deciding between a grievance and forgiveness.

Be thankful. A short command, but it is the first of three calls to thanksgiving in three verses (vv. 15, 16, 17), and thankfulness runs all through this letter (1:3, 12; 2:7; 4:2). It belongs beside peace, because gratitude crowds out the grumbling and grievance that breed strife and anxiety, and the person counting his mercies has no room left to nurse his complaints (Philippians 4:6–7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a feeling of peace is always a sign of God’s will, or that a feeling of unease always means no. Feelings can be mistaken, and a person can feel very peaceful about a sinful decision he has already made. The peace of Christ is not a mood to be consulted like an oracle. It governs decisions as we ask what would honour him and keep peace with God and with his people, tested always by Scripture.

So how do I let Christ’s peace decide something? Take a real decision or conflict. First ask what Scripture says about it; Christ’s peace never contradicts his word. Then ask which course keeps you at peace with God, with a clear conscience, and which course serves peace in the body of Christ rather than division. Ask whether a choice is being driven by fear, pride or the wish to win, and rule those out as referees. Pray, seek wise counsel from mature believers, and then act in faith. If two good options remain, you are free to choose, and the peace you have with God does not depend on choosing perfectly.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. In Ephesians the same overflow of teaching, singing and thanks follows the command to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18–20); here it follows the command to let Christ’s word dwell richly. The two are not rivals, for the Spirit fills a church by means of Christ’s word. In a letter answering teachers who promised fullness through visions and rules (2:8, 18), this is Paul’s reply: you have been filled in Christ (2:10), and you go on being filled as his word makes its home among you.

The word of Christ. The phrase the word of Christ is rare in Paul (elsewhere only Romans 10:17). It means the message of which he is the heart, the word of the truth, the gospel (1:5): not narrowly the words of Jesus printed in red, but the whole word that proclaims him, all of Scripture. Note the contrast: let Christ’s word fill you, not the philosophy and empty deceit of the false teachers (2:8).

Dwell in you richly. To dwell (enoikeō) means to take up residence, to make a home, not to drop by as an occasional visitor. So the word of Christ is to be a resident, not a guest, furnishing every room of the heart. And “in you” is plural: among you, as a church. Paul pictures a congregation saturated with Scripture. This is how the putting off and putting on actually happens: the mind is renewed (v. 10) as the word takes up rich residence within.

Teaching and admonishing. Teaching is the positive passing on of truth; admonishing (noutheteō) is the corrective side, warning and urging a brother away from wrong. Paul used the same pair of his own ministry (1:28). And mark one another: this is not the task of the official teachers alone but of every member, ordinary believers ministering the word to each other (Romans 15:14). It is done in all wisdom, knowing what word the moment needs. A verse thrown at a grieving friend can wound; the same verse given gently, at the right time, can heal.

Psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. The third overflow is song. Psalms are the inspired Old Testament songbook; hymns are songs of praise, perhaps like the great hymn to Christ in 1:15–20; and spiritual songs are songs prompted by the Spirit and full of his truth. Together they mean the full range of sung worship, and singing is itself a way of teaching one another (Ephesians 5:19).

With thankfulness. Literally, with grace, or gratitude, in your hearts: from the heart, not just the lips, and aimed at God, not at the audience.

Where Christians differ: what should churches sing? Some Reformed churches hold to exclusive psalmody, singing only the inspired Psalms in worship. They note that all three words, psalms, hymns and songs, appear in the titles of the Greek Psalter, and that only inspired songs are fit for God’s worship. Others sing a wide range of songs. This commentary’s view: the Psalms should have a central place in Christian worship, and many churches would be richer for singing far more of them. But the three terms most naturally describe a variety of songs, and the New Testament itself contains early Christian songs about Christ (1:15–20; Philippians 2:6–11; 1 Timothy 3:16). Churches may sing new songs that are faithful to Scripture and centred on Christ. The test is whether the word of Christ dwells richly in what is sung. Those who hold to exclusive psalmody do so out of reverence for God’s word, and they deserve to be honoured as brothers.

How do I know if a song is good to sing? Ask whether the word of Christ dwells in it richly. Is it true, faithful to Scripture in what it says about God, Christ, sin and grace? Is it about God more than about my feelings, though feelings are welcome? Does it teach something, so that singing it plants truth in the heart? Can a congregation actually sing it together, or is it a performance to watch? And does it lead to thankfulness? A song can be old or new, simple or complex. What matters is whether it carries Christ’s word to the heart.

For worship. The Word who was with God in the beginning became flesh and dwelt among us, and now he sends his word to dwell in us. He sang a hymn with his disciples on the night he was betrayed (Matthew 26:30), and walked out to Gethsemane very likely with the Passover psalms on his lips. He is the theme of every true song the church has ever sung, and he has put his own word in our mouths.

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever you do. This sums up the whole section. Word and deed are the two halves that cover the whole of life: not merely the religious parts, but the entire ordinary round: work, family, meals, rest. There is no secular corner walled off from Christ.

In the name of the Lord Jesus. To act in someone’s name is to act as his representative: under his authority, for his honour, in dependence on him. So to do everything in Jesus’ name is to drive the van, pay the bill, speak the word and do the task as Christ’s representative, for his glory, by his help, in a manner that would not shame his name. This consecrates the ordinary and constrains the sinful, for you cannot do in his name what dishonours it. So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Not a fence but a lordship. The false teachers wanted a fence of external rules: do not handle, do not taste, do not touch (2:21). Paul gives instead the lordship of Christ, reaching into every word and deed from the inside. Rules cover the situations someone thought of in advance; the name of the Lord Jesus covers the rest. And the human heart prefers the fence. A list of rules can be completed and ticked off, and then we feel safe and in control, with God in our debt. A Lord cannot be ticked off. He asks not for a list kept but for a life given, and the only way to give it gladly is to know that he gave his life first.

Giving thanks through him. The third call to thanksgiving closes the paragraph. Our thanks, like all our approach to God, comes to the Father through Christ, the one Mediator. This is the quiet final answer to the angel mediators of chapter 2: no other channel is needed, and none is allowed (1 Timothy 2:5). He did everything in his Father’s name: he worked in the carpenter’s shop, ate with sinners, slept in a boat and died on a cross, and all of it was worship. Now he takes our clumsy words and ordinary deeds, cleanses them, and carries them to the Father as offerings.

What about the parts of my life that seem to have nothing to do with Jesus? There are none that he has excused himself from. Filling in a spreadsheet, changing a nappy, mowing the lawn and watching a football match can all be done in his name, if they are done honestly, gratefully, and in a way that does not dishonour him. Ask two questions: could I thank God for this, and could I do it with Christ beside me? If yes, do it heartily and enjoy it as his gift. If no, the verse has just answered the question for you. And if there is a part of your life you would rather he did not see, that is the part this verse is most kindly aimed at.

In everyday life. Take an ordinary task today, the most ordinary one you have, and before you start it, say quietly: Lord Jesus, I do this as yours. Then do it well, and thank the Father for it when it is done. You may find that the task has not changed, but you have.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul now carries Christ’s lordship into the household, the basic unit of ancient society. Each member is addressed directly, as someone who answers to Christ, and those who hold power are given the harder command.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lordship of Christ in the Household

The household code shows that there is no corner of life outside Christ’s rule. The Lord praised in the hymn of chapter 1 is Lord of marriage, parenting and daily work; Abraham Kuyper’s “every square inch” is what 3:17 means in practice. A faithful spouse, a patient parent and an honest worker are living out their theology in its most concrete form.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In the Roman household the father held near-absolute legal power over children and slaves. Paul does not abolish the structure, but he fills it with a different spirit: love, not domination; encouragement, not provocation; justice, not exploitation. Now: The same witness shows wherever a Christian works honestly when no one is checking, treats employees fairly, or encourages a child instead of crushing him.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The household code. Now Paul brings the lordship of verse 17 into the home (3:18–4:1, as in Ephesians 5:21–6:9). Greek writers had household codes too, telling the head of a household how to manage his wife, children and slaves. Paul’s addresses the weaker parties, wives, children and slaves, directly, as responsible persons who stand before Christ for themselves. And it places real duties on the stronger parties, husbands, fathers and masters, all of whom are themselves under a Master. The phrase in the Lord, or its like, appears in almost every line. The household is not a little kingdom under the husband; it is an outpost of Christ’s kingdom, and everyone in it answers to him. On leadership and submission in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Wives, submit to your husbands. Submit (hypotassō) means to order or arrange oneself under, and the form is voluntary: the wife places herself under, freely. Nowhere in the New Testament are husbands told to make their wives submit. It is her own glad, chosen deference to her husband’s God-given role of loving leadership, the headship of Ephesians 5:23. And it is to your own husbands: one marriage, not women in general deferring to men in general. Positively, it is respect, support and trust: honouring and strengthening his leadership rather than competing with it, and, when a real decision must finally be made and they still differ, trusting his lead. Paul frames it as the reflection of something beautiful: the church’s glad submission to Christ (Ephesians 5:24).

As is fitting in the Lord: “do it for my sake”. A friend going abroad asks you to look after his elderly father: “Do it for me.” You really do help the father, but you do it for your friend. “In the Lord” works the same way (see on Ephesians 5:22). A wife really does follow her husband’s lead, but she does it for Christ’s sake. So it is an act of devotion to Christ, not a concession to a husband’s superiority, and it rests on Christ, not on shifting custom. And because it is for the Lord, it can never require what the Lord forbids: to sin, to lie, to hide abuse or to give up her faith (Acts 5:29). The same phrase that asks for her submission also guards her. See also As to the Lord in the Theological Dictionary.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the wife is inferior: she is fully equal in worth and standing before God, a fellow heir of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7; Galatians 3:28). Submission is a matter of role, never of value, as the Son is equal to the Father and yet gladly does his will. It does not mean slavish obedience: tellingly, Paul tells children and slaves to obey (vv. 20, 22) but tells wives to submit, the gentler word. It does not mean silence or having no voice: she is a strong helper and counterpart (Genesis 2:18) who speaks, advises and may freely disagree, and godly women in Scripture did exactly that (1 Samuel 25). It does not mean obeying into sin: if a husband demands what God forbids, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

Never a cover for abuse. Submission is not a licence for harshness or abuse, and the very next verse forbids the husband to be harsh. A wife is nowhere commanded to submit to cruelty or danger. Abuse, whether physical, sexual, emotional or financial, is a grave sin, and often a crime. A wife who is being abused should seek safety at once, and help from the church and the civil authorities; she is not failing to submit by doing so. Where there is abuse, the church must protect the victim and call the abuser to account, never preach submit to the one being harmed.

Where Christians differ: is a wife’s submission still God’s will? Egalitarian Christians (those who believe husband and wife share leadership equally, without distinct roles) read this in the light of the call to mutual submission (Ephesians 5:21) and Paul’s statement that in Christ there is no male and female (Galatians 3:28). They see the household instructions as a cultural accommodation tied to the ancient world, now outdated, or as mutual only. This commentary’s view: Paul grounds the wife’s submission in the Lord, and elsewhere in creation and in Christ’s relationship with the church (Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Corinthians 11:3, 8–9). That makes it permanent, not merely cultural. And Paul gives husbands a different command, to love, not to submit. But the wife’s submission is her willing response to her husband’s loving, sacrificial leadership, not a licence for him to dominate. It never requires a wife to sin or to endure abuse. Husband and wife are equal heirs of grace (1 Peter 3:7), with different callings in the one marriage. Egalitarian believers who hold their view from Scripture are brothers and sisters, and the debate should be carried on with charity.

What does it look like in an ordinary marriage? Most decisions in a healthy marriage are simply made together, by agreement, and headship and submission rarely have to come into play. But picture the genuine deadlock. They have prayed, talked it through and weighed it honestly: a move, a major purchase, a direction for the family. They still disagree, and a decision must be made. There the wife trusts and supports her husband’s leading rather than insisting on her own way or making him pay for it afterwards. Day to day it looks like speaking well of him in public and in private, backing his leadership instead of undercutting it in front of the children, and treating him with genuine respect (Ephesians 5:33). The model is Sarah (1 Peter 3:5–6): a woman of strength who freely honoured her husband, not a doormat who had lost her voice.

What if my husband is not a Christian, or does not lead at all? Peter addresses the first case directly: a believing wife may win an unbelieving husband without a word, by her conduct (1 Peter 3:1–2). Her submission is still in the Lord, so she never follows him into sin, and she keeps her own walk with Christ, her church and her conscience. In the second case, where a husband is passive, submission does not mean pretending he leads when he does not. She may lovingly ask him to take responsibility, encourage every step he takes, and pray for him, without either seizing the role in contempt or abandoning the family to drift. And she should not carry it alone: wise counsel from the church can help them both.

In everyday life. Wives, find one way today to honour your husband’s leadership, as to the Lord: a word of thanks, backing a decision you were not sure of. Husbands reading this verse: it was not written to you, and the moment you start quoting it at your wife you have already stopped obeying the next one.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Husbands, love your wives. The word is agapaō, the deliberate, self-giving love of verse 14. His parallel letter spells out the measure: love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). So headship is defined as headship by sacrifice, not by domination: he leads by giving himself away, and keeps on loving.

What love looks like. It is sacrificial, constant and active: it nourishes and cherishes her as a man cares for his own body (Ephesians 5:28–29). It is a husband who puts his wife’s good ahead of his own preferences, who provides and listens, who serves in small unglamorous ways, as the Lord himself knelt to wash feet (John 13:5), and who keeps loving her on the day she is hardest to love, because his love is a covenant, not a mood.

Do not be harsh. The word (pikrainō, from pikros, bitter) means do not be embittered: do not grow sharp or sour with your wife. Paul at once names love’s opposite, because it is the husband’s characteristic temptation: the strength of his position can curdle into domination, and small resentments can harden into a cold, critical spirit toward the one he should cherish most. And Peter adds a sobering reason: a husband who does not live with his wife in an understanding way finds his prayers hindered (1 Peter 3:7).

The familiar clothes of harshness. It wears many disguises: the cutting tone, the sarcasm, the criticism that is never satisfied, contempt, the short temper, silence used as a weapon, and the winning of every argument by sheer sharpness. Often it is the sin of the man who is pleasant with everyone else and saves his harshness for his wife. The cure is the character of verses 12–13: compassion, kindness, meekness, patience and a readiness to forgive. A wife was never given to her husband to be a target for his bitterness, but to be loved as Christ loves.

What do I do if I have been harsh with my wife? Confess it, first to God and then to her, plainly and without excuses: not I’m sorry you felt hurt, but I was harsh with you, and it was wrong. Ask her to tell you, honestly and without punishment, when it happens again, and receive it when she does. Look for the root: harshness usually grows out of an expectation she has failed to meet, or a pressure elsewhere you are taking out on her. Bring that to Christ. And if the harshness has become a pattern of control or intimidation, seek help from your pastor or a trusted counsellor at once. That is no longer a bad habit; it is a danger to her.

For worship. The love that defines a husband’s duty was first poured out on a bride who was nothing to look at. Christ loved the church when she was unfaithful, unlovely and in rags, and he gave himself up for her, to sanctify her, cleanse her and present her to himself in splendour. Every Christian husband is a small, flawed picture of the greatest Husband there is, and every Christian marriage points to the wedding supper of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children, obey. Paul speaks directly to the children, present when the letter was read aloud and real members of the covenant community. Obey (hypakouō) is built on the verb to hear, and it means to heed and do: not merely to feel respect but to act on what is said. For a young child it is glad, prompt obedience in the daily round, the nursery of discipleship where a little one first learns to submit to God. For the teenager the call remains, now expressed as honour and trust: keeping the household’s rules and receiving correction without rebellion.

In everything. The sweep is wide, but not absolute, for all human authority is held under God’s. The parallel reads obey your parents in the Lord (Ephesians 6:1), and a child is never bound to obey a parent who commands him to sin (Acts 5:29). But that exception is rare: for nearly every child on nearly every day it means obey, gladly, even when you do not see the reason.

Obedience and honour. For the grown child who has formed his own household, the word shifts. The duty to obey belongs to the years under the parental roof, but the duty to honour never expires; it is the first commandment with a promise (Ephesians 6:2; Exodus 20:12). The adult child no longer takes orders, but he never stops respecting and providing for his parents as they age (1 Timothy 5:4, 8).

For this pleases the Lord. Literally, this is well pleasing in the Lord. Above all because in obeying, a child walks in the footsteps of the Lord Jesus himself, the great obedient Son, who said I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me (John 6:38), and who became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:8). He was submissive to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51), so an obedient child bears the family likeness of the Son. And the child’s obedience to his parents is, underneath, obedience to God, who set them over him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean children must obey parents who command sin, or who abuse them; God’s authority is higher, and a child who is being harmed should tell a trusted adult. And it does not mean adult children must obey their parents in everything. They honour them, listen to them with respect, and care for them, but they make their own decisions before God, especially within their own marriages (Genesis 2:24).

What about a child whose parents are not Christians? The command still holds, and in fact it may shine brighter there. A Christian child or teenager in an unbelieving home is to obey and honour his parents in everything that is not sin, and his cheerful obedience can be one of the most powerful testimonies they ever see. Where a parent forbids something God commands, such as faith in Christ itself, the child must follow Christ, but he should do so respectfully and humbly, without contempt, and look for every lawful way to honour his parents at the same time.

In everyday life. Children, obey cheerfully today, the first time you are asked. And if you are grown, ring your parents this week, or visit, and ask what you can do for them. Honour does not retire.

For worship. The Lord of glory once had a bedtime. He learned his letters, carried water, swept the workshop and did what he was told, and every hour of that hidden obedience was pleasing to his Father. He obeyed perfectly where we have not, and his obedience is counted to every child of God who trusts him, so that the smallest believer in the house is clothed in the obedience of the eternal Son. He became a child so that children might become the sons and daughters of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers, do not provoke your children. The word (erethizō) means to irritate, exasperate, stir up to resentment. The parallel puts it sharply: do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4). As with the husband and the master, the one who holds the power is given the restraining word. It is addressed to fathers because they bear the chief responsibility for the home, but it applies to mothers as well. The ways to provoke are many: harshness, unfairness, favouritism, punishing in temper, hypocrisy, cold neglect.

Across the years. It looks different at each stage. A young child is provoked by a sharp tongue over the spilled cup, by anger out of proportion, by rules that change with the father’s mood; the good way is gentleness, clear boundaries held with warmth, and expectations that fit his age. The school-age child is provoked by constant criticism, comparison with a sibling and praise that never comes; the good way is to notice and encourage honest effort, and to discipline fairly and with reasons.

The teenager and the grown child. The teenager is provoked by a control that will not loosen as he grows, by being treated as a little boy, by endless lecturing, by belittling, and by because I said so where a reason was owed. The good way is to let trust and responsibility grow together, to listen and reason, and above all to point the young person to Christ rather than merely enforce a rulebook. Even a grown child can be provoked by a father who still dictates his choices; the good way now is to advise when asked, and to bless rather than control.

Lest they become discouraged. The word (athymeō) means to lose heart, to have the spirit go out of you. It shows as a little heart in tears and timidity; a school child who gives up trying, because I will never be good enough for him; a teenager whose discouragement erupts as rebellion or sinks into withdrawal and joyless compliance. Fathers are responsible for the spirit they create in the home.

The Father who sets the pattern. The earthly father is to father as God fathers his own: as a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him (Psalm 103:13). God disciplines, but he never crushes; he is firm and tender, the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named (Ephesians 3:14–15; Hebrews 12:7–11). And the Christian father parents as himself a dearly loved child of that Father, passing on the grace he has received.

Arms that blessed children. The Father’s heart toward children has been shown in a face (John 14:9). When the disciples tried to send them away, he was indignant and said, let the children come to me; do not hinder them. Then he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them (Mark 10:14, 16). He never treated a child as an interruption, and he kept some of his sternest words for anyone who causes a little one to stumble (Matthew 18:6). A father who wants to know how not to provoke his children has only to watch the Son with them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fathers should not discipline. They must; a father who never corrects his child does not love him (Hebrews 12:7–11; Proverbs 13:24). It means discipline must be loving, fair, controlled, and aimed at the child’s good, never at venting the father’s anger. And it never means violence that injures, terrifies or humiliates a child; that is abuse, not discipline.

Is it too late if I have provoked my children? No. One of the most powerful things a father can do is go to his child, whether he is six or forty-six, and say: I was wrong, I was too harsh, I am sorry, will you forgive me? Many grown children have waited their whole lives to hear it. It does not undo the past, but it often opens a door that has been shut for years, and it shows the child the gospel in a way no lecture could. Then change the pattern, with God’s help and the counsel of others if needed. The Father in heaven delights to redeem what earthly fathers have damaged.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bondservants, obey. The word is doulos, slave. Slaves were a large share of the empire’s population and probably of the early church; Onesimus, returning to Philemon with this letter, was one (4:7–9). Paul addresses them as full members of the church, responsible before Christ for themselves. Obey in everything means the master’s lawful direction, done thoroughly, never into sin, for the Lord outranks every master. And earthly masters, literally masters according to the flesh, are masters only on the passing, earthly level. On authority and submission at work and elsewhere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Roman slavery and ours. Roman slavery was harsh, and nothing here excuses it. But it was not the race-based slavery of the later Atlantic trade. People became slaves by capture in war, by birth, or by selling themselves to escape debt, and many were educated, held some money, and could in time be freed. Paul is not blessing the system. Elsewhere he quietly undermines it: if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity (1 Corinthians 7:21); he lists enslavers among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10); and he asks Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). He teaches believers how to live for Christ inside a system the gospel would in time dissolve. The how-to-work of these verses carries straight across to any modern job; the conditions do not.
