Not by way of eye-service. Eye-service (ophthalmodoulia, a word Paul may have coined) is work that only happens while the master’s eye is on you: busy when watched and idle when his back is turned. It has not aged a day: the employee who looks busy when the manager passes, games the figures for the review, and skimps the task nobody sees. The gospel has no room for as long as nobody is looking, because Someone always is.

Sincerity of heart. An undivided heart, the same whether watched or not: you work well not because the master deserves it but because you stand in awe of the Lord. The audience of your work is no longer the boss; it is God.

Work heartily. The Greek is vivid: work from the soul, putting your whole self in, not skipping the menial or unseen task. Here drudgery becomes worship: you are working not for the man who signs your orders but for the Lord. Hand the swept floor to Jesus, and a mean master cannot rob it of its glory (Ephesians 6:7). The Reformers drew from this the dignity of every lawful calling: the maid sweeping a room and the minister in the pulpit both serve God, and no honest work is too lowly to be done for him. In plain words, “as for the Lord and not for men” means do it for my sake: as you might care for a friend’s elderly father while he is abroad, really helping the father, but doing it for your friend (see on Ephesians 5:22, and As to the Lord in the Theological Dictionary).

The inheritance as your reward. Under Roman law a slave owned nothing in his own right, and unless his master freed him he could inherit nothing; inheritances went to sons. Yet Paul promises this slave the inheritance, the whole eternal estate of God’s people (1:12), an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4). The man who can inherit nothing on earth is a full heir of God; he may get no wage or thanks, but the Lord sees and will repay, with glory. And the inheritance is not wages earned. You receive it as a son, by grace; the reward is God graciously crowning the very service his own grace enabled.

You are serving the Lord Christ. The lowliest labour, done in faith, is service to Christ (Matthew 25:40). There is no higher title in the universe than servant of the Lord Christ, and Paul hands it to the people at the very bottom of Roman society.

No partiality. The warning reaches both ways. To the slave: do not imagine your low place lets you get away with lazy or spiteful work. To the master, whom 4:1 turns to address: the one who wrongs his servant will not escape. God plays no favourites (Romans 2:11). He weighs the deed, not the rank: the powerful cannot buy their way out of judgment.

What it does not mean. It does not mean slavery is good, or that the Bible endorses the trade that later carried millions from Africa in chains. Scripture condemns man-stealing as a capital crime (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10), and Christians who used these verses to defend that trade twisted them. Nor does it mean a worker must accept abuse, fraud or unsafe conditions without seeking redress. It means that within whatever situation God has placed him, the believer serves Christ with an undivided heart.

How does this apply to my job today? Directly. Your employer is your earthly master in the sense Paul means: someone with lawful authority over your work. So work as well when the manager is on holiday as when he is in the room. Do not pad your hours, take credit for others’ work, or skimp on the parts nobody checks. Do the job in a way you could hand to Christ. If your boss is unfair, you may seek a fairer job, raise concerns properly, or use lawful means of redress; Paul encouraged slaves to gain freedom where they could. But while you are there, your work is for the Lord, and he is the one keeping the record.

What if my work feels meaningless? Then this passage was written for you. Paul wrote it to people who did the most repetitive, unseen and unrewarded work in the empire, and he told them they were serving the Lord Christ. Meaning in work does not come only from the task itself; it comes from the One you are doing it for. The cleaner mopping an empty corridor, the clerk filling the same forms, the carer washing a body no one else will touch, the parent changing the same nappy for the fifth time today: when it is done for the Lord, it is laid into the hands of the King. Your foreman may never say thank you. The Lord is keeping account, and he forgets nothing.

For worship. The Lord Christ himself took the form of a slave. He who flung the stars into space knelt with a towel and washed his disciples’ feet, and then went out to be sold for thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32). He served without eye-service, for no audience but his Father, and he was paid with a cross. Because he did, the servant who owns nothing and is invisible to the great of this world is the heir of all things.
verseByVerse.note: One of the slaves in the church was Onesimus, returning to his master in Colossae with this letter.

4.title: Devoted to Prayer: Wisdom, Words, and the Gospel Network
4.overview: The household code ends with a word to masters: they too have a Master in heaven (v. 1). Then Paul turns outward: keep praying, alert and thankful, and pray for his gospel work; live wisely towards outsiders, with speech that is gracious and seasoned with salt (vv. 2–6). The letter closes with a page of names that shows the gospel in human form, from the runaway slave now called a faithful brother to the restored deserter and the friend who would later leave. Paul signs with his chained hand, and his last word is grace (vv. 7–18).

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Colossians 4 finishes the household code and closes the letter. Masters must treat their slaves justly and fairly, since they too have a Master in heaven (v. 1). Then come three last exhortations: keep at watchful, thankful prayer, praying for Paul’s gospel ministry; walk wisely toward outsiders, making the most of every opportunity; and let your speech be gracious and seasoned with salt (vv. 2–6). Finally Paul sends news and greetings through a remarkable list of fellow workers, among them Onesimus the slave, now a faithful brother, and Mark the restored deserter, and signs with his own hand (vv. 7–18). The letter that exalted Christ over the whole universe ends with the same Lord ruling Tychicus’s journey, Onesimus’s homecoming and Archippus’s unfinished task.

Masters. The word is kyrioi, the very same word as Lord. In the Roman world a master could command, punish and sell his slaves, and in law even kill them; Aristotle had called a slave a living tool. The duties of the household ran one way only, from slave up to master. So Paul quietly overturns the order when he turns and addresses the masters, and lays an obligation on them.

Justly and fairly. Justly (dikaios) means rendering what is right and due: honest dealing, fair provision, discipline that is just and not arbitrary. Fairly (isotēs) is literally equality, or equity: even-handed, impartial treatment, with a hint of the deeper truth that in Christ this slave is your equal and your brother. This went far beyond anything Roman law asked: the slave is a person to whom justice is owed. Think of Philemon, a master in this very church, about to be told to welcome Onesimus back no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16).

A Master in heaven. Here is the whole motive: the master (kyrios) is told he has a Master (Kyrios). The man at the top of the earthly ladder is himself a servant. So Paul levels the hierarchy not by abolishing it but by pointing straight up. Deal justly with those beneath you, because you will answer for it to the Lord above you, the same Lord with whom there is no partiality (3:25; Ephesians 6:9). The law of Moses had already said it of Israel’s own servants: you shall not rule over him ruthlessly but shall fear your God (Leviticus 25:43).

Side by side at one throne. Master and slave kneel side by side at one throne, equals before the God who made them both and the Saviour who bought them both. At the foot of the cross the boss and the worker are two sinners saved by the same grace, and the Christian who holds authority wields it not as a little lord but as a fellow servant who never forgets the Master over his own shoulder.

What does this look like for an employer or manager today? The old temptation survives intact: to see workers as resources, replaceable parts valued only for their output. We even call the department human resources. Justice and fairness look like a fair wage paid on time, honest contracts kept, safe conditions, no favouritism, and no treating people as disposable when it is convenient. They look like the owner who shares the gain fairly, the manager who disciplines by principle rather than mood, and the boss who treats the night cleaner and the senior partner with the same human dignity. They also look like telling people the truth about their position, and listening when they raise a grievance. The Christian in authority should be the most just and humane employer in town, because he knows whose servant he is.

What if I have power over others but not as an employer? The principle reaches further than the workplace. Teachers over pupils, officers over soldiers, landlords over tenants, carers over the vulnerable, church leaders over congregations, older siblings over younger ones: wherever you hold power over someone, you hold it on loan from the Master in heaven. Ask of every use of that power whether you would be glad to explain it to him. Power is not sinful; it is a stewardship, and the Lord pays particular attention to how the strong treat the weak.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s closing commands face two ways: toward God in steady, thankful prayer, including prayer for his own preaching, and toward outsiders in wise conduct and gracious speech.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer as Steady Devotion, Not Occasional Request

The verb Paul uses for continuing in prayer (proskartereō) is the one Acts uses of the first disciples in the upper room and of the early church’s life together (Acts 1:14; 2:42). Prayer is not an emergency measure but the ordinary stance of creatures who depend on their Creator. A church that keeps at it shows that it knows its need.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In prison, Paul could not open doors for the gospel himself. He could pray, and ask the Colossians to pray with him, leaving the gospel’s advance in the hands of the One who controls it. Now: A church that wants to reach the lost but neglects praying together has forgotten where open doors come from.

verseByVerse.quote: Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. Paul’s closing commands face two ways: toward God in prayer (vv. 2–4) and toward outsiders in wise conduct and gracious speech (vv. 5–6). The letter began with Paul praying for the Colossians without ceasing (1:3, 9); now it ends by asking them to pray for him. A letter about the sufficiency of Christ fittingly ends on prayer, the plain confession that everything we need must come from him.

Continue steadfastly in prayer. The word (proskartereō) means to persevere, to hold fast, to keep at something doggedly. It is the word used of the first church, who devoted themselves to prayer (Acts 1:14; 2:42). And the fact that Paul must command it tells us steadfast prayer is hard.

Why prayer is hard. Prayer is hidden labour with nothing visible to show for it, answers seem to tarry, the flesh is weak, and there is an enemy who would rather we did anything than pray. So Paul says keep at it. It was for exactly this that Jesus told the parable of the persistent widow, to show that they ought always to pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). The Spirit who taught you to call God Father keeps you at it (Galatians 4:6), so do not stop.

Being watchful in it. The word (grēgoreō) means stay awake, alert, on guard, like a sentry on night watch who dare not doze. It carries the memory of Gethsemane, where the Lord found his disciples asleep and said watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation (Matthew 26:41; Mark 14:38). To be watchful is to pray awake, alert to what needs praying for, expectant for God’s answer, and vigilant against temptation. Prayer’s great enemy is less hostility than drowsiness.

With thanksgiving. Thankfulness sounds yet again in this short letter (1:3, 12; 2:7; 3:15–17), now woven right into prayer. It keeps prayer from collapsing into a list of demands, and the grateful person keeps praying; prayer without thanksgiving soon turns into complaint. We do not come to wring favours from a reluctant stranger, but as children to a Father who has already given us his Son (Philippians 4:6; Romans 8:32).

What can I do when my mind wanders every time I pray? Many believers find this, so do not conclude you are unfit to pray. Try praying out loud, quietly, or writing your prayers down; both keep the mind on track. Pray with an open Bible, turning a psalm or passage into prayer phrase by phrase, so you are answering God rather than inventing from nothing. Keep a short list of people and needs, so you are not searching for what to say. When your mind drifts, do not scold yourself; turn the distraction into a prayer and come back. And remember that the Spirit helps us in our weakness, interceding for us when we do not know what to pray (Romans 8:26).

Does persistent prayer change God’s mind? God is not reluctant, and he is not informed by our prayers of things he did not know. But he has ordained that many of his purposes are carried out through the prayers of his people, so that prayer is a real cause in his world, though never a lever on his will. Persistence is not wearing him down; it is depending on him, and in the waiting he is often changing us. Keep asking, because he invites you to, and trust that he will answer as a wise Father, sometimes with yes, sometimes with wait, and sometimes with something better than you asked.

In everyday life. Pray today for one thing you have stopped praying for because the answer seemed slow, and begin with thanks before you ask.

For worship. In the garden the disciples slept, and Jesus kept watch alone. He watched and prayed so that his drowsy people might be kept, and the one who keeps his people neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4). We have a Saviour who stayed awake for us, and a door into the Father’s presence that no drowsiness of ours can close.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison— that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pray also for us. The apostle caught up into paradise, writer of Scripture and planter of churches, leans on the prayers of ordinary, faraway believers. Even the most mature Christian never outgrows his need of his brothers’ prayers (Romans 15:30; Ephesians 6:19), and the humblest believer’s prayers truly count. Your prayers for your pastor are no formality.

A door for the word. The open door is Paul’s picture for a God-given opportunity to preach (1 Corinthians 16:9; Acts 14:27; Revelation 3:8). It is God who opens it, not our cleverness. And a man in chains does not ask for the prison door to open. He asks for a door for the word. His freedom is not his first concern; the gospel’s is. He could write elsewhere that he was bound with chains as a criminal, but the word of God is not bound (2 Timothy 2:9).

The mystery of Christ. A mystery in Paul is not a puzzle but a secret long hidden in the heart of God and now thrown open: Christ in you, the hope of glory, including Gentiles in God’s people (1:26–27). The gospel is not a system or a secret technique, as the false teachers offered their initiates, but a Person: God’s mystery, which is Christ (2:2).

In prison. Paul names the reason for his chains without complaint against Rome, his accusers or God, and without self-pity. He looks past the magistrates and soldiers to the sovereign hand behind them, and calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:1). He so believed in the reign of God that he could write from a cell that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Philippians 1:12). That is what believing in God’s sovereignty looks like: peace where there might have been bitterness.

That I may make it clear. An open door needs a clear word. The verb (phaneroō) means to reveal, to make plain. Even this gifted preacher does not presume on his own eloquence.

What about my own prisons? The verse searches us. Most of us will never be in chains for the gospel, but we have our own confinements: unjust treatment, a shut door, an illness, a hard providence that will not lift. What do we do with them? Grumble at people and at God, or trust the sovereign hand and ask how Christ might be made known even here? The hospital ward, the job you cannot leave, the town you did not choose: each may be the place God has opened a door for the word. Pray for release if you wish, and pray first for the door.

How do I pray for missionaries and pastors? Use this verse as your outline. Pray that God would open doors: real opportunities, people ready to listen, freedom to speak. Pray for clarity: that they would explain Christ plainly and faithfully, without obscurity or compromise. Pray for courage, since Paul asked for boldness in the parallel (Ephesians 6:19–20). Pray for contentment and faith in hardship. And then ask them what they need, and pray specifically. A missionary’s newsletter is a prayer list in disguise.

For worship. The word that Paul longed to declare is the Word himself, who was made flesh and whom no chain could bind. They bound Jesus, nailed him down and sealed his tomb, and on the third day he walked out, and the word of the gospel has been running through the world ever since. The Lord who holds the keys of death and Hades opens doors that no one can shut, and his gospel cannot be imprisoned.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walk in wisdom toward outsiders. Paul has asked them to pray for his witness (vv. 3–4); now he turns to theirs. Outsiders are the non-Christians among whom they live, and Paul cares greatly how the church appears to them, because the world reads the gospel first in the lives of those who profess it (1 Thessalonians 4:12; 1 Peter 2:12).

In wisdom. To walk is the whole conduct of life, and in wisdom means with the skill and tact of the wisdom hidden in Christ (2:3), so as to adorn the gospel. It looks like integrity, kindness, a blameless life that disarms criticism, and the tact to know when to speak and when to stay quiet. And it avoids two ditches at once: compromise, blending into the world until no one can tell the difference, and harsh superiority, the sour, judgmental believer the world rightly recoils from.

The only offence. Christ crucified is a stumbling block to some and folly to others (1 Corinthians 1:23), and Paul would not remove that offence for anyone (Galatians 5:11). But he took great care that nothing else, no rudeness, hypocrisy or foolishness of ours, should stand in its way. If outsiders stumble, let it be over Christ and not over us. Be honest about the opposite danger. Often what keeps us quiet is not wisdom but the wish to be liked: we fear the raised eyebrow more than we love the neighbour. The cure is not to care less about people but to care more about Christ’s approval than theirs (Galatians 1:10), and the believer who has that approval already, by grace, is free to speak. Your daily conduct before unbelieving colleagues is itself an argument, for Christ or against him.

Making the best use of the time. Literally, buying up the opportunity (exagorazomai ton kairon). The word for time is not the ticking clock (chronos) but the opportune moment (kairos), the open window. The picture is a shrewd merchant snapping up a bargain: seizing every God-given opening to commend Christ before it passes, because the days are evil, as the parallel adds (Ephesians 5:16). The open window with this neighbour may not come again. Christ walked in perfect wisdom among outsiders: he ate with tax collectors, spoke with a Samaritan woman at a well, touched lepers and welcomed children. He never wasted a moment, and he never forced one, and every opportunity we are given to speak of him was bought by the time he spent for us.

How do I spot an opportunity without forcing one? Listen more than you speak. Opportunities usually arrive as questions, griefs or crises: someone mentions a death in the family, asks how you stay so calm, confesses a fear, or notices you went to church. The window is often a single sentence, and the wise response is often a single sentence back, honest, gentle and brief, with an open door to say more: can I tell you what has helped me? Pray each morning that God would put such moments in your path and make you notice them. Then, when one comes, take it, and leave the result to him.

If I am shy, am I failing at this? No. Walking in wisdom is first a matter of how you live, and a shy believer who is honest, kind and faithful is already speaking loudly. You do not need to be an extrovert to buy up opportunities. A card to a neighbour who has lost someone, an invitation to a carol service, a book given with a short note, or a quiet answer when asked why you believe: these are open to anyone. God has used quiet people in countless conversions that no one outside heaven has ever heard about.

In everyday life. Name one unbeliever you see regularly. Pray for them by name, ask God for one opportunity this week, and when it comes, buy it up.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Always gracious. All your talk, not merely your religious talk. Gracious, literally with grace, means speech that is kind and winsome, not harsh, sarcastic or preachy, and speech that actually gives grace to those who hear (Ephesians 4:29), as the gracious words that came from the mouth of Jesus drew the crowds (Luke 4:22).

Seasoned with salt. Salt gave food flavour and kept it from spoiling, and Greek writers used salt as a picture of wit. So salted speech is not bland, insipid talk but speech with savour, interest and substance, worth listening to; and it is wholesome, free of what is corrupt or coarse. Not the modern salty speech, which is crude.

Grace and salt together. Speech that is gracious but not salted is kind but bland: gushing, sentimental, saying nothing memorable. Speech that is salted but not gracious is clever but cruel, witty at someone else’s expense. The Christian’s tongue is to be both: kind and interesting, truthful and winsome. In practice it is answering a hostile remark with unexpected kindness, seasoning a hard truth so it can be heard, and trading the coarse joke and the sour complaint for words that build people up.

How you ought to answer. Mark each person: not a single canned formula fired at everyone, but an answer suited to this individual, his question, his objection, his need. The watching world asks: why do you live like that? Why are you so hopeful? Peter says the same: always be prepared to give a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Wisdom listens before it speaks.

The soil and the fruit. Gracious, flavourful speech is the soil, and readiness to answer is the fruit. Winsome everyday words draw people to ask; harsh or insipid talk shuts the conversation before it begins. You need not have a sermon by heart, only a gracious, salted tongue and a heart ready with a fitting word (Proverbs 15:23).

What if someone asks a question I cannot answer? Say so honestly. I don’t know, but I would like to find out, is a gracious answer, and it often opens a second conversation. You are not required to win every argument; you are asked to give a reason for your hope, and the simplest reason is often the strongest: what Christ has done for you, and why you trust him. Then go and find out, read, ask your pastor, and come back. People are usually more moved by a Christian who is humble and honest than by one who has a quick reply for everything.

For worship. No one ever spoke like this man. Grace was poured upon his lips; he knew how to sustain with a word him who is weary; he silenced his accusers and comforted sinners in the same afternoon. He answered the rich young ruler, the woman at the well and the thief on the cross each in the way that fitted, and every word was true and every word was kind. The Word made flesh is full of grace and truth, and he is teaching our clumsy tongues to speak with his accent.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul closes with news and greetings, a roll call of the people behind his mission, and one charge, to Archippus. He signs in his own hand: remember my chains; grace be with you.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body of Christ in Named People

The list of names puts flesh on 1:18, where Christ is the head of the body, the church. The body is not an abstraction; it is Tychicus and Onesimus and Luke and Nympha. That is why Reformed teaching has stressed the visible local church: not an ideal church somewhere, but these people, in this place.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The runaway slave Onesimus is commended to the church as a “faithful and beloved brother,” and the teaching of 3:11 walks through the door: in the church, slave and free no longer decide anyone’s standing. Now: The church is still a gathering of people who would never otherwise share a room, brought to the same table because Christ is all, and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tychicus. A modern reader is tempted to skim a page of ancient names, but this roll call is a photograph of the gospel at work. Listen to the words Paul keeps reaching for: beloved brother, faithful minister, fellow servant, fellow prisoner, a comfort to me. These are not colleagues but family. The first name, Tychicus, is the courier, a native of Asia (Acts 20:4) who carried these pages to Colossae with Onesimus beside him, and the letter we call Ephesians on the same journey (Ephesians 6:21–22).

Beloved, faithful, fellow servant. Beloved brother: family. Faithful minister: dependable service, the word from which we get deacon. Fellow servant: partnership, literally fellow slave, standing beside Paul under the same Master.

For this very purpose. Tychicus has two jobs, and the second is the larger: news of Paul, for a church anxious about him, and then to encourage their hearts, the same longing Paul expressed for them in 2:2. Scripture reaches most people through somebody, and the messenger’s character is not incidental to the message. Paul could have sent a courier. He sent a brother.

As the Father has sent me. Behind Paul’s sending of Tychicus stands a greater sending. The Father sent the Son into the world not to condemn it but to save it (John 3:17), and the risen Jesus said to his disciples, As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you (John 20:21). So a messenger who travels a long road to encourage hearts is doing in small what Christ did in full: coming in person, at cost, to people who needed more than a letter. The Lord of glory did not run his church by dispatching instructions from a distance; he came himself, the message and the messenger one and the same.

Why does sharing news matter in the church? Because the church is a family, and families want to know how their members are. Paul thought it worth a long, dangerous journey for the Colossians to hear how he was. News is the raw material of prayer and love: you cannot pray for someone whose circumstances you never hear about, or rejoice with someone whose joys are never shared. Prayer letters, a word of news after the service, a visit to someone housebound: these are not trivial. They knit the body together and encourage hearts, which is exactly why Tychicus was sent.

In everyday life. Think of the Tychicus in your own church, the person who sets up chairs, drives the elderly, sends the news, and thank them this week.

verseByVerse.quote: and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Onesimus. We know who this is, because Paul wrote a whole letter about him. Onesimus was a slave in the household of Philemon, a member of the Colossian church. He had almost certainly run away (that is the usual reading of Philemon), and in Roman law a runaway could be branded, flogged, or worse. Somewhere in his flight he had met Paul in prison and been converted (Philemon 10). Now he is walking back into the town he fled, carrying a letter to his master.

Our faithful and beloved brother. Paul introduces him to a congregation that knew him as somebody’s runaway property with not a word about his legal position, but with almost the very words he has just used of Tychicus (v. 7), very likely a free man and an apostolic delegate. The gospel has transformed his status before the church long before it changes his status before the law.

Who is one of you. Then four words that go further still. He is not an outsider being tolerated but a member of that church, with the same standing as the man who owns him. Paul simply states it, in a public letter that would be read aloud in the room where Philemon was sitting.

The doctrine walking through the door. Set this beside 3:11, a few paragraphs earlier: here there is not Greek and Jew, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all. Here it walks through the door on two legs. Paul does not stage a revolt against Rome’s slave system; he does something slower and more corrosive to it, putting a runaway and a delegate side by side with the same titles. And there is a gentle play on the name, which Paul makes openly in Philemon 11: Onesimus means useful. Formerly he was useless, Paul says, but now he is indeed useful.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul excused Onesimus’s wrong. The letter to Philemon shows that he sought reconciliation and offered to make restitution himself: if he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account (Philemon 18). Grace did not pretend the wrong had not happened.

What should a church do with a new believer who has a criminal past? Receive him as Paul received Onesimus: as a faithful and beloved brother, one of us, not a project or a risk to be managed in whispers. That does not mean ignoring wisdom. Where there is a real danger to others, especially to children, safeguards are a form of love, and a genuinely repentant person will understand them. Where restitution is owed, it should be made, as Paul arranged. But the man’s name in the church is no longer his record. Do not keep reminding him of his past, do not introduce him by it, and do not hold him at arm’s length. Christ has not.

For worship. Onesimus walked home with a letter that said charge it to my account, and in that sentence the whole gospel was written small. We were runaways from our Master, and the Son of God said to the Father: if he owes you anything, charge it to me. He paid what we had stolen and more, and then sent us home with a new name. He is the Saviour who makes the useless useful and the outcast family.
verseByVerse.note: Onesimus was the runaway slave of Philemon, a member of the church at Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him), and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aristarchus my fellow prisoner. Aristarchus was a Macedonian from Thessalonica (Acts 20:4). He had been seized by the mob in the theatre at Ephesus (Acts 19:29) and had sailed with Paul on the voyage that ended in shipwreck (Acts 27:2). Now he is in custody with him. The word Paul uses (synaichmalōtos) is literally fellow prisoner of war, a man captured alongside him in the same campaign. (In Philemon 24 the title goes to Epaphras, so perhaps they took turns.) Here is a Christian whose name we would never have known but for a greeting, who followed the apostle into a riot, a shipwreck and a cell.

Mark the cousin of Barnabas. This phrase is the sound of a wound healing. This is the John Mark who abandoned Paul and Barnabas partway through the first missionary journey and went home (Acts 13:13). When Barnabas wanted to take him again, Paul refused, and the disagreement was sharp enough to split the two men and end their partnership (Acts 15:37–39). Now Paul is writing ahead to make sure Mark gets a warm reception.

Welcome him. A church might have heard the story and be wary. Years later, near the very end, Paul will send for him: get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). Grace does not discard those who have failed. It restores them, and it restores the people they failed, too, for Paul’s own heart had to change toward Mark.

The Gospel a restored man wrote. The early church held that this Mark wrote the second Gospel, and the book bears the marks of a man who knew both failure and grace. It does not spare the disciples: when Jesus was arrested, they all left him and fled (Mark 14:50). Yet it also records the angel’s message at the empty tomb: go, tell his disciples and Peter (16:7). The Gospel that bears Mark’s name preaches what his own life proved: a deserter can be called back. The Lord chose a deserter to write the Gospel of the Servant who never deserted. The welcome Paul now asks for him is simply the risen Christ’s way with his failures, passed on.

Jesus who is called Justus. Jesus was a common Jewish name, the Greek form of Joshua, and this man also used the Roman name Justus. He is otherwise unknown, an ordinary believer with an ordinary name, remembered for ever because he stood by Paul.

The only men of the circumcision. Only three Jewish believers in Paul’s circle, and the word only carries a quiet ache from the man who could wish himself accursed for the sake of his kinsmen (Romans 9:3). Some Jewish believers opposed his mission to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:4), and many of his own people worked against him (Acts 21:27–28).

A comfort to me. The word (parēgoria) appears only here in the New Testament. It is a medical term, the root behind paregoric, a soothing medicine that eases pain. These men were medicine to the apostle’s soul. Paul was no self-sufficient hero; he needed friends, and said so.

Fellow workers for the kingdom of God. Some conclude the kingdom is not the church’s present business, that it belongs to Israel or waits wholly in the future, and it is true that its full visible glory is still to come. But Paul writes that these men are, right now, fellow workers for it, and earlier he said that God has already transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (1:13). So the kingdom is already here, wherever Christ is owned as King, and not yet consummated, awaiting his return in glory. We live in it now and labour for its advance, while we wait for its dawning in full (Romans 14:17; Acts 28:31).

If I have failed in serving God, can I be used again? Yes. Mark deserted in the middle of a mission and became the man Paul asked for at the end of his life. Peter denied Christ three times and was restored by the lakeside to feed his sheep. God’s grace is not only for the start of the Christian life but for its failures along the way. Be honest about what happened, put right what you can, accept that trust may need to be rebuilt over time, and then take up whatever service is put in front of you, however small. The question is not whether you have failed but whether you will let him restore you.

In everyday life. Is there a Mark in your life, someone who let you down and whom you have quietly written off? Ask whether God is asking you to welcome him back.

For worship. When Jesus was bound, no Aristarchus stood beside him to share his chains. He went into the dark without a comforter, so that none of his servants would ever be without one. Now the King gathers the failures, the fearful and the forgotten and makes them his fellow workers, and as his sufferings overflow to his people, so through him their comfort overflows too (2 Corinthians 1:5).
verseByVerse.note: Mark had once left Paul, causing a split with Barnabas; he is now restored.

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphras. Without Epaphras there would be no church at Colossae: he first brought them the gospel. Paul called him our beloved fellow servant and a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf (1:7), and it was his report that prompted this letter. Paul gives him the title servant of Christ Jesus, literally slave (doulos), a title Paul uses of himself elsewhere (Romans 1:1; Philippians 1:1) and in this letter gives to no other individual.

Always struggling. The word (agōnizomai) is the athlete’s straining word, the root of our agony, used of a wrestler in the contest. Paul used it of his own labour (1:29; 2:1). Most of us think of intercession as the least strenuous thing a Christian does. Epaphras is far from home and can do nothing else for these people, and the New Testament calls what he is doing combat. If prayer is genuinely wrestling, then the person who says all I can do is pray has misunderstood which activity is the strenuous one.

Mature and fully assured. His prayer is the whole letter distilled into one petition. Stand: firm, not shifted off Christ (2:6–7). Mature (teleioi): full-grown, the goal Paul named in 1:28. The false teachers offered an advanced inner circle, but Paul’s maturity is not a grade above ordinary Christians; it is the growing up of people already filled in Christ (2:10). Fully assured (peplērophorēmenoi) means carried all the way to settled conviction, not swayed by every new teacher. And all of it in all the will of God: not in esoteric secrets, but resting in the whole will of God made known in his Son.

Laodicea and Hierapolis. Three towns in the Lycus valley. Epaphras had evidently cared for the whole valley, and Paul, who had never been there, vouches for him; such a word steadies a congregation’s confidence in the man who taught them, especially when other teachers are trying to undermine him.

What do I actually pray for the people I love? Most of our praying, if we are honest, is for their circumstances to improve: health, jobs, exams, journeys. Those are good things to pray, and God invites them. But Epaphras wrestles for their maturity and assurance. He wants them standing, grown and certain. It is a larger ambition than comfort, and it is the one that survives whatever happens to their circumstances. Try praying Paul’s and Epaphras’s prayers for your children, your friends and your church: that they would stand firm in Christ, grow up into him, and be fully assured of his love and his will. Use the prayers of 1:9–12 as your words.

For worship. Behind Epaphras on his knees stands a greater Intercessor. In Gethsemane Jesus wrestled in prayer until his sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44, verses missing from some early manuscripts though found in many others), and in the upper room he prayed for his disciples and for all who would believe through their word. He still prays at the Father’s right hand that we may stand. The church at Colossae was held up by the prayers of a faithful pastor and by the prayers of the Son of God, and so are we.
verseByVerse.note: Hierapolis lay across the valley from Laodicea.

verseByVerse.quote: Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke the beloved physician. Two names, and between them a sad contrast nobody could yet have known. This is, by early and consistent tradition, the author of the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, and it is the only place in the New Testament where we are told his trade. It fits how he writes: the careful research of one who had followed all things closely (Luke 1:3), and a warm interest in illness and healing. He is not listed among the men of the circumcision (v. 11), so he was most probably a Gentile, perhaps the only Gentile writer in the New Testament. In the we passages of Acts he quietly writes himself into the story.

Beloved. Paul was a man with a physical affliction he could not shake (2 Corinthians 12:7; Galatians 4:13–14), flogged five times, beaten with rods three times, stoned once and shipwrecked three times (2 Corinthians 11:24–25). Travelling with him, for years, was a doctor. And at the very end, when everyone else had gone, Paul wrote: Luke alone is with me (2 Timothy 4:11). The apostle who healed others by God’s power still travelled with a physician: using doctors and medicine is no lack of faith.

As does Demas. Every other name gets a title; Demas gets his name and nothing else, though here he is still a fellow worker (Philemon 24). The sequel is on record. Years later Paul wrote: Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica (2 Timothy 4:10). Not scandal or heresy: he fell in love with this present world, the ordinary, respectable pull of comfort, safety and a quieter life, and the pull was stronger than his attachment to a chained old man in Rome. That is how most people leave: not with a repudiation but with a drift.

Two loves. A few lines before he writes that Demas loved this present world, Paul speaks of the crown laid up for all who have loved the Lord’s appearing (2 Timothy 4:8, 10). The same verb stands in both places. Demas did not lose interest in religion; he found something he loved more than the coming of Christ. That is the root of every drift, answered not by trying harder to love the world less, but by seeing more of the one who is coming. Christ who is your life will appear (3:4), and a heart that longs for that day has less room for the pull of this one.

Two possibilities side by side. The verse holds the man who stayed to the end and the man who did not, and nobody in Colossae could have told them apart. Let it make us watchful rather than smug, and let it make us pray, as Epaphras did, that we may stand. And there is one friend who never deserts. When all forsook Paul, the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16–17), and he has promised never to leave or forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5).

Was Demas a true believer who lost his salvation? Scripture does not tell us his final state. Here he is a fellow worker; later he deserts. If he never returned, the Reformed reading is that he showed he had never truly belonged, for they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). And he may have returned; we are not told, and we should not pronounce on him. What we do know is that those whom God has truly called and justified, he keeps to the end (Romans 8:30; John 10:28–29). That is the doctrine called the perseverance of the saints: the truly saved continue in faith to the end, and it is his keeping, not the strength of our grip, that guarantees it (Philippians 1:6). The doctrine of perseverance does not make warnings like this unnecessary. It is one of the means by which God keeps his people: he warns them, and they take heed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Demas was certainly lost, or that every Christian who goes through a cold or weary season is a Demas. Tiredness and grief are not the love of the world, which rarely announces itself and usually looks perfectly reasonable.

How do I know if I am drifting like Demas? Watch for the quiet signs rather than the dramatic ones. Prayer becoming rare and then optional. Gathering with God’s people slipping from weekly to occasional, always for a good reason. Scripture squeezed out by screens. Conversations with believers becoming awkward because you have less to say. Decisions about jobs, homes and money made without any reference to Christ’s kingdom. A growing irritation with Christians who seem too serious. None of these alone proves anything. Together they are a direction. The very fact that you are asking the question is a sign that you have not let go. If you see them, do not despair; turn back now, tell a trusted friend, and go back to the means of grace. The Shepherd goes after drifting sheep.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, the author of Luke and Acts, was a doctor. Demas later deserted Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers at Laodicea. Laodicea, a rich banking town about ten miles off, keeps appearing in this letter (2:1; 4:13, 16), and Paul is knitting these valley congregations together: greet them, swap letters with them, pray for them. Brothers here, as often in Paul, includes the sisters.

Nympha. A woman is named, and a congregation meets in her home. For two centuries Christians met in houses, whose owners had to be willing to fill them every week with people who might attract official attention. Nympha had means, and used them. The New Testament names several such women: Lydia at Philippi (Acts 16:15, 40), Priscilla with Aquila (1 Corinthians 16:19), and Mary the mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12). The early church would have been homeless without them.

The church in her house. The church in her house tells you what a first-century congregation actually looked like: not a hall but a room; not an audience but a group small enough to eat together. When Paul writes about bearing with one another and forgiving each other (3:13), he is describing people who sat in the same room every week and could not avoid one another’s faults. Our arrangements are different. The demand is not. And the Son of Man, who had nowhere to lay his head, has made his home in his people: where two or three gather in his name, he is there among them, in every crowded room in Laodicea and every kitchen where believers meet today.

A textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read a man’s name, Nymphas, and his house, as the ESV footnote mentions. The feminine reading is better supported, and it is the one most modern translations follow.

A shadow over Laodicea. A generation later the risen Christ dictates a letter to this same church, rebuking it because it says it is rich, has prospered, and needs nothing, not realising that it is wretched, pitiable, poor, blind and naked (Revelation 3:17). Churches can be greeted warmly by an apostle and still drift. Yet even there the risen Lord does not give up on them. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, he says, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Revelation 3:20). The Lord who rebukes them still wants a place at their table.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Nympha was the pastor or elder of the church. Hosting a church was a valuable and costly ministry of hospitality and generosity, and the New Testament honours it by name; the oversight of the church was given to qualified elders (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). Christians who read the New Testament as opening church oversight to women see such hosts differently, and they are brothers and sisters; this verse itself tells us nothing about how her church was led.

Could my home be used for the church? Very likely, and in more ways than you think. You do not need a large house. A kitchen table is enough for a Bible study for four, a meal for a lonely student, coffee after a funeral, a prayer meeting, or a place where a new family in the church can be made welcome. Hospitality is commanded of all believers (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9), not only of the gifted. It will cost time and tidiness, and it will sometimes be inconvenient. That is what made Nympha’s gift a gift.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes.

verseByVerse.quote: And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read among you. Read among you means read aloud, to the gathered congregation (1 Thessalonians 5:27). For most Christians through most of history Scripture came in through the ears, in a room full of other people, and the public reading of Scripture is still a central part of Christian worship (1 Timothy 4:13).

Also in the church of the Laodiceans. From the beginning these were public documents for the whole people of God, not private mail. Paul expects congregations to swap his letters, copy them, and read one another’s. That habit is one of the first stirrings of what became the collected New Testament.

The word of Christ, passed hand to hand. A prisoner’s letter carried such weight because the apostles did not speak on their own authority. Jesus promised them that the Spirit would teach them all things and bring to their remembrance all that he had said (John 14:26), and Paul received his gospel through a revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:12). What the Colossians were sending on to Laodicea was the word of Christ that Paul had told them to let dwell in them richly (3:16). In the apostles’ letters the risen Lord is still speaking to his churches.

The letter from Laodicea. We do not know what it was. It may simply be lost: a letter of Paul’s that God did not intend to preserve, which need not alarm us, since Paul wrote at least one other letter to Corinth that we do not have (1 Corinthians 5:9). Many have thought it is the letter we call Ephesians, written as a circular to several churches and reaching Laodicea before Colossae; some early manuscripts lack the words in Ephesus in Ephesians 1:1. A later forged Epistle to the Laodiceans was never widely received as Scripture, and rightly so.

Where Christians differ: lost letters and the canon. The canon (the word means a measuring rule) is the list of books that are Scripture, the rule by which the church’s faith is measured. If an apostolic letter is lost, is the New Testament incomplete? This commentary’s view: no. God in his providence preserved the books he intended for the permanent canon. Not every apostolic letter was meant to be Scripture for all time; or, if the letter from Laodicea is Ephesians, it was not lost at all. That a letter written by an apostle might not be preserved is not a gap in the Bible. It means God gave his church what he meant it to have. The canon is not everything the apostles ever wrote; it is what God caused to be kept. It is complete and sufficient for all things necessary for his glory and our salvation, faith and life (the Westminster Confession 1.2–3, 6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.2–3, 6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church created Scripture, or gave the books their authority by voting on them. The church recognised the Scriptures God had given, as a child recognises his father’s voice. The authority comes from God who breathed them out, not from the church that received them.

Should I worry that books were left out of the Bible? No. The books sometimes promoted as lost gospels were written long after the apostles, usually in the second century or later, and they teach things the apostles never taught. The early church did not suppress them out of fear; it recognised that they did not carry the apostolic voice. The books we have were received widely and early because they came from the apostles and their close companions and agreed with the faith once for all delivered. God, who inspired his word, has also preserved it. You can read your Bible as complete.

In everyday life. Read Colossians aloud this week in one sitting, as the Colossians first heard it; it takes about fifteen minutes, and you will hear the flow of the argument as never before.
verseByVerse.note: The letter from Laodicea has not survived; some think it may be the letter we know as Ephesians.

verseByVerse.quote: And say to Archippus, “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Archippus. We meet Archippus once more, in the letter to Philemon, where Paul calls him our fellow soldier and names him alongside Philemon and Apphia (Philemon 2). He was probably a member of that household (many have guessed their son, though we are not told), and seems to have had some ministry in the church, perhaps leading it while Epaphras was away. Something had stalled. Paul does not say what, and there is no rebuke in the words, but the charge would not be needed if all were well.

A public charge. Paul does not write privately to Archippus; he tells the whole congregation to say it to him. Encouragement is a duty of the whole church, and a man who has gone quiet in his work is better served by a room full of people who expect something of him than by everyone politely looking away.

Fulfil the ministry. The ministry is one he has received, a trust handed to him by Christ, not a career he chose. You may resign from a job you selected, but a trust is somebody else’s property left in your hands. And he is to fulfil it (plēroō), literally to fill it full, to carry it through to the end. Not to maintain it respectably, but to finish (2 Timothy 4:5). The pattern is Christ’s own. On the night before he died he said to the Father, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). He too had received a work, and he carried it through to the cross. He did not leave his work half done, and he will not leave ours. Every ministry in his church is a small trust handed down from that finished one.

The household on the road. Archippus belongs to Philemon’s household, and Philemon’s household is exactly where Onesimus is walking back to as this letter travels (v. 9). Whatever ministry had stalled, it had stalled in the one home in Colossae about to be tested hardest, the home that must decide how to receive a returning runaway. Paul does not join the two threads for us, and we should not force them.

The charge turns to face us. This is the only name in the roll call handed a charge of his own, and it swings the list round to face the reader. The one charge lands on an ordinary Christian whose ministry we cannot even identify. You have been given something too. See that you finish it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Archippus was in serious sin or being publicly shamed; the tone is encouragement to persevere. Nor does it mean only ordained ministers have a ministry to fulfil. Every member of the body has been given gifts and work by the Lord (1 Corinthians 12:7; 1 Peter 4:10).

How do I know what ministry I have received? Begin with what is already in your hands. Your ministry is rarely something exotic. It is usually the people God has placed around you and the gifts he has given you: the children you are raising, the Sunday school class, the elderly neighbour, the welcome team, the friend who is struggling, the work you were asked to do and said yes to. Ask mature believers where they have seen God use you. Notice what needs you see that others miss. And look at what you have started and let slide. That may be the very thing the Lord is asking you to finish.
verseByVerse.note: Archippus was probably a member of Philemon’s household.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With my own hand. Paul usually dictated his letters (Romans 16:22) and took the pen himself at the close. It authenticated the letter, his handwriting being the seal of genuineness against forgeries (2 Thessalonians 3:17). And it was a piece of pure affection, his own hand reaching across hundreds of miles to a church that had never seen his face.

Remember my chains. Roman custody often meant a wrist chained to a guard, so the hand that took the pen may well have been in iron. The man who wrote that Christ is the image of the invisible God was a prisoner while he wrote, and the last thing he does is ask them not to forget it.

Not self-pity, but an argument. It is partly a request for prayer (v. 3), and a call to solidarity, to remember those who are in prison as though in prison with them (Hebrews 13:3). But the chains are also an argument, and he knows it. People do not usually wear irons for what they know to be a lie. A church being offered a more sophisticated religion by teachers who risked nothing had been sent the gospel by a man paying for it in metal.

Grace be with you. The last word answers the first. The letter opened with grace (1:2), and everything between, the supremacy of Christ, the new life, the transformed household, the page of names, stands inside grace. To a congregation being told they could climb nearer to God by rules, festivals, visions and severity to the body, the final word is the first word: not effort, not secret knowledge, but grace, the free gift of God in the Christ in whom they have already been filled. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add Amen.

How do I remember the chains of Christians today? Paul’s request outlived him. Many believers today are imprisoned, beaten, or cut off from family and work for following Christ. Remember them first in prayer, by name and country where you can; organisations that serve the persecuted church publish specific requests. Write to prisoners where that is possible and safe. Give to support their families. Speak up for them to those in authority. And let their faithfulness shame our complaints and strengthen our courage. The same grace that held Paul in chains is holding them.

In everyday life. End your own day where Paul ended his letter. Whatever you did well or badly, whatever you finished or left undone, you go to sleep inside grace.

For worship. The hand that wrote this greeting was chained for the sake of a Saviour who was himself bound and led away, so that his people might be set free; he wore the chains of our sin so that grace might be with us for ever. Grace will be the last word of history too, when the Lord Jesus comes and every chain falls away.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then signed the greeting himself.
